text:
Immigrants detained in the U.S. by President Donald Trump’s administration have no constitutional right to a bond hearing, a federal appeals court ruled Friday.

According to Reuters, the ruling came out of the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans.

Fewer rights for detained migrants

What we know:

The court’s conservative majority ruled 10-7 that the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment does not apply to immigrants who are detained and seeking a bond hearing.

What they're saying:

"To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be ​free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by ​agreeing to leave the country," US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote.

READ MORE: 6 charged in decade long, multi-million dollar marriage fraud ring

In a social media post, James Percival, general counsel for the US Department of Homeland Security, called the decision a "big win in the 5th Circuit on mandatory detention ​for illegal aliens."

What we don't know:

It’s unclear whether the ruling will stand; the Supreme Court has agreed to take up the issue as federal courts are flooded with lawsuits by migrants who say they’ve been unflawfully detained. Lower courts remain divided on what rights migrants should have amid the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Big picture view:

If the ruling stands, detained migrants in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi (the 5th Circuit’s jurisdiction) will have fewer avenues to lobby for their release.

Local perspective:

Texas and Louisiana house more immigrant detainees than any other state.

‘Devastating consequences’

The other side:

"Unchecked, executive authority to ​arrest and detain, indefinitely, echoes fearfully from history," US Circuit Judge Dana Douglas, one of the dissenting judges, wrote in the opinion.

"This ruling opens ​the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences ​for them, their ⁠loved ones and their community," Ellie Norton, a lawyer for the non-US citizens in the case at the National Immigration Project, said in a statement to Reuters.

text:
A Nashville judge temporarily blocked Tennessee health officials from requiring immigration status checks of HIV-positive individuals enrolled in a healthcare safety-net program.

Chancellor I'Ashea L. Myles issued the temporary restraining order late Wednesday. The order prevents the Tennessee Department of Health from moving forward with a demand that organizations revise their contracts to include immigration status verification as a condition of serving patients in the Ryan White HIV/AIDS program.

The order extends to a companion program known as HOPWA, or Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS. Myles set a Nov. 4 hearing in the case.

The decades-old, federally-funded Ryan White program provides millions of dollars to every U.S. state to serve low-income individuals living with HIV/AIDS. States in turn distribute funding to healthcare and other providers who work directly with patients.

On Oct. 1, the Tennessee health department sent a memo to these providers citing new state law that requires verifying anyone seeking federal, state or local public benefits to be lawfully present in the United States. The law also comes with criminal penalties for employees who fail to verify patient status.

Nashville CARES, one of the Tennessee's largest participants in the program, filed suit challenging the mandate earlier this week. The federal government does not require immigration status checks as a condition of receiving services through Ryan White or HOPWA and federal law exempts such checks for programs targeting communicable diseases, it noted in legal filings.

Hundreds of its patients would be at risk of losing life-saving medical, prescription drug and support services -- including financial assistance that pays the costs of private health insurance, Nashville CARES said in legal filings.

Represented by attorneys with the Tennessee Justice Center, the organization said the mandate violated state rule-making procedures and federal law.

Attorneys representing the Tennessee Department of Health objected to a temporary injunction in a legal response to Nashville CARES' initial petition. They argued that Nashville CARES was "essentially (asking) the Court to intervene in a contract dispute." State attorneys also disputed the right of Nashville CARES to broadly challenge the state's imposition of the new contract rules on all Tennessee organizations that participate in Ryan White program, arguing the case should focus only on Nashville CARES' dispute.

Myles' temporary restraining order applies to all organizations that contract with the state to provide Ryan White services.

The order blocks any effort to require immigration or citizenship status verification for any individual currently enrolled in the program, and any new applicant. Myles also blocked the state from restricting enrollment only to those able to provide proof of legal immigration or citizenship status.

text:
FOLKSTON, Ga. — Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old Salvadorian illegal alien, died while in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center Oct. 23, 2026. Sandoval’s criminal history includes convictions for aggravated assault, making terroristic threats, receiving stolen property, and theft by unlawful taking as well as a charge for drug possession.

At approximately 1:46 a.m. Oct. 23, facility staff found Sandoval with a ligature around his neck. Staff immediately began life-saving measures. The Charlton County Emergency Medical Services arrived to the scene and provided additional lifesaving measures. Despite those efforts, Sandoval was pronounced dead at approximately 2:28 a.m.

Sandoval’s death is under investigation. An autopsy will be conducted to determine the official cause and manner of death.

On an unknown date, Sandoval entered the United States at an unknown location without being admitted, inspected or paroled by an immigration officer. On October 2, 2026, Sandoval was arrested by ICE Newark and issued a notice to appear before an immigration judge. He arrived at Folkston on Oct. 8, 2026 pending his first removal hearing.

Consistent with ICE policy, Enforcement and Removal Operations has completed all required notifications to the Department of Homeland Security, the ICE Office of Inspector General and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility via the Joint Intake Operation Center.

ICE makes official notifications to Congress, non-governmental organization stakeholders and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.

ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility; a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility; access to medical appointments; and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.

title: ICE's Cruelty Is Becoming America's M.O. - The Bulwark
description:

A masked agent then draws a gun, yelling, “Get on the ground.” Gonzalez appears to respond, “Fuck you.

text:
“ICE is facial recognition, ICE is surveillance, and ICE is coming after you regardless of your status.”

SO SAID REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ at a “Students vs. Billionaires” town hall event in late September.

And while her rhetoric is heated, the New York congresswoman has a point.

Since the beginning of Trump 2.0, we’ve seen ICE perpetrate wanton violence, especially against Latino fathers and husbands. The agency relies on a gigantic, AI-powered surveillance network to pursue its targets and intimidate protesters. And ICE has assaulted and detained U.S. citizens, showing that in the minds of their agents, the actual legal status of the people they accost does not seem to be a primary concern.

Take Ricardo Gonzalez in Long Beach, California. A U.S. citizen and former city employee, Gonzalez was riding an e-bike near his home when ICE agents set upon him. A video of the episode shows an unmarked car driving the wrong way down a one-way street, then swerving at Gonzalez, obscuring him from view.

A masked agent then draws a gun, yelling, “Get on the ground.” Gonzalez appears to respond, “Fuck you. You hit me with your fucking car. I’m a fucking U.S. citizen.”

A neighbor and witness said an agent jumped out of the car and tackled Gonzalez, and video footage shows Gonzalez yelling in pain that his arm is broken as an ICE agent kneels on his back. The Long Beach Post reports Gonzalez was tased twice, and that one agent taunted the growing crowd of protesters at the scene, saying they didn’t “look legal.” Gonzalez’s daughter confirmed the tasing and said the family is raising money for his hospital bills and recovery.

Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson has filed a complaint on behalf of the city asking for a formal investigation into the ICE operation, and answers to questions such as whether an ICE vehicle hit Gonzalez, whether he was tased, and why medical aid was not rendered immediately.

“Many people—they relegate use of force to ‘this person must have done something wrong,’” Richardson told me. “[Gonzalez] was a U.S. citizen. But even if he wasn’t, do these agents have the right to brutalize who they want with no accountability and no oversight? Because if they do, no one is safe.”

Share

ICE has also run up a body count this year. Some of the men killed or brutalized—fathers, brothers, and sons—have been undocumented, it’s true. But none deserved the brutal treatment they received for it. And neither did their children or spouses (many of whom are U.S. citizens) do anything to warrant having their fathers or husbands violently taken away. Sometimes the children were with these men when they were attacked.

That’s what happened to 24-year-old Sebastian, who was dropping off his two children at their babysitter at 7:30 a.m. on Tuesday when ICE drove him off the road, wrecking his car. The hard-to-watch video shows Sebastian desperately holding onto his toddlers as ICE agents methodically pry his fingers off them. As the two children cry, a crowd gathers, filming the encounter. In this case, the agents eventually let the terrified father go, telling him to report to ICE, the Boston Globe reported. He was apparently not even the man they had come to find.

Sometimes the agency’s actions are much more targeted. ICE’s investigative arm raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) last week, carrying out a plan clearly intended to get the congresswoman denaturalized and deported. The whole episode was defined by the deeply anti-Somali racism rampant on the right, and it sends a message to naturalized citizens across the country: The White House could send law enforcement after you, too.

A Less-Welcoming Society

ICE is not just Trump’s mass deportation tool. It has also become a vector for the sort of basic mean-spiritedness that he’s spent the past decade giving permission for his followers to emulate. Sometimes the agency’s name is used to inflict casual cruelty upon kids, as a woman at a high school volleyball game did in Houston last week when she yelled, “We’re going to call ICE on your parents” and “Go back to Mexico!” Other times it lets petty people settle scores in horrifying ways, like when a man filed a theft charge against a 25-year-old former employee who had bought a $12 meal not realizing her phone’s McDonald’s app was still linked to her former company’s credit card. As reported in Baltimore Brew, when she went to court to settle the matter, she was grabbed by ICE; she apparently remains in ICE detention. (It’s unclear whether the former boss, who reportedly showed a pattern of disturbing behavior toward the former employee, alerted ICE.)

In this climate that the president has cultivated—defined by growing acrimony, suspicion, and downright cruelty, sometimes causing irreversible consequences—it’s no wonder that Latino truancy is up in places like Washington, D.C. After his father was deported, one child reportedly described feeling “genuinely afraid to step outside.”

Columbia University’s Mae Ngai, a leading historian of immigration, told me the Trump administration treats U.S. citizens who are Latino as illegitimate or second-class citizens based on their racial or ethnic background—a concept she calls “alien citizenship.” Ngai says black and brown Americans have long faced this type of suspicion, and that you can draw a straight line from Mexican repatriation during the Great Depression—which saw 450,000 people of Mexican descent, half of whom were U.S. citizens and many of whom were children, removed from the country—to the anti-immigrant fervor of the Trump administration.

“Mexicans and Asians were never considered to be the ‘right kind’ of immigrant,” she said. “Mexicans were written off as birds of passage: They just come and go, they don’t settle here, but many Mexicans did settle here. . . . There’s this idea that Mexicans and by extension other Latinos are not bona fide immigrants, they don’t become Americans.”

She said what ICE is doing is citizenship nullification. “With Asians and Latinos, even their citizenship is shaky—it’s suspect.”

To make the United States even less hospitable for Latinos, the administration has also slashed the number of people it is naturalizing. The numbers are lower now than they were during COVID, when some operations of the federal government virtually ground to a halt. The administration’s reduction of the number of people being granted citizenship has coincided with its willful destruction of the visa process for highly skilled workers and its breaking of the asylum process for those seeking refuge.

SPEAKING OF THE ASYLUM PROCESS: CNN reported this week that the State Department has been using two different, contradictory sets of assessments of the safety of some Latin American countries. In public travel advisories, the department has been warning Americans about the dangers of visiting Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala, and El Salvador. But in assessments sent to asylum officers, the department suggests the level of danger there is lower than in some U.S. cities like Houston and Baltimore. The upshot is that future asylum claims from Latin America are more likely to be denied.

This change follows a 2025 law creating an annual asylum fee—one that was applied retroactively, which left many asylum seekers unsure not just how much they owed but also how to prove they had paid the fee.

The Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project (ASAP) recently won a lawsuit in district court against the method the Executive Office for Immigration Review used to charge the fees, partly because the agency failed to address the difficulties applicants faced in producing their payment receipts. (The practical effect of the ruling is not yet clear, though, and the court did not invalidate the fee itself.)

“Wait until you see what we do next year,” border czar Tom Homan boasted earlier this month.

One indication of what’s to come, according to the American Prospect, is that ICE is “fast-tracking a $100 million domestic surveillance program,” which includes plans to deploy 142 intelligence contractors across the United States to create network analyses and possibly targeting packages using classified and open-source material. According to an ACLU senior policy analyst quoted by the Prospect, “It looks dangerously like the construction of an internal spying agency.”

A FORMER OBAMA OFFICIAL once told me that you either inspire people to vote or you scare them into voting. What is happening is scary, to be sure. But the way people have responded to that fear—sometimes, that itself is inspiring.

I’ve had a lot of cause this year to write about the late Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Which is why it caught my attention when the veteran immigration activist Erika Andiola posted that people are leaving their “I Voted” stickers on a memorial local residents have set up to honor him in Houston.

“Guys, seventy of these stickers. We counted,” Araujo’s son Ronaldo beamed in a video as he showed stickers dotting the area under the words “Justice for Lorenzo.” “Thank you guys for voting and thinking about my dad.”

text:
An immigrant detained at a sprawling detention center complex in Georgia died on Friday, local and federal officials confirmed, after the facility has already faced national scrutiny for its response to an ongoing hunger strike inside.

The death inside the D Ray James facility in Folkston, Georgia, comes as federal immigration officials and private contractors are allegedly threatening hunger strikers there with force-feeding, a detained hunger striker, his wife, attorneys and advocates all said this week. Detainees are refusing food to protest prolonged captivity and bad conditions.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Saturday confirmed the death inside the facility, which is adjacent to the Folkston ICE processing center. Together, both facilities make up a large detention complex. GEO Group, the private prison company that runs the facilities under contract for the federal government, referred all questions to ICE.

The Georgia bureau of investigation (GBI), a state law enforcement agency, confirmed in an email that the local sheriff’s office requested the GBI conduct an “in-custody death investigation” at the D Ray facility, the Guardian can reveal. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its umbrella agency, did not respond to requests for comment about the death or the hunger strike.

“This was a preventable tragedy,” said Azadeh Shahshahani, the legal and advocacy director for Project South, a social justice organization based in Georgia. “We hold ICE and the private prison corporation fully responsible for any harm that migrants suffer at Folkston. We call for an immediate independent investigation into this tragic death and for accountability. Folkston must be shut down immediately.”

The man, Luis Sandoval, was 48 and from El Salvador, ICE said in its statement, adding that at about 1.46am on Friday, facility staff found Sandoval with a ligature around his neck. He was pronounced dead less than an hour later.

Sandoval was arrested by ICE officials earlier this month, and transferred to the Folkston facility on 8 October. In its press release, the agency said Sandoval had prior convictions for aggravated assault and other crimes, and that his death was under investigation.

It was unknown on Saturday whether Sandoval had participated in the hunger strike. The GBI said it could not share more details because of its active investigation.

Sandoval is the 60th person to die in ICE custody since the start of the second Trump administration, as ICE continues with its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown.

Austin Kocher, president of Relevant Research, which studies the immigration enforcement system, and who is a research fellow at American University, said that this year, there have been an average of one death every 10 days in the custody of ICE. That figure includes people dying in detention centers or in nearby hospitals while still in the custody of ICE.

“Even in the past, there has not been such an overt dehumanization and overt view that migrants’ lives are expendable,” Kocher added. “I worry that that tone [from the Trump administration] has a tendency towards neglect and viewing migrants as disposable.”

Tens of thousands of people have been arrested and detained by ICE, leading to prolonged detention, as immigrants and asylum seekers fight their cases, and the agency has been stepping up its offensive in recent months despite a less showy presence on the streets.

One man currently in the Georgia detention center is Andrei Gerdiukov, a Russian asylum seeker who is participating in the hunger strike.

Nearly three weeks ago, Gerdiukov and dozens of others launched a hunger strike to demand their legal cases be processed more quickly through the US immigration system and to protest the conditions of their confinement. The hunger strikers were placed in solitary confinement, according to Gerdiukov and attorneys.

“I feel tired, I feel dizzy. Every move, it is hard,” Gerdiukov said in an interview by phone on Saturday from detention. “They threatened us that they were going to force-feed us.” He had heard about the death but did not know Sandoval.

Gerdiukov and his wife, Polina Chertushkina, came to the US from Russia to seek asylum after they faced persecution for their opposition to the war in Ukraine, Chertushkina said. Their cases are ongoing, but as the couple were driving through Florida this February, they were pulled over and detained by immigration officials. Chertushkina was released, but Gerdiukov was taken to Folkston eight months ago.

“I am so worried about him, I don’t know what to do,” Chertushkina said about the force-feeding threats, speaking on Saturday by phone. Chertushkina is asking lawmakers to assist her husband.

At least 12 hunger strikers are still participating, despite the threats of force-feeding, Gerdiukov said, adding that several had been fainting.

On Friday, the hunger strikers were moved to a nearby unit, where medical officials “wearing combat boots” took their vital signs, raising fears of imminent force-feeding, Gerdiukov said.

It was not clear on Saturday whether or when the authorities intended to use force-feeding.

The process to force-feed hunger strikers is secretive, with court records often sealed.

A judge has to approve the procedure, and then detention guards restrain a hunger striker while medical staff push tubing up the nose and down the throat to pump nutritional liquid into the stomach. Medical ethicists and human rights organizations have called the practice torture.

ICE generally says in court filings that force-feeding is necessary to maintain “good order” in detention centers as well as to keep detainees alive.

Kocher decried the contradictions.

“On the one hand, they’re trying to force-feed people [to keep them alive],” Kocher said. “And yet at the same time, in that same [Folkston] facility, you have someone who died and possibly was able to kill themselves.”

text:
Georgia’s two U.S. senators have asked federal officials to determine whether officers at the ICE processing center in South Georgia, the nation’s largest, have retaliated against hunger strikers at the sprawling facility, including placing at least 13 of the protesters into solitary confinement.

The Current GA reported Monday that about 500 detainees had gone on a hunger strike in the first week of October to protest conditions at the Folkston installation and what lawyers representing some of the detainees say are violations of U.S. law for processing asylum seekers.

In a letter on Thursday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and the agency’s inspector general, the senators, Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff, urged DHS to conduct an “immediate investigation” to ensure the facility, located 50 miles southwest of Brunswick in Charlton County, is complying with federal detention standards.

Their request follows what they described as “reports of medical neglect and retaliation by custodial officers in response to the hunger strike.” The alleged retaliation included putting at least 13 of the hunger strikers into solitary confinement, write Ossoff and Warnock, citing “reports from local advocates.”

The assertion that at least 13 detainees have been put into solitary confinement could not be independently confirmed, though the wife of one detainee told The Current last week that her husband, a hunger striker, had been placed in isolation. Attempts to contact detention center officials on Saturday were unsuccessful.

“We support Senators Warnock and Ossoff’s inquiry into the conditions at the Folkston ICE Processing Center. We are also deeply concerned about reports of punishment and retaliation against those speaking out. We hope this inquiry will be the first step toward transparency, accountability, and meaningful action to protect the human rights, dignity and well-being of every person detained,” said Daniela Rodriguez, co-founder and executive director at Migrant Equity Southeast in a statement to The Current.

Besides urging DHS’ inspector general to carry out an unannounced inspection of the detention facility, Ossoff and Warnock also asked Mullin to disclose how many, if any, of the hunger strikers have received a medical evaluation and how many, if any, have been transported offsite for hospital care.

Another death at Folkston

The reported hunger strike at Folkston and allegations of retaliation against participants again focused attention on the treatment of detainees at the installation. On Saturday, ICE announced that a 48-year-old Salvadoran man had died at the facility in the early morning hours Friday.

The man, Luis Sandoval, was found with a ligature around his neck at 1:46 a.m., ICE said in a news release. Despite receiving medical attention, he was pronounced dead 42 minutes later.

The statement did not say whether Sandoval was a current or past participant in the hunger strike. It recounted what it said was Sandoval’s illegal entry into the U.S. and his criminal record, and said an investigation into Sandoval’s death, including an autopsy, would be conducted, adding that ICE is “committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments.”

Sandoval is the second person to die in custody at Folkston; Jaspal Singh died on April 15, 2024. Singh was placed under medical observation after complaining of chest pain and was later found unresponsive.

The facility’s medical care contributed to his death, according to an ICE review of the case.

A record of lax enforcement

The senators’ Oct. 22 letter is also addressed to J. David Donahue, the CEO of the GEO Group, which has operated the D. Ray James facility since 2010 and has operated the Folkston immigrant detention center since 2017.

In June 2024, ICE, or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, awarded the Boca Raton-based company a new, $47 million contract to consolidate the installation — formally known as the Folkston ICE Processing Center — with the D. Ray James Correctional Facility. The contract called for expanding the resulting complex to accommodate 3,000 beds, which would make it the largest immigrant detention center in the U.S. and as of 2025, one of 20 ICE facilities the company operates nationwide.

The company has a record of lax enforcement of federal detention standards at Folkston. It received the highest number of violations during the first Trump administration, according to oversight reports examined and reported by The Current last year.

In 2019 alone, ICE inspectors recorded 38 violations, ranging from poor medical care and food handling to mistreatment of detainees from certain nations.

Some of those conditions appear to persist at Folkston.

“Some of us have been detained for months. Some people have been here for years. We are not serving criminal sentences. We are asking the United States for protection,” one of the detainees said in an audio recording obtained by The Current earlier this month.

“We are afraid that what inspectors see will not show how we normally live. We have serious concerns about the food, sleep conditions, medical care, and the length of our detention,” the detainee said.

Also, the current hunger strike at Folkston is not its first.

In 2018, Indian and other South Asian migrants at Folkston went on a hunger strike to protest their prolonged detention and to call attention to what they said was ICE’s inhumane practice of refusing to release individuals.

In their letter this week, Warnock and Ossoff ask Mullin to indicate whether ICE or the GEO Group has “sought or obtained any court order for involuntary feeding or hydration of any detainee.”

Polina Chertushkina, the wife of Andrei Gerdiukov, a Russian national detained at the facility, said that she is grateful for the intervention of the senators.

“I’m especially glad they addressed the issue of forced feeding, as my husband and other hunger strikers were moved to a different pod yesterday for medical examinations in preparation for possible forced feeding,” she wrote Saturday in a message to The Current.

text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Russell K. Robinson, Mullin v. Doe: Whitewashing Anti-Blackness, 17 Cal. L. Rev. Online 65 (July 2026) (Full Document)

Mullin v. Doe is notable for the logical contortions that the Court performed to deny what was right in front of its face. It also raises stark questions about this Court’s ability to detect and condemn anti-Black racism. President Trump’s stigmatizing statements about Haitian immigrants should have easily sufficed to show racial animus when the administration terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) status for Haitian immigrants. This brief essay describes and dissects the various arguments that Justice Alito’s majority opinion unfurled to avoid that conclusion. It then concludes by linking the opinion to a broader cultural phenomenon of “performative politics,” and shows that it extends to the right wing.

The majority worked hard to launder the Trump administration’s virulent racism. The Court’s initial method was to bury the comments--to refuse to print them in the U.S. reports. As Justice Kagan pointed out in dissent, Justice Alito declined to recount the actual statements by President Trump and former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem that gave rise to the respondents’ claim of racial animus. This is extremely unusual and suspect. How can a court analyze statements if it can’t bear to face them?

[ . . . ]

Make no mistake. Republican-appointed Justices are actively facilitating Trump’s racist immigration agenda, but they want readers to know that they are not personally racist.

Russell K. Robinson is Walter Perry Johnson Professor at Berkeley Law and Faculty Director of the Center on Race, Sexuality & Culture.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

The Department of Homeland Security agreed in a settlement with the state to alert city officials at least 30 days before environmental permitting would get underway.

No new Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers are slated for construction in Newport, Oregon, anytime soon, and the federal government will provide at least a month’s notice to city officials before any environmental permitting would get underway.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security agreed to those terms through Aug. 1, 2027, as part of a settlement with the Oregon Department of Justice filed in federal court in Eugene on Friday.

“ICE doesn’t get to skirt the law to build a facility for locking up and deporting our neighbors,” said Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, in a news release. “Oregon stood up, we made the federal government answer for its plans in court, and now they have to follow the law.”

The possibility of a new ICE detention center coming to Newport arose last fall amid concerns that federal immigration authorities were scouting the Oregon Coast for a long-term holding facility, including at Newport’s U.S. Coast Guard municipal airport site.

Newport’s city leaders went public with their concerns shortly after, and strong opposition grew from residents and the state’s Democratic leaders, who also took issue with the temporary removal of a life-saving rescue helicopter from the city’s Coast Guard facility.

Rayfield successfully sued the Homeland Security Department over the helicopter’s removal, securing a court order that it be returned to Newport, and asked a federal judge to halt any construction on an immigration detention facility at the site.

In that case, which is behind the recent settlement, lawyers for Oregon’s Justice Department argued that the federal government had been skirting federal environmental and coastal land use regulations by trying to build a facility on the municipal airport site without providing advanced notice to state and local leaders. The Oregon Justice Department agreed to drop the case following the federal government’s commitment to providing advance notice should efforts to build a detention center in the area resume.

The notice period required in the lawsuit does not apply to other Oregon cities, though the settlement notes ICE is not planning to expand or create any detention facilities or processing centers in the state.

text:
The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

Greg Bovino also told the BBC that he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".

Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. US President Donald Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".

A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".

Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".

He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".

Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".

Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.

"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".

The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.

When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."

Kristi Noem, who was Homeland Security secretary at the time of the operation, was fired by Trump in March.

Bovino has since retired from the US border patrol. He has become known for his hardline stance on immigration, often going further in his statements than Trump's own officials and claiming without evidence that 100 million people are illegally in the US and should be deported.

He has called for "total spectrum immigration enforcement" with support from the US military involving "cruise ships packed to the gills, cars, planes, trains, automobiles, all headed out of the United States packed with illegal aliens".

When asked about Bovino's comments about Minneapolis, a White House spokesperson said "the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history".

"He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," they said.

text:
Transcript

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

This week, the Department of Homeland Security was accused of deliberately slowing down hundreds of thousands of immigrant visa applications for people from 75 countries in defiance of a federal court order. And protests hit a sleepy Vermont town that's a hub for ICE intelligence gathering. NPR's Vanessa Romo joins us now for the latest immigration briefing, a regular look at the administration's crackdown. Vanessa, thanks for being with us.

VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: Hi, Scott. Thanks for having me.

SIMON: And let's begin with that last story. You've been reporting on this - ICE surveillance headquarters in Vermont. What did you find? What does ICE do there?

ROMO: ICE has three targeting surveillance centers in the country. One is in California, and the other two are in this very beautiful, quiet town of 10,000 people in Williston, Vermont, just outside of Burlington. I was there when a group of protesters was holding a demonstration outside of what's called the Law Enforcement Support Center. ICE describes this as a single national point of contact for law enforcement around the country. And here's Leif Taranta, one of the protest organizers, describing some of the work that goes on there.

LEIF TARANTA: This is the only ICE tip line in the country. So when people call to report someone they think might be undocumented, those calls go here, and then the people here coordinate with ICE agents about going to pick up people. And so they do a lot of the dispatching for ICE nationally from here.

ROMO: So you know how the Trump administration has consistently said that the ICE sweeps that we're seeing around the country are deliberate and that officers have specific targets in mind when they're deployed? Well, this is where those lists are coming from.

SIMON: What do we know about what information law enforcement officers might be using to put those lists together?

ROMO: Well, this law enforcement center is also home to ICE's massive database of a hundred million electronic records. So that includes immigrant status information, court and law enforcement records and even biometric data. And so analysts there pull from all of that information to create those target lists.

SIMON: You said Williston's home to two of these surveillance headquarters. Please tell us about the second.

ROMO: The second is just about a mile and a half away. It's called the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center. And the work going on here is of really great concern to privacy rights advocates who say that DHS is pulling information from commercial databases and social media. So everything from Google to Instagram, WhatsApp and even YouTube.

And based on a federal contract proposal, they allege that the Trump administration is now scouring the internet for what's called sentiment analysis to create these profiles on people who might be expressing anti-ICE views. Here's Kabbas Azhar, a lawyer with the Electronic Privacy Information Center.

KABBAS AZHAR: Of course, there's a lot of issues with that. Speech is very ambiguous, very contextual. And oftentimes, this threat analysis that they're doing can sweep in a lot of protected First Amendment activity.

ROMO: So we asked ICE about whether they're doing that, and they did not respond to my questions.

SIMON: And I gather this small town in Vermont has become the scene of regular demonstrations. What do the protesters hope to achieve?

ROMO: They hope to draw attention to the fact that these intelligence facilities are here and that they're at the heart of the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown. So the thought is that if more people in a very blue, progressive state knew, then that would spark public outrage and that could lead to their ouster.

SIMON: And now, Vanessa, the other topic that we mentioned earlier. Two months ago, federal judge struck down a blanket Trump administration pause on issuing immigrant visas to people from 75 countries. Is the State Department complying with that order?

ROMO: Lawyers say no. My colleague Sergio Martínez-Beltrán spoke with immigration attorneys and people affected by this policy who say not only is the State Department not following the judges' directives, but it's intentionally slow-walking the processing of nearly 300,000 visas from people from those previously banned nations. That has, in effect, left all of those applicants, who are largely spouses and children or other family members of U.S. citizens, trapped in their home country.

And again, we reached out to the State Department, and citing pending litigation, they declined to comment on that charge that they're foot-dragging reviewing these visas. The agency did pause visa processing worldwide to conduct a training program for consular officials. And in an email statement to NPR, they said that the goal of the training is to identify immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers, a so-called public charge.

SIMON: NPR's Vanessa Romo with this week's immigration briefing. Vanessa, thanks so much.

ROMO: Thank you.

title: He Went to Document an Anti-ICE Protest. He Left Without an Eye
description:
And on March 28, he lost an eye from an injury sustained at a protest against federal immigration enforcement.
When he moves, his hair sweeps away just long enough to reveal a large black eye patch covering a glass eye underneath.
The fragments destroyed the structure of Collins’ eye.
Each of them later had to have an eye removed.
That kind of precision work is “so much harder now that I have one eye,” Collins said.
text:
This article was produced by Capital & Main. It is co-published by Rolling Stone with permission.

Tucker Collins, 19, has undergone a series of changes since last year. He started his freshman year as an astronautical engineering student at the University of Southern California. He moved to a new part of Los Angeles. And on March 28, he lost an eye from an injury sustained at a protest against federal immigration enforcement.

That afternoon, the amateur photographer and filmmaker decided to go to a No Kings protest in downtown Los Angeles with a new camera his parents gave him as a Christmas gift, he told Capital & Main. He was there to film and photograph Department of Homeland Security agents who have carried out a series of aggressive immigration raids under President Donald Trump.

”I think we’ve seen with DHS specifically, in this case, being used, weaponized into a force of terror against everyday citizens,” he said. “I was there to document any potential crimes.”

Collins was walking as part of a large group of protesters, holding up his camera toward DHS agents near the Metropolitan Detention Center, a prison in downtown L.A. used to detain immigrants, when he was hit in the face with a kinetic impact projectile — also known as a less-lethal round — according to video taken by another protester and provided to Capital & Main by Collins’ attorney V. James DeSimone. Collins crumpled to the ground and began to scream, the video showed, and strangers pulled him to safety. Another protester drove him to the hospital, he said, and the injuries were so severe that his eye had to be surgically removed.

Collins is soft-spoken with long blond hair covering the right side of his face. When he moves, his hair sweeps away just long enough to reveal a large black eye patch covering a glass eye underneath.

“This was a crime, and it was, I guess, surprising that it happened to me,” he said. “But not surprising that it happened.”

Editor’s picks

Collins is one of numerous people injured by local police or federal agents during protests that have continued in Southern California in the year following the Trump administration’s surge of immigration enforcement actions that began in June 2025.

In dozens of cases, local and federal officers, often outfitted in riot helmets and bulletproof vests, have fired kinetic impact projectiles, including plastic or rubber bullets commonly referred to as less-lethal rounds, into crowds of demonstrators. Los Angeles Police Department officers fired at least 2,587 such rounds at protesters between June 6, 2025, and March 28, 2026, according to use-of-force reports published by the department.

While there is no official tally of the number of people injured during protests in Southern California, the Los Angeles Press Club has documented in a federal lawsuit over a dozen incidents in which journalists in the area were injured covering the protests. Some of the people injured recovered in the days and weeks after, but others were left with life-altering wounds. Those with serious injuries have filed claims or lawsuits against police or federal law enforcement.

A Capital & Main review of claims and lawsuits filed since June 2025, as well as interviews with attorneys and reviews of bystander videos, documented at least five people who were, like Collins, shot in the eye with a projectile. Capital & Main spoke with three of them, each of whom described feeling anxiety and a sense that something deeply unjust had happened to them. They said they were also continuing to reckon with their lives being suddenly and permanently altered.

Related Content

All of the five injured men lost vision in at least one eye. Three of them required surgeries to remove their injured eyes, according to legal claims filed against the agencies whose officers they believed to be responsible. Each of them has had to navigate the new challenges of living with a significant visual impairment.

The Los Angeles Police Department and U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to Capital & Main’s questions about the complaints filed against them by five people who were shot in the eye. The agencies have said elsewhere that they do not keep internal records of the total number of injuries to protesters since June 2025.

Lost Forever

Due to the severity of his injury, Collins was transferred to another hospital where a surgeon removed five plastic fragments of a projectile from his skull, said Collins and his attorney, V. James DeSimone. The fragments destroyed the structure of Collins’ eye. And the collection of blood and fluid that made up the remains of his eye were determined to have passed the point of repair, they said, so the eye was removed.

The first few weeks of his recovery were filled with agonizing headaches, Collins said. “The pain was still too much for me to want to do anything but lie in bed all day,” he said. “It hurt to move my head.”

Since losing his eye, Collins said he has had to relearn dozens of basic tasks, from walking without running into people and objects to completing his schoolwork.

“I’m worried how much it will, you know, impact my ability to do the things I love,” he said. “I’d like to think that I’ll still be able to do my career path as normal, but in reality I don’t know.”

Marcos Lemor, an ophthalmologist affiliated with Adventist Health-White Memorial and East Los Angeles Doctors Hospital who surgically removed what was left of Collins’ eye, said that the gravity of his injury presented a significant challenge. Without both eyes, Collins has lost his depth perception.

“He’s never going to be able to really do that kind of very fine manual work because he does not have that perception,” Lemor said, “That’s lost forever.”

Collins is still grappling with his new reality and said he feels a great sense of loss.

“It’s strange to think of my life now having a before and after,” Collins said.

Lives Changed

Collins isn’t the only protester or bystander to sustain a life-altering eye injury from a law enforcement projectile at a Southern California protest.

During a previous No Kings rally on June 16, 2025, an LAPD officer shot photographer Marshall Woodruff, 29, in his right eye, according to a lawsuit filed against the department. His eye had to be removed, leaving the aspiring filmmaker with an uncertain future in film, said his attorney, Aaron Liskin, a partner at Kinsella Holley Iser Kump Steinsapir LLP in Los Angeles.

Homeland Security agents shot both college student Kaden Rummler, 21, and visual artist Britain Rodriguez, 31, in the face during a protest outside Santa Ana City Hall on Jan. 9. Video captured an agent in body armor dragging Rummler by the collar of his hoodie, covered in blood. Both Rodriguez and Rummler were hit in the eye, according to claims they filed against the Department of Homeland Security. Each of them later had to have an eye removed.

Rummler was initially charged with felony assault on a federal agent. His charge has since been reduced to an infraction of “creating a hazard on federal property.” He paid a fine of $250 and a $30 processing fee, according to federal court documents reviewed by Capital & Main.

Jesus Javier Gomez Islas, 23, was riding a scooter home from work near a demonstration at the Metropolitan Detention Center on Jan. 31 when he was shot in the eye by a Los Angeles Police Department officer, according to his attorney, Jamal Tooson, a partner at Lessem, Newstat & Tooson, LLP in Los Angeles, and a claim filed by Gomez Islas against the department. Gomez Islas had his eye surgically removed, according to Tooson and the filing.

Tooson said that his client has developed sympathetic ophthalmia, a rare, auto-immune condition that occurs when the inner eye tissue is exposed and the body does not recognize it as its own. The immune system then launches an attack to destroy the healthy eye. He said Gomez Islas is in danger of losing his remaining eye due to the severity of the original injury.

In an email, a Los Angeles Police Department spokesperson Norma Eisenman declined to respond to questions about Gomez Islas’ cases because it is “pending litigation.”

In July, then-spokesperson Department of Homeland Security spokesperson Lauren Bis did not answer questions about Rummler’s, Rodriguez’s and Collins’ injuries or its practices, but sent a statement saying, “We remind the public that rioting is dangerous — obstructing law enforcement is a federal crime and assaulting law enforcement is a felony.”

The statement also included the following statement in response to questions about photographers and reporters injured while covering protests.

“We remind members of the media to exercise caution as they cover these violent riots and remind journalists that covering unlawful activities in the field does come with risks — though our officers take every reasonable precaution to mitigate those dangers to those exercising protected First Amendment rights.”

Undeterred

Collins said he is resolute in his commitment to return to a normal life. He dreams of being an astronautical engineer; he wants to build rockets that go into outer space. A few weeks after he was discharged from the hospital, he joined USC’s Rocket Propulsion Lab in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert for a launch. He has been able to stay engaged in the field with the help of the university’s rocketry team for now.

That kind of precision work is “so much harder now that I have one eye,” Collins said.

Trending Stories

But Collins said his experience has left him more confident in the importance of documenting what he sees.

He plans to pick up his camera again and return to protests to bear witness.

Federal appeals court judges broke with their Republican-appointed colleagues on Friday, accusing them of issuing a ruling that “detonates the core” of the Constitution’s Due Process Clause.

In a scathing dissent from a ruling that upheld the Trump administration’s policy of detaining certain undocumented immigrants without bond hearings while their immigration cases proceed, Judge Dana Douglas—joined by four colleagues—wrote that the court was relying on “sham history” to support the Trump administration’s policy.

“The Government proposes a seismic change in how this country’s immigration law functions,” she said. “It may come, but it cannot come wrapped in the mantle of history. Nor should judges do it the favor of wrapping it in the mantle of a sham history cobbled together by the government.”

The full 5th Circuit Court of Appeals heard the case and ruled 10–7 against three noncitizens who had been detained while their immigration cases proceeded.

Each of the three men, from Mexico and Honduras, has lived in the United States for at least 14 years. They were detained after traffic stops, and two have children who are U.S. citizens.

Lower courts ordered the men released, but Friday’s ruling reversed those decisions. The Supreme Court will also consider the broader legal question.

Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote the majority opinion. Five of the other nine judges who sided with him were also appointed by Trump.

Even Judge Leslie Southwick, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented, warning that by upholding the administration’s detention policy, “this court has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents, a wall not designed, recognized, or even suggested by the Supreme Court.”

The other four—Chief Judge Jennifer Elrod, Priscilla Richman, Edith Jones, and Jerry Smith—were appointed by Republican presidents George W. Bush and Ronald Reagan.

The heart of the case is whether the Trump administration can detain undocumented immigrants without giving them an opportunity to seek release on bond.

While the majority acknowledged that the men have due process rights under the Fifth Amendment, it ruled that those protections do not entitle them to individual bond hearings while their immigration cases proceed.

“The practice (challenged here) of seeking out persons unlawfully present in this country in the interior and subjecting them to detention without meaningful process or the possibility of bail—that is, to what was long understood to be the statute applicable at ports of entry, rather than the interior detention statute—is a recent invention of the Department of Homeland Security in the last year or so contradicting its almost three decades old practice,” Judge Douglas, a Biden appointee, wrote.

The majority opinion acknowledged that the men have due process rights under the Constitution, but found that those rights do not guarantee them a hearing to seek release on bond while their cases are decided.

The Trump administration has pursued a ruthless immigration agenda, sending ICE agents into major cities and pulling people from the streets, their homes, and their cars. Federal immigration agents have also fatally shot people during enforcement operations, including U.S. citizens.

“Historically, and for obvious reasons, courts have jealously guarded against executive attempts to claim sweeping detention mandates that, among other things, may make sudden, unannounced arrests and detentions a part of ordinary life in the interior of this country,” Douglas said.

title: Santa Maria Special-Education Adult Student Says ICE Agents Caused Broken Wrist
authors: Pricila Flores, Noozhawk Staff, Pricila Flores, Noozhawk Staff
description:
Federal immigration enforcement agents detained and allegedly injured an adult special-education Santa Maria High School student Wednesday morning while he was en route to school.
ICE agents were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation in Santa Maria” when they encountered someone they believed matched the description of who they were looking for, a spokesperson told Noozhawk Friday.
Santa Maria Joint Union High School District’s spokesperson Kenny Klein on Thursday confirmed that ICE agents detained a student on Wednesday while the student was on their way to school.

Most recently, she spoke out against the federal agency in Santa Maria amid a surge in activity that immigrant activists say is linked to a statewide immigration operation.
text:
Federal immigration enforcement agents detained and allegedly injured an adult special-education Santa Maria High School student Wednesday morning while he was en route to school.

The student was identified to Noozhawk as Erick Zepeda, a 20-year-old U.S. citizen, by his former special education teacher, Glenn Goldin.

Goldin, who described himself as Zepeda’s mentor and father figure, sat down with his former student Thursday morning. Zepeda recounted the incident to him over breakfast and “broke down,” Goldin said.

“He really did think they were going to kill him,” Goldin told Noozhawk, overcome with emotion.

Goldin told Noozhawk that Zepeda was detained at around 6:45 a.m. Wednesday by two agents wearing “Police” and “ICE” vests who exited a black SUV at the corner of Enos Drive and Broadway.

The incident left Zepeda with a wrist broken in two places, a black eye and lacerations, Goldin said.

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) representative confirmed to Noozhawk that the agents temporarily detained an individual in Santa Maria Wednesday but did not name the person.

A spokesperson also denied the claim that the individual suffered broken bones, calling it “FALSE” in an emailed statement.

The spokesperson said the individual never requested medical assistance during the incident.

ICE agents were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation in Santa Maria” when they encountered someone they believed matched the description of who they were looking for, a spokesperson told Noozhawk Friday.

The ICE spokesperson alleged the “individual resisted officers” and “refused lawful commands and assumed a fighting stance with clenched fists.”

“They relied on their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity, whereupon he was released,” the spokesperson added.

Santa Maria Joint Union High School District’s spokesperson Kenny Klein on Thursday confirmed that ICE agents detained a student on Wednesday while the student was on their way to school.

The school district did not share the student’s identity but confirmed the person was detained and then released one-half mile from the high school campus at 901 S Broadway.

The student continued walking to school, where school administrators called an ambulance, and the student was transported to the hospital, Klein said.

Goldin said school administration called an ambulance upon seeing his injuries, and that the Santa Maria Police Department also responded to the school.

Afterwards, Zepeda was taken to Marian Regional Medical Center in Santa Maria, and his group home manager told Goldin about the student’s broken wrist that reportedly needed surgery, according to Goldin.

Goldin said there are photographs of Zepeda’s injuries, including a black eye and some lacerations.

Klein said the Santa Maria Police Department “confirmed” it notified “all appropriate agencies,” including the District Attorney, the California Attorney General, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement through the Los Angeles Office.

A Santa Maria police spokesperson told Noozhawk on Thursday that the department would not comment and also directed any requests for comment to ICE.

Klein also said the school community was notified of the immigration enforcement-related detention.

Student Recounts Getting Detained

Goldin is a former Santa Maria High School special education teacher who taught Zepeda for the last two years and heard of the arrest from other former students.

He said the 20-year-old, who lives in a group home, has “enunciation problems” and “trouble expressing himself.”

Special education students can remain in high school until they are 22 years old, according to Goldin.

Goldin recalled feeling “horrified” while hearing his former student recount the story.

“For me, as a special education teacher, it’s triply horrifying because it took us a year to convince him that he could walk to school by himself, that he didn’t have to get in a shitty yellow school bus that made him feel different,” he said.

Goldin said Zepeda has “a weird gait,” and “he couldn’t protect himself” when the agents allegedly tackled him to the ground.

The ICE agents then handcuffed Zepeda while he repeatedly told them, “You’re hurting me,” before loading him into the vehicle, Goldin said.

Once loaded into the vehicle, the agents reportedly asked Zepeda about his identity while they circled the block for a brief time before releasing the 20-year-old back to the site where he was detained, Goldin added.

Community Backlash to Incident

Local immigrant activists and community groups, including 805UndocuFund, have planned a protest for Saturday at 5 p.m. at 625 S. McClelland Ave.

Santa Maria City Council member Gloria Soto denounced the Wednesday incident on social media.

She said in a statement on Thursday that the student was racially profiled by ICE.

“This is unacceptable. Our children should never have to fear for their safety in their own community,” she wrote.

Soto also said she called the city mayor, Alice Patino, and requested she call a special Santa Maria City Council meeting “to address this incident.”

“To my colleagues who remain silent: Where is your leadership? Our community deserves accountability, not silence.”

No Santa Maria City Council meeting was scheduled as of Friday morning.

Soto has been vocal in condemning local ICE activity.

Most recently, she spoke out against the federal agency in Santa Maria amid a surge in activity that immigrant activists say is linked to a statewide immigration operation.

Congressman Salud Carbajal also took to social media Friday to call the incident “outrageous.”

“Our schools must remain safe places for students and families, free from fear, intimidation, and racial profiling,” he wrote.

text:
President Donald Trump administration deported 980,000 migrants during the first 18 months of the second term, according to a new Migration Policy Institute (MPI) analysis.

The analysis showed that the deportations were higher than under the former president Joe Biden administration and Trump’s first term, but still well below early-2000s levels.

It noted that the Trump administration was on track to complete about 660,000 deportations in fiscal year (FY) 2026, up from an annualised count of 620,000 during the first year of his current administration.

“That is 26 per cent above the average for FY 2021–2024 but below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in FY 2000 and well short of the administration’s goal of 1 million a year,” the MPI analysis stated.

According to the MPI, 69 per cent of the 980,000 deportations carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) between January 20, 2025 and July 31, 2026 were of unauthorised immigrants initially intercepted at the border despite U.S.-Mexico border encounters at historic lows.

The MPI Visiting Senior Fellow Marc Rosenblum, noted that arrests that originated in communities in the U.S. interior accounted for a growing share of deportations, rising from 28 per cent in 2025 to 39 per cent in July 2026.

Mr Rosenblum, who is a former executive director of the DHS Office of Homeland Security Statistics, further stated that the pace of deportations resulting from interior arrests had doubled, increasing from 8,000 per month on average in the first three months of Mr Trump’s second term to 19,000 per month on average between May and July 2026.

“At a time when unprecedented resources and policy attention are being directed at increasing arrests and deportations, this analysis fills a critical gap in understanding immigration enforcement trends,” stated Doris Meissner, director of MPI’s U.S. Immigration Policy Program.

The analysis noted that 61 per cent of ICE deportations, which excluded those resulting from a border turnaround, were of non-citizens who had been in the U.S. at least two years, adding that 390,000 deportations in all—and 15 per cent (90,000) were of immigrants who had been in the country 10 or more years.

“Among deportations of individuals with two or more years of U.S. residence, 71 per cent (about 280,000) had no criminal conviction. For those with 10 or more years of U.S. residence, 61 per cent (57,000) had no criminal conviction.

“Across all 980,000 deportations carried out by ICE or CBP, 20 per cent (190,000) involved a non-citizen convicted of a crime. And just 31 per cent of removals were of convicted criminals, compared to an average 44 per cent criminality rate for FYs 2009–2021,” it noted.

Noting that the most common convictions were for illegal entry or re-entry (23 per cent of all criminal removals) and traffic offences, including driving under the influence (21 per cent), the analysis showed that a growing share of deportations had been returns rather than formal removals in a major break with the pre-COVID-19-pandemic period.

“While the total number of immigrants departing the United States through deportation or ‘self-deportation’ are much higher than at any previous time dating back at least to 2014, it is highly unlikely that 3 million immigrants have departed the country—much less 3 million unauthorized immigrants,” it added.

text:
Ogden • About 50 people gathered Saturday in Ogden to call for the release of a young couple detained by federal immigration agents after a traffic stop earlier this week.

Protest organizers say the couple left their 2-month-old child in the care of a family member.

Pablo Oyarce, 25, and Javiera Galvez, 26, were booked into the Weber County Jail on Oct. 22, booking records show. The Weber County Sheriff’s Office pulled them over for a traffic stop and contacted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to Ogden United, the group organizing Saturday’s protest.

Neither had charges listed in the jail’s booking records as of Saturday morning.

Jared Rosser, an Ogden resident who knows the family, said Galvez’s mother had been visiting from Chile to help care for the couple’s newborn. She was the one who told Rosser the couple had been arrested, he said, and he started to spread the word.

Now, she’s scrambling to figure out how to bring her daughter home, unsure how to “navigate any of it,” Rosser said.

“I think we can all agree that a 2-month-old baby should be with their mother,” protest organizer Kim Haslam told the crowd.

Rosser said Galvez has been calling her mother from jail and told her that officers were pressuring the couple to self-deport as early as Sunday, leaving them little time to speak with an attorney.

The couple came to the U.S. through the visa waiver program, he said, which allows eligible travelers from certain countries to visit for tourism or business for up to 90 days. During that time, he said, they filed paperwork seeking asylum.

The protest began at 11:30 a.m. Saturday outside the Weber County Building, with attendees calling on the sheriff’s office to explain why deputies contacted ICE and what policies or agreements govern the agency’s cooperation with federal immigration agents.

For Arlene Anderson, who attended the protest, the couple’s detention was an example of what she believes immigration enforcement is doing to families.

“This is happening in Ogden,” Anderson said. “Contrary to what people are saying, we are seeing families torn apart. This is not what we wanted in our community.”

Margaret Kluthe, a retired pediatrician, said she worries about how separation from the mother could affect the 2-month-old baby. In her career, she said, she saw how separation can put children at risk of health problems and illness.

The Weber Sheriff’s Office signed a 287(g) task force model agreement with ICE in July 2025.

The task force model is the most intensive of ICE’s 287(g) agreements. It allows designated local officers to investigate and make immigration arrests as part of their regular police duties, including during traffic stops.

Lt. Sean Endsley said Saturday that a Weber County officer trained under the agreement detained the couple and made the arrest while acting on ICE’s behalf. Endsley said he did not immediately have further information about what prompted the traffic stop or the couple’s immigration status.

Protestors are also calling for an emergency stay of removal while the couple’s immigration case is pending and for Galvez to be released so she can care for their child.

Haslam said she hopes to see the Sheriff’s Office end its agreement with ICE completely.

“Sheriff Arbon says that they’re going after the worst of the worst,” Haslam said. “And this couple is not the worst of the worst.”

text:
A small but determined group of Oceanside residents gathered along Mission Avenue Friday evening to call for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to leave their streets, sharing a message they say is at the heart of their protest: They are a community, not a target.

Car horns and cheers filled the air as demonstrators lined the busy roadway between Armando's and Tierra Mia Coffee, catching the attention of passing drivers and drawing honks of support throughout the evening.

The gathering was organized by Noelia Hernandez, who arrived prepared with signs, snacks and aguas frescas for those who came out to participate.

“The thing that matters is that at least a little bit of people are here,” Hernandez said. “And the honking and everything lets us know that they're supporting us, even if they're not here today, but they let us know that they're here in some way.”

Hernandez said providing refreshments and supplies was the least she could do for those who took time to join the demonstration.

As the evening continued, more signs and flags appeared along the stretch of Mission Avenue, with participants expressing concerns about increased immigration enforcement in Oceanside and its impact on local residents.

Among those who attended was Lucia Farmer, an Oceanside resident who said she felt compelled to speak up for people who may be afraid to do so themselves.

“I want to speak out for the people who can't, who are too afraid to speak out, who don't have that privilege to do that,” Farmer said.

Born and raised in Oceanside, Farmer said it was important to show up for her hometown, adding that smaller community demonstrations deserve attention and support, too.

“I think our local community needs a lot of love, too,” she said. “So I'm gonna speak out for the ones here.”

Farmer also voiced concern about what she described as a growing presence of ICE activity in Oceanside.

“It's really sad seeing the surge of ICE activity growing in Oceanside, and I don't think that's OK,” she said. “This is our community. These are our people. These are our friends and family that live here.”

For demonstrators, the response from passing motorists became a meaningful part of the evening. Each honk and cheer offered a reminder that others in the community shared their concerns, even if they could not attend in person.

Farmer said the support gave her hope and reassured her that others felt the same way.

“It gives me more hope, but there's a lot of people who feel like they're on the same boat as us,” she said.

Despite the group's small size, participants said they intended to continue making their voices heard.

“A lot of people want us to be quiet and silence us, but they won't be able to do that anymore,” Farmer said. “We're here and we're together to speak up.”

For those gathered along Mission Avenue, the demonstration was about more than signs or slogans. It was an opportunity to stand with neighbors, support people who may feel afraid to speak publicly and remind the community that they are not alone.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court will hear several cases during its current nine-month term.

Here’s a look at some of them; rulings are expected by the end of June.

1. Climate suit

The justices heard arguments Oct. 5 in a bid by ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colo. The companies appealed after Colorado's top court allowed Boulder's lawsuit, which seeks monetary damages and accuses the companies of violating state law. The Trump administration backed the companies. The justices voiced concerns about unduly limiting states’ authority to pursue climate-related litigation, as well as the potential to unleash chaos if local governments across the country were permitted to sue these companies.

2. Immigration detention

The court will decide the legality of President Donald Trump's policy that subjects millions of immigrants in the U.S. illegally to mandatory detention during deportation proceedings. The justices took up the Trump administration's appeal of a lower court's ruling against the policy in a case involving a Brazilian national. The administration abandoned the longstanding interpretation of federal law that immigrants living in the U.S. could be released on bond while their cases play out in immigration court. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

3, Deportations

The justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own — so-called "third countries" — without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. On Sept. 29, the court paused a federal judge's ruling that deemed removing migrants to third countries unlawful. More than 25,000 migrants were deported to 29 countries under the policy, according to human rights groups.

4. Asylum and terrorism

The court will hear the Trump administration's bid to deny asylum to a ​man who was forced to prepare meals for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen, which U.S. officials considered to be a terrorist organization, in Nigeria — a case that could expand what officials ‌may deem terrorist activity under U.S. immigration law. The Justice Department appealed a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba that said cooking did ​not qualify as "material support" for terrorism. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

5. Firearms

The justices will hear arguments Dec. 2 in a challenge to the legality of state prohibitions on assault-style rifles, another chance to expand gun rights in a case that ​involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings. Lower courts upheld bans on powerful ‌semiautomatic rifles, such as AR-15s, in Cook County, Ill., and Connecticut. The lower courts rejected arguments that the measures violate the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and bear arms." Gun rights groups and other challengers said Supreme Court precedents concerning the ​Second Amendment protect these firearms, which they described as in "common use."

6. Voting rights

The justices will hear arguments Dec. 8 in a Republican-led bid to revive voter restrictions in Arizona that would stiffen proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registrants ‌and purge state voter rolls of alleged noncitizens. Republicans appealed after a lower court halted provisions of Arizona's law because they were found to violate a federal voting registration statute. Critics said the Arizona measure adds extra mandates for voting ​that unfairly target Latino, Native American and student voters. Those groups tend to favor Democratic candidates.

7. Race in admissions

The justices will consider whether to revive a lawsuit against a Maryland county's lottery admissions policy for four elite public middle ​schools that some parents claim unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants. The case has the court delving again into the contentious issue of race in student admissions. A coalition of parents appealed a lower court's decision rejecting their claim that Montgomery County's policy violates the U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment guarantee of equal protection under the law. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

8. LGBTQ+ rights

The justices will hear arguments Nov. 3 in a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver ​and other Catholic entities to be exempted from a Colorado preschool funding program's ‌nondiscrimination requirement. The Catholic plaintiffs objected to the state's requirement ⁠that schools receiving funding under the program give all children "equal opportunity" to enroll in preschool regardless ​of certain characteristics, including the sexual orientation or gender identity of students or their family members. A lower court found the program did not violate ​the religious rights of the plaintiffs under the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment.

9. DOGE

The justices will decide whether the Trump administration can avoid handing over records to a watchdog group about its Department of Government Efficiency, an initiative that slashing agency budgets and workers spearheaded last year by the president's former adviser Elon Musk. The administration appealed a judge's order for DOGE to respond to requests by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington for information about its operations. The judge found DOGE likely is a government agency covered by the federal Freedom of Information Act, or FOIA. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

10. Home distilling ban

The court will decide the legality of a federal ban on ​home distilling of alcoholic spirits enacted in 1868 to crack down on liquor tax evasion. The dispute pits the Trump administration, which defends the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds Congress’ authority under the U.S. Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states backed the legal challenge ​to the statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

11. Apple suit

Justices will hear Apple's bid to escape being found in contempt ​in its legal fight with "Fortnite" maker Epic Games after the iPhone maker was deemed in violation of a ‌judicial order mandating sweeping changes to its App Store in the antitrust litigation. Apple appealed a lower court's ruling upholding a decision by an Oakland, California-based federal judge finding Apple in contempt in Epic's 2020 lawsuit contesting App Store fees. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

12. PepsiCo trademark

The court will hear arguments in a bid by ​canned-coffee maker Rise Brewing to hold PepsiCo liable for alleged trademark infringement ‌concerning Pepsi's morning energy drink "Mtn Dew Rise." Rise appealed a lower court's ruling rejecting the company's claim that the product name "Mtn Dew Rise" infringes its trademarks and creates customer confusion with ​its coffee brand. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.
