ORO VALLEY, Ariz. (KGUN) — EDITOR'S NOTE: KGUN 9 reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security for a response to the claims made at the protest. Neither agency had responded as of the time of publication. This story will be updated if a response is received.

Dozens of people gathered in Oro Valley to protest outside a building they say houses a Department of Homeland Security office that runs activities with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

KGUN 9 reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security for comment prior to publication. Neither agency responded, and we were unable to independently confirm whether an ICE facility operates at that location.

The demonstration comes as DHS reports increased enforcement activity. According to the agency, ICE arrested more than 50,000 undocumented immigrants in August — a record, and the second consecutive month with arrests at that level.

Rolande Baker, an Oro Valley resident, said she came out after witnessing what she described as the removal of neighbors in her community.

"It has been a nightmare across this nation and here in Tucson," Baker said.

Baker said the scale of enforcement activity prompted her to speak out publicly.

"This is horrendous what is going on in this country. It has to stop. We cannot be kidnapping our neighbors," Baker said. "This is not what this country is about."

A protester who identified himself only as Jason said the size of the crowd at the demonstration stood out to him.

"It's really encouraging to me; it's impressive," Jason said. "It shows how mad people are. It shows how determined people are to resist these kinds of attacks on not only civil liberties, but just on decency in general."

Jason also described the enforcement climate as alarming.

"It's terrifying," Jason said. "I mean, when people don't know that they're going to be snatched. When they're on their way to work, when they're alone, when no one can see them."

Organizations from around Tucson joined in the demonstration.

Dugan Meyer, a volunteer with Rapid Response, said the goal was to keep the public engaged with what is happening in the community on a daily basis.

"We want people to make noise and understand that this is happening every single day and that we can do something about it." Meyer said.

title: Detained migrants have no constitutional right to bond hearings, US court rules
description:
A U.S. appeals court ruled on Friday that President Donald Trump’s administration is not required under the U.S. Constitution to give detained immigrants a chance to seek release on bond.
Circuit Court of Appeals decided that the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment due process protections do not require that immigration detainees receive bond hearings.
Numerous lawsuits by migrants arguing they were being unlawfully detained have flooded the courts as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, implemented Trump’s mass deportation agenda.
The Supreme Court is considering only whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the Constitution, the issue the 5th Circuit addressed with Friday’s decision.
But the full 5th Circuit agreed to rehear the case, and on Friday reversed course, concluding that detained immigrants are not constitutionally entitled to proceedings in immigration court beyond what Congress provided by statute.
text:
A U.S. appeals court ruled on Friday that President Donald Trump’s administration is not required under the U.S. Constitution to give detained immigrants a chance to seek release on bond.

In a 10-7 ruling powered by its conservative majority, the New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals decided that the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment due process protections do not require that immigration detainees receive bond hearings.

“To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country,” U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote in the decision.

The ruling, if left to stand, would eliminate a key avenue for detained migrants in the three states under the 5th Circuit’s jurisdiction — Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi — to argue for release, especially if the U.S. Supreme Court decides the administration’s detention practice complies with immigration law.

The Supreme Court this month agreed to consider the issue, which has divided lower courts. Numerous lawsuits by migrants arguing they were being unlawfully detained have flooded the courts as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, implemented Trump’s mass deportation agenda.

The Supreme Court is considering only whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the Constitution, the issue the 5th Circuit addressed with Friday’s decision.

While the 5th Circuit in February had adopted the administration’s reading of immigration law as requiring mandatory detention, a 2-1 panel of the court in July held that ICE could not constitutionally detain people for more than 90 days without providing hearings to argue for release on bond.

The decision, which came in lawsuits by two Mexican citizens and one Honduran, carried particular importance because Texas and Louisiana, within the 5th Circuit’s jurisdiction, house the nation’s largest numbers of immigration detainees.

But the full 5th Circuit agreed to rehear the case, and on Friday reversed course, concluding that detained immigrants are not constitutionally entitled to proceedings in immigration court beyond what Congress provided by statute.

“This ruling opens the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences for them, their loved ones and their community,” Ellie Norton, a lawyer for the non-U.S. citizens in the case at the National Immigration Project, said in a statement.

James Percival, the general counsel for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, in a social media post hailed what he called a “big win in the 5th Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens.”

Among the dissenting judges was U.S. Circuit Judge Dana Douglas, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, who wrote that “unchecked, executive authority to arrest and detain, indefinitely, echoes fearfully from history.”

text:
A Santa Maria High School student with disabilities was allegedly assaulted by two ICE agents on his way to school.

The 20-year old U.S. citizen was reportedly tackled by two federal immigration agents and forced into their car, according to a news release from Indivisible Santa Maria on Friday.

The ICE agents questioned the student about his name, date of birth and citizenship status before leaving him in an alleyway with bruises, lacerations and a broken wrist that required surgery.

“The student then proceeded to walk to school,” said Kenny Klein, public information officer for the Santa Maria Joint Union High School District, in a statement. “School administration called an ambulance, and the student was taken to the hospital to receive medical care.”

805 UndocuFund is organizing a protest at 5 p.m. on Saturday at 625 S. McClelland Ave. in Santa Maria in support of the student who was allegedly assaulted by ICE.

Klein said the Santa Maria Police Department responded to the event and has notified the District Attorney, the California Attorney General and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Parents, students and staff were also notified of the alleged assault, Klein added.

The event comes amidst a surge in immigration enforcement across the Central Coast. Over 200 people have been detained or remain unaccounted for across San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara and Ventura counties since Oct. 5, according to data from 805 UndocuFund.

The non-profit organization responds to ICE activity in the region and supports families affected by immigration enforcement with legal and financial assistance.

An ICE spokesperson said the student matched the description of someone the agents were targeting in Santa Maria on Wednesday, and “when the individual resisted officers, refused lawful commands, and assumed a fighting stance with clenched fists, they relied on their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity, whereupon he was released.”

The ICE spokesperson also denied that the student had broken his wrist from the incident.

“Claims that the individual suffered broken bones are FALSE,” the spokesperson wrote in an email to the News-Press. “He never requested medical assistance.”

Santa Maria City Councilwoman Gloria Soto took to social media on Thursday in response to the event.

“This is unacceptable,” Soto wrote in an Instagram post. “Our children should never have to fear for their safety in their own community.”

Rep. Salud Carbajal, D-Santa Barbara, also shared his disbelief via his X account on Friday.

“The student is a U.S. citizen and sustained injuries severe enough that they needed surgery,” Carbajal wrote. “This is outrageous and we should not tolerate these tactics.”

Santa Maria has been among the hardest hit communities for federal immigration enforcement in Santa Barbara County since the start of the second Trump administration.

On Oct. 15, Alexandria Quintanar, a volunteer for 805 UndocuFund, was detained by ICE after an agent followed her while allegedly driving recklessly in Santa Maria.

Quintanar was released from ICE custody shortly after.

805 Undocufund, alongside CAUSE, Future Leaders of America, The Fund for Santa Barbara, MICOP, Immigrant Legal Defense Center, Santa Maria Indivisible and the California Immigrant Policy Center has also called for an investigation into the case, as well as an official stance from the city of Santa Maria that it will not support or facilitate ICE enforcement.

description:
Babushahi Bureau Washington DC (US), October 24, 2026: A US federal appeals court has ruled that the government is not constitutionally required to provide detained immigrants with bond hearings to seek release while their deportation proceedings are pending.
In July, a three-judge panel of the appeals court had ruled that immigration authorities could not constitutionally detain individuals for more than 90 days without providing hearings at which they could seek release on bond.
Supreme Court to consider related legal question The US Supreme Court has agreed to hear a related case concerning whether federal immigration law requires bond hearings for certain detained migrants.

text:
Babushahi Bureau

Washington DC (US), October 24, 2026: A US federal appeals court has ruled that the government is not constitutionally required to provide detained immigrants with bond hearings to seek release while their deportation proceedings are pending.

In a 10-7 decision on Friday, the full US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, based in New Orleans, held that the due process protections of the Fifth Amendment do not guarantee immigration detainees the right to such hearings.

The ruling applies to Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the three states within the court’s jurisdiction, and could significantly affect migrants seeking release from immigration detention while challenging their removal from the United States.

The case involved lawsuits filed by two Mexican nationals and one Honduran national. In July, a three-judge panel of the appeals court had ruled that immigration authorities could not constitutionally detain individuals for more than 90 days without providing hearings at which they could seek release on bond.

However, the full court agreed to reconsider the cases and overturned the panel’s decision.

Writing for the majority, US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson said that individuals seeking freedom from physical restraint could leave the country, a position that drew criticism from dissenting judges and immigrant rights advocates.

The ruling comes amid the Trump administration’s expanded immigration enforcement and mass deportation efforts. The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency has faced numerous legal challenges from migrants arguing that their detention is unlawful.

Supreme Court to consider related legal question

The US Supreme Court has agreed to hear a related case concerning whether federal immigration law requires bond hearings for certain detained migrants. However, the question before the Supreme Court concerns statutory protections, whereas the Fifth Circuit’s latest ruling addresses whether such hearings are required under the Constitution.

The appeals court’s decision could restrict a key legal avenue for detained migrants in the three states to challenge their continued detention, particularly if the Supreme Court separately upholds the administration’s interpretation of federal immigration law.

Ellie Norton, a lawyer representing the migrants through the National Immigration Project, criticised the ruling, warning that it could lead to more people being detained without adequate justification and cause serious harm to families and communities.

James Percival, general counsel for the US Department of Homeland Security, welcomed the decision, describing it as a significant victory for the administration’s mandatory detention policy.

Dissenting from the majority, US Circuit Judge Dana Douglas warned that unchecked executive authority to arrest and detain individuals indefinitely raised serious historical concerns.

The ruling marks a significant development in the ongoing legal battle over the scope of immigration detention powers in the United States.

text:
The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

Greg Bovino also told the BBC that he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".

Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. US President Donald Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".

A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".

Watch: Renee Good's partner speaks publicly for first time since her death

Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".

He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".

Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".

Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.

"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".

The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.

When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."

Kristi Noem, who was Homeland Security secretary at the time of the operation, was fired by Trump in March.

Bovino has since retired from the US border patrol. He has become known for his hardline stance on immigration, often going further in his statements than Trump's own officials and claiming without evidence that 100 million people are illegally in the US and should be deported.

He has called for "total spectrum immigration enforcement" with support from the US military involving "cruise ships packed to the gills, cars, planes, trains, automobiles, all headed out of the United States packed with illegal aliens".

When asked about Bovino's comments about Minneapolis, a White House spokesperson said "the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history".

"He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," they said.

Bovino has also floated "exploring" a presidential run in 2028. "If politicians aren't going to step up and do their job then you might see something happen," he told the BBC when asked about his intentions.

Bovino recently addressed a far-right rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Abdul El-Sayed, a US citizen and Democratic candidate running in the state's tightly fought race for a Senate seat.

American-born Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate if he wins the seat against Republican Mike Rogers.

The incident has raised concerns about student safety among some local residents.

Danny Mogg, a Santa Maria resident and grandfather of a student who attends Pioneer Valley High School, said he plans to accompany his grandson on his daily walks to and from school.

“I am a grandfather and life coach to an autistic teenager that attends Pioneer High School. He walks to school every day. This is a complete outrage and it will not stand. I plan to walk my grandson every morning and home,” Mogg said.

KSBY News reached out to the school district and the teacher for additional information but did not receive further details.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation in Santa Maria when they encountered an individual they believed matched the description of their target.

According to the agency, the individual refused lawful commands and assumed a fighting stance. ICE said agents used "their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity."

The agency also denied claims that the individual suffered broken bones, saying he did not request medical assistance.

Immigration attorney Rodolfo Marquez said racial profiling has become a growing concern in immigration enforcement.

“There has been cases that almost allow them to racial profile, in which the Ninth Circuit ruled, and we see that happening now,” Marquez said.

Marquez shared advice for potential encounters with ICE.

“One of the first questions you should ask is, ‘Am I free to go?’ If they say no, then you know it’s a detention, right? Then the third thing would be to exercise your right to remain silent. ‘I exercise my right to remain silent, and I don’t consent to any searches,’” Marquez said.

He also encouraged people who witness an ICE detention to record what they see, as long as they do not interfere with the agents.

“I think it’s important to bring accountability with recording. This can be used in court cases,” Marquez said.

805 Undocufund plans to hold a protest Saturday, Oct. 24, at 5 p.m. to show support for the student and respond to the reported detention.

Introduction

On October 23, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that three long-term undocumented residents were not constitutionally entitled to individualized ICE bond hearings while awaiting immigration removal proceedings. The decision does not itself establish a violation of international law. However, mandatory immigration detention without sufficient individual justification or effective judicial review may conflict with Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which binds the United States.

Sitting en banc, the Fifth Circuit reversed district court judgments that had ordered the detainees' release and prohibited their renewed confinement without hearings assessing dangerousness and flight risk. The majority concluded that the Fifth Amendment did not require those procedures under the applicable statutory detention regime. Its ruling addressed constitutional rights under American law rather than the separate obligations imposed by international human rights law (Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara, 2026).

Article 9 of the ICCPR prohibits arbitrary deprivation of liberty and guarantees access to judicial proceedings capable of reviewing unlawful detention. It does not require every immigration detainee to receive a hearing identical to those conducted by American immigration judges. The UN Human Rights Committee nevertheless interprets the Covenant as requiring immigration detention to remain reasonable, necessary, proportionate, and subject to appropriate review (Human Rights Committee, 2014, paras. 18, 39–48).

The legal controversy consequently extends beyond the authority of Congress to prescribe mandatory custody. It concerns whether immigration status can justify confinement without an individualized assessment and whether the remaining judicial remedies provide adequate protection against arbitrary detention. The answer depends on the Fifth Circuit's actual holding, the disputed interpretation of federal immigration legislation, and the distinct standards governing detention under the ICCPR.

1. The Fifth Circuit's Decision on ICE Bond Hearings

The October 23 judgment arose from three consolidated appeals: Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara, Villegas Angel v. Mullin, and Gomez Alvarado v. Vergara. The Fifth Circuit, sitting with 17 judges, reversed habeas corpus relief granted to three men detained under 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A). Ten judges supported the judgment, while seven dissented. Separate concurring and dissenting opinions revealed substantial disagreement over the constitutional protection of personal liberty.

The principal question was whether the Fifth Amendment required immigration authorities to conduct hearings assessing the petitioners' dangerousness or flight risk before detaining them during removal proceedings. Judge Cory T. Wilson's majority opinion concluded that the Constitution imposed no such requirement under the statutory regime applicable to these individuals. The court also found that their actual detention periods did not establish constitutional grounds for habeas relief.

The ruling establishes an important precedent within the Fifth Circuit, which covers Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi. It does not decide every constitutional question involving immigration detention. The majority expressly left open challenges concerning confinement that no longer serves a legitimate immigration purpose, removal proceedings used as a pretext for imprisonment, or detention continuing when removal becomes practically unattainable (Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara, 2026, pp. 28–30).

1.1 The Three Detainees and the Reversal of Habeas Relief

Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, a Mexican national, had lived in the United States without formal admission for more than 22 years. Immigration authorities detained him following a traffic stop in December 2025. He filed a habeas petition on February 13, 2026, and obtained relief from the federal district court on February 25, after approximately two months in detention.

Alejandro Villegas Angel, also a Mexican national, had lived in the country since 2011 and was the father of two U.S.-citizen children. Following a police stop in February 2026, he was transferred to ICE custody. A district court granted his habeas petition on March 3, after approximately three weeks of confinement. Miguel Angel Gomez Alvarado, a Honduran national who had lived in the United States since 2012, was detained following a traffic stop in November 2025. He obtained habeas relief on March 2, 2026, after approximately three months in custody.

All three were detained under § 1225(b)(2)(A), which the government interpreted as requiring their confinement pending removal proceedings. The district courts concluded that continued detention without individualized custody hearings violated procedural due process. They ordered the petitioners' release and prohibited renewed detention unless authorities first provided hearings assessing dangerousness and flight risk. The men were released shortly after the district court judgments (Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara, 2026, pp. 4–5).

A divided Fifth Circuit panel affirmed the district courts in July 2026. It adopted a constitutional requirement for individualized hearings within 90 days of detention, although two petitioners had obtained habeas relief before reaching that period. The panel nevertheless affirmed their release orders, reasoning that continued detention without hearings would have exceeded the proposed limit by the time the panel ruled. The full court subsequently granted rehearing en banc, vacating the panel opinion.

Following argument on September 24, the en banc court reversed the district courts on October 23. It rejected the petitioners' claimed constitutional entitlement to individualized dangerousness or flight-risk hearings and concluded that their detention periods did not warrant habeas relief. The judgment vacated the lower courts' grants of relief; it did not itself order the three men returned to custody or establish their subsequent detention status.

1.2 The Majority's Interpretation of the Fifth Amendment

The majority began from the petitioners' classification as applicants for admission under federal immigration legislation. Section 1225(b)(2)(A) requires detention of covered individuals pending removal proceedings but does not provide an ordinary administrative bond procedure. The petitioners' constitutional argument was that due process required an additional opportunity to establish that confinement was unnecessary because they presented neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community.

Judge Wilson expressly acknowledged that the petitioners enjoyed Fifth Amendment protections. The majority nevertheless emphasized Congress's broad immigration authority, drawing on Mathews v. Diaz (1976) and Department of Homeland Security v. Thuraissigiam (2020). Those decisions recognize substantial legislative authority over immigration while addressing different questions concerning the constitutional status and procedural rights of noncitizens.

The procedural due process analysis concentrated on whether the proposed hearings would determine facts relevant under the governing detention rule. The majority reasoned that statutory custody depended on admission status, not individualized dangerousness or flight risk. It relied partly on Connecticut Department of Public Safety v. Doe (2003), in which the Supreme Court rejected a procedural claim seeking a hearing on a fact that was immaterial under the applicable registration statute.

The court separately rejected the substantive due process argument. It considered mandatory detention rationally related to legitimate governmental objectives, including securing attendance during removal proceedings and facilitating removal when legally authorized. Its reasoning drew on Demore v. Kim (2003), which upheld mandatory detention of certain criminal noncitizens during removal proceedings.

The majority also discussed Jennings v. Rodriguez (2018), where the Supreme Court rejected interpretations of immigration detention statutes that would have required periodic bond hearings not provided by Congress. Jennings did not conclusively decide whether prolonged detention without individualized review would violate the Constitution in every circumstance. Likewise, Demore concerned a distinct statutory category and did not establish unlimited authority to detain all noncitizens without individualized assessment.

The Fifth Circuit applied these precedents to the petitioners' specific claims under § 1225(b)(2)(A). Its conclusion was that the Constitution did not require the hearings they requested, even though their prolonged residence in the United States distinguished them factually from individuals apprehended at the border.

1.3 The Dissents and the Limits of the Holding

Judge Leslie Southwick, joined by five colleagues, rejected the majority's constitutional analysis. His dissent emphasized the significance of physical liberty and questioned whether Congress could require detention throughout removal proceedings without allowing long-term residents to challenge the individual justification for their confinement. He considered the majority's approach insufficiently protective of individuals already living within the United States.

Judge Catharina Haynes advanced a narrower dissenting position. She agreed with the principal objections raised by Judge Southwick but would have limited the analysis to individuals resembling the petitioners: people with more than ten years of residence, no criminal history, and close American relatives. Her opinion attached particular constitutional significance to established residence and personal circumstances rather than treating every undocumented individual as identically situated.

Judge Dana Douglas separately challenged the majority's reliance on Doe and its treatment of procedural due process. Judge Stephen Higginson also dissented, examining the relationship between immigration detention legislation and constitutional protection. These opinions reflect distinct lines of disagreement; none represents the controlling judgment of the en banc court.

Judge Priscilla Richman concurred in the judgment but expressly declined to decide whether immigration officials could proceed under § 1226 in different circumstances or what procedures might then be required. She also emphasized that the petitioners had not independently challenged the constitutionality of prolonged detention based on its duration.

The majority distinguished Zadvydas v. Davis (2001), which concerned detention after a removal order, from the pre-removal custody before it. It rejected the application of Zadvydas' six-month presumptive period as a fixed limit on detention pending removal proceedings. The court stressed that the three petitioners had been confined for approximately three months, two months, and three weeks, respectively.

The opinion nevertheless recognized constitutional limits. Different due process questions might arise if detention stopped serving its immigration purpose, proceedings became a pretext for imprisonment, or removal could no longer realistically be achieved. The judgment consequently cannot be treated as unconditional constitutional approval of indefinite immigration detention (Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara, 2026, pp. 28–30, 98–159).

2. Why ICE Can Deny Bond Hearings Under U.S. Law

The dispute arose from competing interpretations of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). Federal law establishes different detention arrangements depending on a noncitizen's legal classification and the circumstances of immigration proceedings. Individuals detained under discretionary custody provisions may generally request bond redetermination, subject to statutory and regulatory limits. Covered individuals detained under § 1225(b)(2)(A) ordinarily cannot obtain the same administrative hearing.

The distinction acquired new significance when the Department of Homeland Security changed its interpretation of detention authority in July 2025. The administration treated individuals who had entered without admission, including some apprehended after years of residence inside the United States, as subject to mandatory detention. The position departed from longstanding administrative practice and generated litigation across the federal courts.

The controversy is principally statutory: whether Congress intended § 1225(b)(2)(A) to apply to everyone present without admission or only to individuals seeking admission in the relevant statutory sense. The constitutional question becomes decisive when a person is classified under the mandatory detention provision but argues that the Fifth Amendment independently requires individualized custody procedures.

2.1 The Dispute Over Sections 1225 and 1226

Section 1225(a)(1) defines an applicant for admission to include a noncitizen present in the United States who has not been admitted, as well as someone arriving in the country. Formal admission ordinarily requires lawful entry following inspection and authorization by an immigration officer. The statutory definition can consequently encompass individuals who entered without inspection and remained in the United States for years.

Section 1225(b)(2)(A), however, directs detention when an immigration officer determines that a covered individual seeking admission is not clearly entitled to admission. The distinction between applicant for admission and seeking admission lies at the center of the circuit split. The Fifth Circuit interpreted the provisions together, concluding that individuals present without formal admission remain subject to the mandatory detention rule. Other circuits have held that the latter expression imposes an additional limitation involving persons seeking lawful entry.

Section 1226(a) permits discretionary detention pending a removal decision and authorizes release on bond or conditional parole. Where regulations give an immigration judge custody jurisdiction, a detainee can seek reconsideration of the initial custody decision. Release is not automatic: the judge must evaluate legally relevant factors, including danger and flight risk, within the applicable statutory and regulatory limits.

The modern provisions emerged from the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996. That legislation substantially reorganized immigration proceedings and replaced much of the former division between exclusion and deportation with a unified removal system. Before the reforms, individuals apprehended after entering without inspection generally had greater access to bond procedures than those stopped while seeking entry.

The subsequent administrative practice is relevant to interpreting congressional intent. Federal immigration authorities continued for nearly three decades to treat many noncitizens apprehended within the country after entry without inspection as eligible for discretionary detention procedures. Courts rejecting the 2025 policy have regarded this history as evidence against the government's newer interpretation.

Section 1226(c) establishes another mandatory detention regime for specified criminal and security-related categories, including provisions amended by the Laken Riley Act of 2025. Its targeted requirements provide additional context for statutory interpretation but should not be conflated with § 1225(b)(2)(A). The applicability of each provision depends on its own legal conditions.

2.2 The 2025 ICE Policy and the Circuit Split

In July 2025, ICE adopted interim guidance interpreting § 1225(b)(2)(A) as requiring detention of certain individuals physically present in the United States without formal admission, including those who had entered years earlier. The Congressional Research Service documented the policy change in its September 17, 2026, analysis, Mandatory Detention During Removal Proceedings: Circuit Split.

The reported ICE guidance was not publicly available on the agency's website when the Congressional Research Service examined it. Its operative interpretation is nevertheless reflected in subsequent agency guidance and adjudication. Under the revised approach, affected individuals were generally ineligible for an ordinary immigration judge's bond determination, although statutory discretionary parole authority remained available in qualifying circumstances.

On September 5, 2025, the Board of Immigration Appeals adopted the government's interpretation in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, 29 I&N Dec. 216. The Board concluded that immigration judges lacked authority to hear bond requests or grant bond to individuals present in the United States without admission when covered by § 1225(b)(2)(A). Its decision concerned administrative custody jurisdiction rather than an individualized finding of dangerousness or flight risk.

The Fifth Circuit subsequently accepted the broader statutory interpretation in Buenrostro-Mendez v. Bondi, 166 F.4th 494 (5th Cir. 2026). The Eighth Circuit reached a similar conclusion. These decisions read the statutory definition of an applicant for admission as supporting mandatory detention of the affected category, even when authorities apprehended individuals after substantial residence inside the country.

Other appellate courts disagreed. By September 17, 2026, the First, Second, Third, Fourth, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits had rejected the government's broad interpretation, according to the Congressional Research Service. Their reasoning differed, but the prevailing statutory objection was that being classified as an applicant for admission did not necessarily mean the person was presently seeking admission within § 1225(b)(2)(A).

In Barbosa da Cunha v. Freden, 175 F.4th 61 (2d Cir. 2026), the Second Circuit interpreted the statute as placing the affected detention under § 1226 rather than § 1225. On September 25, it denied rehearing en banc. Separate opinions accompanying that denial exposed judicial disagreement about the statutory language, nearly three decades of administrative practice, and the availability of habeas relief.

The Sixth Circuit's decision in Lopez-Campos v. Raycraft, 175 F.4th 713 (6th Cir. 2026), is especially important because its analysis extended beyond statutory construction. On May 11, the court concluded that individuals living within the United States who were not seeking lawful entry fell outside § 1225(b)(2)(A). It affirmed habeas relief and declined to disturb district court findings that the long-term residents were constitutionally entitled to individualized bond hearings.

The Sixth Circuit thus addressed the Fifth Amendment question that later divided the Fifth Circuit. Its majority considered the petitioners' established residence and personal circumstances legally significant. Judge Eric Murphy dissented, arguing that federal legislation authorized detention and that Supreme Court precedent did not require the individualized hearings requested.

The conflicting constitutional approaches cannot be reduced to the statutory circuit split. Some courts resolved detention disputes through interpretation of the INA without independently deciding whether the Constitution required bond hearings. Others, including the Sixth Circuit and the Fifth Circuit's October en banc court, addressed constitutional protection more directly.

2.3 The Supreme Court Review in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

On October 1, 2026, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, No. 26-104. The case arose from the Second Circuit's ruling concerning Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national whose detention generated litigation over the relationship between §§ 1225 and 1226.

The question accepted for review is whether § 1225(b)(2)(A) mandates detention pending removal proceedings of noncitizens present in the United States without having been admitted. The Court's decision to grant review followed the Second Circuit's September 25 denial of rehearing en banc. As of October 24, 2026, the Supreme Court had not issued a merits decision.

The pending case concerns statutory authority for mandatory detention. If the Supreme Court rejects the government's broad interpretation, affected individuals may become eligible for custody procedures under § 1226(a), subject to other applicable restrictions. If it accepts the government's interpretation, separate constitutional challenges and questions concerning international human rights obligations will remain.

The Fifth Circuit's October 23 judgment and the Supreme Court's pending proceedings are connected but distinct. The Supreme Court is reviewing which statutory detention regime applies; the Fifth Circuit decided whether the Fifth Amendment required particular hearings under the detention provision applied to the three petitioners.

3. Bond Hearings, Humanitarian Parole, and Habeas Corpus

An immigration bond hearing allows an immigration judge, where authorized by law, to determine whether a detainee should remain confined or may be released under specified conditions. The assessment ordinarily concerns the risk of absconding, danger to the community, and other relevant circumstances. A favorable bond determination does not resolve the person's immigration status or establish a right to remain in the United States.

The authority to conduct these hearings depends on the governing detention provision. Section 1226(a) permits discretionary custody and release, subject to statutory and regulatory limitations. Section 1225(b)(2)(A), by contrast, requires detention of covered individuals pending removal proceedings and provides no ordinary bond procedure. The Board of Immigration Appeals confirmed this distinction in Matter of Yajure Hurtado (2025).

The absence of an ordinary immigration bond hearing does not eliminate every possible release mechanism. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(d)(5)(A), the Secretary of Homeland Security may authorize temporary parole on a case-by-case basis for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit. Parole does not constitute admission to the United States, and the statutory provision establishes a discretionary executive power rather than an individual entitlement to release.

Humanitarian parole also differs from an independent custody determination. An official may consider serious personal circumstances when deciding whether parole is appropriate, but the existence of discretionary authority does not establish that the necessity of detention has been judicially assessed. Nor does it guarantee that a person who presents little danger or flight risk will be released.

The power to arrest and detain individuals within national territory forms part of a state's enforcement jurisdiction under international law. States retain authority to implement immigration legislation, including through deprivation of liberty when legally justified. That authority operates alongside domestic constitutional requirements and applicable international human rights obligations.

Federal habeas corpus provides a separate means of challenging unlawful detention. Under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, individuals may seek judicial relief from custody alleged to violate applicable constitutional or federal legal requirements. The three Fifth Circuit petitioners used this procedure successfully in the district courts before the appellate court reversed their judgments.

Habeas proceedings can produce relief beyond immediate unconditional release. Courts may, where the law permits, order release unless the government corrects a legal defect or provides an adequate hearing. The Second Circuit discussed this remedial function in its September 2026 proceedings in Barbosa da Cunha v. Freden, emphasizing that challenges to unlawful immigration detention may fall within habeas jurisdiction.

The practical scope of review nevertheless depends on the claim and the legal standards that federal courts may enforce. A court may have authority to determine whether detention complies with the INA or the Fifth Amendment without possessing an independent basis to enforce every protection contained in the ICCPR. This distinction is central to assessing whether available remedies satisfy international requirements.

4. ICCPR Article 9 and the Prohibition of Arbitrary Detention

The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights establishes binding obligations concerning deprivation of liberty. Adopted by the UN General Assembly on December 16, 1966, the Covenant entered into force internationally in March 1976. The United States deposited its instrument of ratification on June 8, 1992, and the treaty entered into force for the United States on September 8, 1992.

Article 9 protects liberty and security of person. Its guarantees extend to individuals within the applicable territorial and jurisdictional scope, irrespective of nationality or immigration status. This reflects a fundamental feature of international human rights law: protections concerning physical liberty are not generally confined to citizens or individuals with permission to reside in a particular country.

The Covenant does not categorically prohibit immigration detention. States may regulate admission, residence, and removal and may use custody measures for legitimate immigration purposes. However, the state's authority is subject to the prohibition of arbitrary detention under Article 9(1) and the guarantee of judicial review under Article 9(4).

These are binding treaty provisions. Their interpretation has been developed by the UN Human Rights Committee through General Comments, Views on individual communications, and concluding observations on state reports. Those materials carry substantial interpretive authority but must be distinguished from the treaty itself and from binding judgments of international courts.

4.1 Necessity and Proportionality Under Article 9(1)

Article 9(1) prohibits arbitrary arrest and detention and requires deprivation of liberty to occur on grounds and according to procedures established by law. The provision establishes related but distinct safeguards. A detention may be unlawful because it lacks a sufficient domestic legal basis, but detention authorized by national legislation may also be arbitrary under the Covenant.

The Human Rights Committee developed this distinction in General Comment No. 35, adopted in 2014. According to paragraph 12, arbitrariness extends beyond formal illegality and includes considerations of justice, predictability, due process, reasonableness, necessity, and proportionality. These elements require examination of the actual justification for depriving an individual of liberty.

Paragraph 18 addresses immigration detention specifically. The Committee recognizes that confinement for immigration control is not inherently arbitrary. An initial period may be justified by legitimate administrative objectives, including identifying a person, establishing entry circumstances, or conducting necessary immigration procedures. Continued detention requires justification appropriate to the individual's circumstances and reassessment as confinement extends.

The Committee identifies individualized risks of absconding, criminal danger, and threats to national security as circumstances potentially relevant to continued detention. Such risks cannot simply be assumed from membership in a broad immigration category. The Committee's interpretation requires decision-makers to examine whether detention remains necessary and proportionate and whether the relevant objectives can be achieved through less restrictive measures (Human Rights Committee, 2014, para. 18).

Reporting obligations, guarantees of appearance, and appropriate residence conditions may provide alternatives. Their suitability depends on the circumstances of the individual and the requirements of the immigration proceedings. International law does not require the state to choose an ineffective alternative, but the Committee's approach rejects a mandatory rule covering an entire category as a substitute for considering less restrictive options.

This interpretation is particularly relevant to the Fifth Circuit controversy. Section 1225(b)(2)(A), as construed by the majority, authorizes detention based on statutory immigration classification rather than a separate administrative determination of danger or flight risk. The resulting tension with Article 9(1) concerns whether confinement receives sufficient individual justification, especially as its duration increases.

4.2 Judicial Review Under Article 9(4)

Article 9(4) guarantees that anyone deprived of liberty may bring proceedings before a court capable of deciding the lawfulness of detention without delay and ordering release when detention is unlawful. Unlike Article 9(3), which establishes particular protections concerning criminal charges, Article 9(4) applies to civil and administrative detention, including immigration custody.

General Comment No. 35 explains that judicial review must be effective in substance. Paragraphs 39–48 address the availability of proceedings, the independence of the reviewing authority, the capacity to order release, and the requirement for a decision without delay. The Committee recognizes that states may establish different procedures for challenging detention, provided those procedures satisfy the Covenant.

Paragraph 44 specifies that unlawful detention includes confinement incompatible with Article 9(1) or another relevant Covenant provision, even when authorized by domestic legislation. The Committee consequently interprets Article 9(4) as requiring a judicial remedy capable of addressing detention that is substantively unlawful under international human rights standards.

The Covenant does not prescribe an American-style immigration bond hearing as the exclusive means of providing that protection. Habeas corpus or another effective judicial procedure may satisfy Article 9(4), depending on its scope and operation. The relevant question is whether a court can examine the applicable grounds of unlawfulness and order release when those grounds are established.

Review confined to statutory detention eligibility raises a particular difficulty. If a court can determine only whether the detainee falls within a mandatory category, it may lack authority to address continued confinement that is arbitrary under the Committee's interpretation of Article 9(1). The mere existence of judicial proceedings cannot conclusively establish compliance when their substantive reach is inadequate.

5. International Decisions on Mandatory Immigration Detention

The Human Rights Committee has considered mandatory immigration detention in communications brought against states that accepted the First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR. Its decisions have developed the interpretation of Article 9 in circumstances where national legislation authorizes detention while restricting individualized release determinations.

The Committee's Views are reasoned determinations issued by the treaty-monitoring body. They are not judgments of an international court and do not create binding judicial precedents against states uninvolved in the communications. Their reasoning nevertheless provides relevant guidance concerning the Committee's understanding of the Covenant's requirements.

Australian immigration detention cases are particularly useful because they address the relationship between mandatory detention legislation, individual justification, and judicial review. They also illustrate the importance of factual circumstances, especially detention duration, security assessments, and the actual remedies available to detainees.

5.1 A v. Australia and F.K.A.G. and Others v. Australia

In A v. Australia, Communication No. 560/1993, the Human Rights Committee considered the detention of a Cambodian asylum seeker who had remained in Australian immigration custody for more than four years. Australia maintained that detention was authorized by national legislation and served immigration control purposes.

In its Views adopted on April 3, 1997, the Committee concluded that the detention violated Article 9(1). It recognized that unlawful entry could justify an initial period of confinement but found that continued detention required sufficient justification in the individual's circumstances. The Committee rejected the proposition that compliance with domestic legislation necessarily established the absence of arbitrariness (A v. Australia, 1997, paras. 9.3–9.4).

The Committee also examined the limitations of Australian judicial review. Domestic courts could determine whether detention complied with the statutory framework, but the available proceedings did not adequately permit release on the ground that confinement was arbitrary under the Covenant. The Committee found a violation of Article 9(4), identifying a substantive deficiency in the scope of judicial protection (A v. Australia, 1997, para. 9.5).

In F.K.A.G. and Others v. Australia, Communication No. 2094/2011, the Committee considered prolonged immigration detention involving refugees and asylum seekers, including individuals affected by adverse security assessments. The case concerned detention arrangements that significantly restricted the possibility of release despite the passage of time and the circumstances of the individuals concerned.

In Views adopted on July 26, 2013, the Committee found that Australia had failed adequately to justify continued detention through individualized necessity and proportionality assessments. It also examined whether less restrictive measures had been sufficiently considered. The Committee identified violations of Article 9, including paragraphs 1 and 4, and made additional findings concerning other rights arising from the particular circumstances of the detainees (Human Rights Committee, 2013, paras. 9.3–9.7).

These decisions are relevant to the American controversy because they reject domestic statutory authorization as a conclusive answer to arbitrariness. Their factual circumstances nevertheless differ considerably from those before the Fifth Circuit. The Australian communications involved prolonged or indefinite confinement and particular restrictions on review, whereas the three Fifth Circuit petitioners obtained district court relief after periods measured in weeks or months.

The Committee's findings support an international legal analysis of categorical detention practices. They do not establish that the United States committed the same violations or that every individual detained under § 1225(b)(2)(A) experiences arbitrary confinement.

5.2 The UN Human Rights Committee's Findings on the United States

The Human Rights Committee expressed concerns about American immigration detention before the policy changes introduced in July 2025. In its concluding observations on the fifth periodic report of the United States, adopted in October 2023 and issued as document CCPR/C/USA/CO/5 in December, the Committee addressed mandatory and prolonged immigration detention, access to legal assistance, and conditions of confinement.

Paragraph 54 recorded concerns about overcrowding, inadequate access to food, water and medical care, deaths in detention, violence, ill-treatment, and prolonged solitary confinement. The Committee also addressed restrictions affecting asylum procedures and the protection of individuals facing removal.

Paragraph 55 recommended that immigration detention be used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest possible period. It called for greater reliance on appropriate alternatives, improved access to legal assistance and interpretation, and detention conditions consistent with international standards (Human Rights Committee, 2023, paras. 54–55).

The observations concern the broader treatment of migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers. Individuals seeking international protection may possess additional safeguards under refugee law, while refugee and asylum-seeker rights must be distinguished from protections applicable to all immigration detainees. Article 9 of the ICCPR is not restricted to persons who qualify for refugee status.

The Committee's observations are relevant because they demonstrate that concerns about mandatory immigration detention existed before the 2025 administrative change. They do not, however, constitute findings concerning the subsequent ICE guidance, Matter of Yajure Hurtado, or the Fifth Circuit's October 2026 judgment.

Concluding observations also differ legally from individual Views. They form part of the Committee's supervisory examination of state compliance and contain assessments and recommendations. They should not be represented as binding judicial determinations that a particular American detention or court ruling violated Article 9.

6. The ICCPR's Legal Effect in the United States

The United States ratified the ICCPR subject to reservations, understandings, and declarations. One declaration states that Articles 1–27 are not self-executing. In American constitutional practice, this substantially limits the ability of individuals to invoke those treaty provisions directly as independently enforceable rights in federal courts without an applicable domestic legal basis.

The distinction between a treaty's international binding force and its domestic enforceability is central to the relationship between international law and municipal law. A state may be bound internationally even when its legal system does not permit individuals to enforce the treaty directly through ordinary judicial proceedings. The rules governing those two questions arise from different legal sources.

The Supreme Court addressed the ICCPR's status in Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, 542 U.S. 692 (2004). The Court acknowledged that the Covenant binds the United States under international law but observed that the American declaration concerning non-self-execution prevented the treaty itself from creating obligations enforceable in federal courts. The case concerned claims arising from an extraterritorial arrest and the Alien Tort Statute, not immigration bond hearings.

The non-self-executing declaration does not extinguish the United States' substantive international obligations under Article 9. Nor did American ratification include a general reservation removing the prohibition of arbitrary detention or the guarantee of judicial review from the state's treaty commitments. The United States remains internationally bound by those provisions, subject to the terms of its ratification.

This distinction is consistent with the principle reflected in Article 27 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which generally prevents a treaty party from invoking domestic law to justify failure to perform a treaty. The United States has signed but not ratified the Vienna Convention. Article 27 does not bind it directly as a party to that treaty, although the corresponding principle is widely recognized as customary international law.

For immigration detainees, the practical difficulty is that a federal court may reject a constitutional or statutory claim without determining whether the underlying detention complies with the ICCPR. A finding that an individual lacks a Fifth Amendment entitlement to a bond hearing does not necessarily establish compliance with Article 9. Equally, the existence of an international treaty obligation does not automatically create a domestic cause of action capable of enforcing it.

Article 2(3) of the ICCPR requires states parties to provide effective remedies for violations of Covenant rights. In the detention context, that obligation operates alongside Article 9(4)'s specific guarantee of judicial review. The adequacy of domestic remedies must be assessed according to their actual capacity to address the relevant violations, rather than their formal existence alone.

International supervision has important limitations. The United States has not become a party to the First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR, which permits individuals to submit communications to the Human Rights Committee concerning alleged violations by participating states. Individuals detained in the United States consequently cannot use that procedure to obtain individual Views against the United States.

The Committee nevertheless retains its reporting and supervisory functions under the Covenant. Its General Comments and concluding observations remain relevant to the interpretation and assessment of American treaty obligations, although they do not operate as domestic judicial orders requiring release from custody.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights provides another institutional avenue for examining American immigration practices. The United States has not ratified the American Convention on Human Rights, but the Commission examines petitions concerning the United States by reference to the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man. The United States disputes the Declaration's status as a source of binding treaty obligations. Findings within that regional system must accordingly be distinguished from obligations arising directly under the ICCPR.

The absence of an enforceable individual international complaint procedure does not remove the possibility of an internationally wrongful act. Under the general law of state responsibility, a breach of an international obligation attributable to a state may engage its responsibility regardless of whether an international court or treaty body has previously issued a determination. Establishing such a breach requires identifying the applicable obligation and the conduct inconsistent with it.

7. Does Mandatory ICE Detention Violate International Law?

The Fifth Circuit's October 23 judgment does not by itself establish that the United States violated international law. The court decided that the three petitioners lacked a constitutional entitlement to individualized hearings addressing dangerousness or flight risk under the applicable statutory detention regime. It did not determine whether their detention, or the broader mandatory detention policy, complied with Article 9 of the ICCPR.

The international question concerns the state's conduct in depriving individuals of liberty. Congress may authorize detention, immigration officials may implement the legislation, and federal courts may determine that particular constitutional challenges are unsuccessful. Those domestic determinations do not conclusively resolve whether confinement is arbitrary under the Covenant or whether the available judicial remedies satisfy Article 9(4).

The government's immigration objectives are legally relevant. States have legitimate interests in establishing identity, securing attendance during removal proceedings, protecting public safety, and implementing lawful removal decisions. The Human Rights Committee's interpretation of Article 9 does not prohibit detention serving those purposes. It requires that confinement remain justified in light of individual circumstances and that judicial protection against unlawful detention be effective.

7.1 When Mandatory Detention Becomes Arbitrary

Mandatory immigration detention raises serious concerns under Article 9(1) when statutory classification replaces an adequate assessment of the reasons for continued confinement. A person's lack of formal admission may establish that particular immigration procedures apply. It does not necessarily establish that the person presents an individualized risk requiring detention throughout those proceedings.

Under General Comment No. 35, the justification for confinement must be evaluated in the individual's circumstances. Relevant considerations may include the likelihood of absconding, concrete public safety concerns, cooperation with immigration authorities, and the availability of effective alternatives. The Committee interprets Article 9 as requiring reassessment as detention continues, rather than permitting its necessity to be presumed indefinitely.

The distinction has particular significance for individuals who have lived inside the United States for many years. Established residence, family responsibilities, and previous compliance with legal requirements may be relevant to evaluating flight risk and the suitability of alternatives. Such circumstances do not guarantee release, but the Committee's interpretation does not permit them to be dismissed merely because the individual falls within a statutory immigration category.

Detention duration also affects the assessment. Custody initially justified for immigration purposes may become arbitrary when its continuation lacks sufficient reasons, proceedings experience excessive delay, or removal becomes unrealistic. The applicable evaluation concerns the actual detention and the grounds advanced to justify it, not simply the passage of a predetermined number of days.

The three Fifth Circuit petitioners were detained for considerably shorter periods than the individuals in A v. Australia and F.K.A.G. and Others v. Australia. Their periods of confinement do not automatically establish either compliance or violation. A case-specific international assessment would require sufficient evidence concerning the justification for detention, available alternatives, and whether the authorities adequately examined the continued need for custody.

A categorical policy applied without such assessment is difficult to reconcile with the Human Rights Committee's interpretation of Article 9(1). That conclusion concerns the potential incompatibility of detention practices with the Covenant; it does not establish that every individual affected by the policy experienced an identical violation.

7.2 Whether Habeas Review Provides Adequate Protection

Article 9(4) requires access to judicial proceedings capable of deciding the lawfulness of detention and ordering release when detention is unlawful. The existence of federal habeas corpus proceedings is relevant to assessing American compliance. It demonstrates that the denial of an ordinary administrative bond hearing does not necessarily eliminate all judicial avenues for challenging confinement.

The three petitioners obtained relief through federal habeas proceedings before the Fifth Circuit reversed the district courts. Their litigation demonstrates the availability of a judicial forum for certain constitutional challenges to immigration detention. The appellate judgment rejected the particular claims presented; it did not hold that every future challenge to detention under § 1225(b)(2)(A) falls outside federal judicial jurisdiction.

The scope of review remains decisive. Under the Human Rights Committee's interpretation, Article 9(4) requires an effective remedy for detention incompatible with the Covenant, including substantive arbitrariness under Article 9(1). Judicial proceedings limited to confirming statutory classification may be inadequate if they cannot address continued confinement that lacks sufficient justification under the international standard.

American habeas review can provide protection against detention exceeding statutory authority or violating enforceable constitutional requirements. The Fifth Circuit also recognized that different due process claims may arise when detention no longer serves a legitimate immigration purpose or removal becomes practically unattainable. Such proceedings could provide meaningful relief in circumstances beyond those considered in the October judgment.

However, constitutional standards recognized by American courts and the Human Rights Committee's interpretation of Article 9 are not necessarily identical. A federal remedy may be effective for particular domestic claims without encompassing every circumstance in which continued detention would be arbitrary under the Covenant.

The absence of a bond hearing is consequently not conclusive of an Article 9(4) violation. The more precise inquiry is whether an affected detainee has access to an independent judicial procedure capable of examining the relevant grounds of unlawfulness and ordering release when those grounds are established.

7.3 The Legal Limits of the October 23 Judgment

The Fifth Circuit resolved a constitutional dispute concerning the three petitioners' requested custody hearings and the detention periods presented in their cases. It did not adjudicate the international lawfulness of mandatory ICE detention. No determination by the Human Rights Committee or another international body has established that this particular October 23 judgment violated the ICCPR.

That absence of international adjudication does not itself establish compliance. State responsibility may arise where conduct attributable to a state breaches an applicable international obligation, irrespective of whether a competent international institution has already issued a finding. The existence and scope of any violation must nevertheless be demonstrated through the governing legal standard and relevant facts.

The distinction between domestic statutory authorization, constitutional permissibility, and international treaty compliance is particularly important while the Supreme Court considers Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha. A ruling narrowing § 1225(b)(2)(A) could change the domestic detention regime and restore access to ordinary bond procedures for affected individuals. It would not eliminate the independent requirements of Article 9 or determine whether previous detentions complied with the Covenant.

Conversely, Supreme Court acceptance of the government's statutory interpretation would not conclusively establish international lawfulness. A congressional mandate may resolve which domestic detention provision applies while leaving unresolved whether continued confinement is sufficiently justified and subject to adequate judicial review under international human rights law.

Neither Article 9 nor General Comment No. 35 establishes an automatic international entitlement to an immigration bond hearing after 90 days. The earlier Fifth Circuit panel's proposed 90-day constitutional rule was vacated. Similarly, the six-month presumption discussed in Zadvydas v. Davis arose from a distinct statutory and constitutional context involving post-removal-order detention and cannot be converted into a universal limit applicable to every immigration proceeding.

The strongest basis for an international legal objection concerns a detention practice that treats admission status as sufficient justification for continued confinement, does not adequately assess individual necessity, and fails to provide judicial review capable of addressing substantive unlawfulness. Such a practice raises substantial concerns under Article 9 as interpreted by the Human Rights Committee.

A determination concerning particular detainees requires closer examination of their circumstances. The relevant evidence includes the purposes served by detention, its duration, individual risks, alternatives, and the scope of available remedies. Without that assessment, the legal consequences of the October ruling cannot properly be characterized as an established violation affecting every person subject to mandatory detention.

Conclusion

The Fifth Circuit's October 23, 2026, ruling rejected a constitutional entitlement to individualized ICE bond hearings for three long-term undocumented residents detained under § 1225(b)(2)(A). The judgment reversed their habeas relief but did not establish that every detention authorized under the provision complies with international law. Article 9 of the ICCPR imposes separate obligations concerning arbitrary deprivation of liberty and effective judicial review.

The Fifth Circuit decision creates a substantial question about the compatibility of categorical immigration detention practices with the United States' obligations under Article 9. Establishing a particular violation requires evidence that the detention lacked sufficient legal justification or effective judicial protection under the applicable international standard. The October judgment leaves that international question unresolved.
