text:
Introduction

On October 14, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland denied a preliminary injunction against Executive Order 14398, permitting the Administration’s March 2026 order related to federal contractor diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices to remain in effect while litigation proceeds. Unlike the earlier litigation involving Executive Orders 14151 and 14173, where courts initially enjoined certain provisions based on concerns regarding vagueness and overbreadth, the court declined to issue similar relief here.

Background

Executive Order 14398 and Enforcement Efforts

On March 26, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order (EO) 14398 – “Addressing DEI Discrimination by Federal Contractors.” Exec. Order No. 14398, 91 Fed. Reg. 16,147 (Mar. 26, 2026). The EO requires covered contractors to agree that, in connection with the performance of work under a federal contract, they will not engage in “racially discriminatory DEI activities.” In turn, the EO defines such activities as “disparate treatment based on race or ethnicity” in recruitment, employment, contracting, program participation, or the allocation or deployment of an entity’s resources. Furthermore, the EO directs federal agencies to implement these restrictions in the federal awards. Section 3 of the EO outlines six requirements, and perhaps most significantly, the order provides that compliance with its requirements is material to the government’s payment decisions, creating a potential False Claims Act (FCA) hook for contractors.1 We have previously covered this executive order and recent FCA settlements relating to allegedly discriminatory DEI-related practices here. These FCA settlements and other more recent ones have made it clear that federal enforcement in this area is aggressive and ongoing.

In April 2026, contracting agencies were directed to include the requirements of EO 14398 in new procurements as described in a Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council Memorandum (FAR Memorandum). The FAR Memorandum directed agencies to incorporate the new contract clause, FAR 52.222-90, into covered new procurements and to make every effort to modify covered existing contracts through bilateral modifications to include the same requirements.2 The clause also requires flowing its requirements down to subcontractors at all tiers.3

Of course, EO 14398 is not the first of its kind to target federal contractor DEI-related practices related to federal procurement. At the beginning of 2025, the Administration issued Executive Orders 14151 and 14173, which similarly sought to restrict certain, arguably broader, DEI-related activities. Those orders were promptly challenged in federal courts, with plaintiffs arguing, among other things, that they were impermissibly broad and failed to define key terms such as “DEI,” “equity-related,” and “illegal DEI.”4 Litigation challenging these two executive orders is ongoing and has yielded mixed results at the district court and circuit court levels.5 However, these provisions may be enforced pending further litigation after the Fourth Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction that had blocked portions of Executive Orders 14151 and 14173.6

Court Challenge to EO 14398

Shortly after EO 14398’s issuance, as expected, a case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland challenging the order and seeking a preliminary injunction. See National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 8:26-cv-01532 (D. Md. Apr. 20, 2026). The complaint asserted multiple grounds, including that the executive order is unconstitutional and violated, among other things, the First Amendment as overbroad and is impermissibly vague under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The complaint also alleged that the FAR Memorandum violated the Administrative Procedure Act because it did not comply with the required rulemaking procedures. If granted, the preliminary injunction would have preliminarily prevented enforcement of the challenged provisions of EO 14398 and stayed the related FAR Council guidance while the litigation proceeded.7

On October 14, 2026, the court denied the plaintiffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction. National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 26-cv-1532-ABA (D. Md. Oct. 14, 2026). The court’s central conclusion was straightforward: the court found that the EO was sufficiently clear as to what conduct it prohibits and therefore concluded that plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed on the merits of their challenge. In its order, the court emphasized that EO 14398 “only prohibits contractors from engaging in conduct that is already prohibited by federal law: intentional discrimination based on race or ethnicity.” The court based its analysis on the Executive Order’s definition of “racially discriminatory DEI activities” as “disparate treatment based on race or ethnicity.” The court further reasoned that “disparate treatment” is a well-established legal term of art and therefore should be interpreted according to its settled legal meaning (since the court noted that there is no evidence that the Executive Order intended otherwise). Accordingly, the court rejected plaintiffs’ argument that the phrase was impermissibly broad or that it reached virtually all race-related contractor speech.

Contractor Takeaways

The court's refusal to grant a preliminary injunction is notable given prior district court decisions related to the earlier, and arguably broader, DEI-related executive orders from 2025. Unlike Executive Orders 14151 and 14173, portions of which were initially enjoined at the district-court level based on concerns regarding vagueness and undefined terms, EO 14398 survived the preliminary injunction stage in this most recent district court decision. Although not a final ruling on the merits, the decision suggests that the court viewed EO 14398 as more narrowly tailored and less susceptible to the ambiguity concerns that drove the earlier injunctions. As a result, contractors should expect the government to continue enforcing the order and its associated contract requirements.

More broadly, the implementation and enforcement of EO 14398 will continue. The contractual requirements implementing the EO are being incorporated into new and already awarded federal contracts and subcontracts, and the government enforcement efforts in this area have yielded multiple False Claims Act settlements and promise additional investigation and enforcement going forward.

As has been the case since early 2025, contractors should continue to carefully evaluate their DEI programs (particularly as related to the limitations and restrictions imposed by EO 14398). In light of the evolving legal landscape, regularly reviewing internal practices for compliance and closely monitoring developments in the pending litigation will be crucial for mitigating risk and preparing for potential enforcement activity. The decision provides some clarity regarding the conduct prohibited by the Executive Order, but only time will tell what will ultimately be expected of contractors in practice.

1 Memorandum on Agency Implementation of Executive Order 14398, Addressing DEI Discrimination by Federal Contractors, Federal Acquisition Regulation Council (Apr. 17, 2026). Other requirements include: (1) prohibiting contractors from engaging in “racially discriminatory DEI activities;” (2) requiring contractors to provide information, records, and access to books and accounts to demonstrate compliance; (3) permitting contract cancellation, termination, or restrictions on future contracting for noncompliance; (4) requiring contractors to report known or reasonably knowable subcontractor violations and take any remedial actions directed by the government; and (5) requiring contractors to notify the government if a subcontractor challenges the validity of the clause in court.

2 Memorandum on Agency Implementation of Executive Order 14398 at 2 (“In accordance with FAR 1.107(d) (May 2, 2025 deviation), contracting officers must make every effort to bilaterally modify existing contracts by July 24, 2026. If a contractor refuses to agree to a bilateral modification, the contracting officer should consider whether, absent the modification, the contract no longer meets the agency’s needs and should therefore be terminated for convenience.”) (emphasis added).

3 Id. at 9; FAR 52.222-90(c) (“The Contractor must include the substance of this clause, including this paragraph (c), in subcontracts at any tier, including those for commercial products and commercial services, for which the place of delivery or performance is in the United States.”).

4 In some cases, district courts have granted preliminary injunctive relief and expressed concern that the lack of clear definitions left federal contractors and grant recipients unable to determine what conduct was prohibited, creating uncertainty regarding compliance obligations and raising constitutional concerns regarding vagueness and protected speech. See, e.g., National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education et al. v. Trump, Case No. 1:25-cv-00333 (D. Md. Feb. 21, 2025); Chicago Women in Trades v. Trump, 778 F. Supp. 3d 959 (N.D. Ill. 2025). Notably, the district court injunction in Chicago Women in Trades was narrower than the Maryland injunction, applying only to enforcement of the Certification Provision of EO 14173, whereas the Maryland court enjoined several challenged provisions of EO 14151 and EO 14173.

5 See, e.g., National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education et al. v. Trump, Case No. 1:25-cv-00333 (D. Md. Feb. 21, 2025), preliminary injunction vacated by National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, 167 F.4th 86 (4th Cir. 2026); Chicago Women in Trades v. Trump, 778 F. Supp. 3d 959 (N.D. Ill. 2025), appeal pending, No. 25-2144 (7th Cir.).

6 National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump,167 F.4th 86 (4th Cir. 2026). On February 6, 2026, the Fourth Circuit vacated the Maryland preliminary injunction, concluding that the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed on their facial constitutional challenges, while leaving open the possibility of challenges to particular applications of the orders.

description:
In recent weeks, Woodward at times has positioned himself as the Justice Department political appointee who could shield career Justice Department attorneys caught between the administration’s controversial positions and frustrated federal judges.
Chief legal punching bag The prominent role Woodward has taken defending Trump’s wishes in court has, at times, made him the administration’s chief legal punching bag — including among critics of Justice Department leadership on the right.
During Woodward’s daylong appearance in Reyes’ courtroom Monday, he was surrounded by no less than eight other Justice Department lawyers and officials in court.
He jumped in several times when Reyes was grilling a greener, career-level Justice Department attorney about the administration’s handling of the case.
A Justice Department spokesperson later clarified that Woodward does meet and speak to Trump, just not regarding official executive privilege assertions.
text:
President Donald Trump said on Friday he wanted an election-related lawsuit to be filed in Alaska.

The man to do it for him was Stanley Woodward, the associate attorney general.

Holding the third highest ranking job at the Justice Department and having never appeared in federal court in Alaska before, Woodward has taken on that case’s unusual task — a fight to potentially block election certification if the incumbent Republican candidate loses — with little apparent help from other parts of his agency. (One assistant US attorney submitted and signed the filing under Woodward.)

In other administrations — and even in prior months — election litigation hasn’t come from the associate attorney general’s office.

Yet the Alaska lawsuit capped a week where Woodward, a longtime DC attorney, had hustled to the forefront of the president’s personal agenda.

Earlier in the week, he spent a full day in court arguing what government witnesses could share in testimony about Trump’s plans for a golf course in Washington, DC. His argument and filings have lately echoed Trump’s frustration with some federal judges.

In recent weeks, Woodward at times has positioned himself as the Justice Department political appointee who could shield career Justice Department attorneys caught between the administration’s controversial positions and frustrated federal judges.

“It’s difficult to put my colleague in a position of contradicting the president,” he told a judge in Washington, DC, at the golf course hearing Monday, where he played clean up after a lower-level DOJ attorney struggled to square the government’s arguments with what Trump had said publicly about the case.

He was ordered to attend the hearing by Judge Ana Reyes after he was the sole signer of a court submission that responded to her yelling at a previous hearing because of the Justice Department’s handling of the case.

A longtime defense lawyer with ample trial-court experience after the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot and during the federal investigations into Donald Trump, Woodward landed in the Justice Department about a year ago, after serving as a White House attorney for Trump. Prior to Trump’s reelection, he had already been in the inner circle of lawyers around the president, personally representing Trump associates in the January 6 and classified documents criminal conspiracy investigations between 2021 and 2024. His clients have included now-FBI Director Kash Patel, and White House advisers Dan Scavino and Peter Navarro.

His work at the time gained notoriety and respect among several judges in the DC District Court for how frequently he was appearing before them.

Yet the persona has shifted this year, as Woodward has increasingly signed more extreme court filings, including ones that have mimicked Trump’s personal tone, in a case challenging the construction of the East Wing ballroom.

Woodward signed a court filing in April that said what the legal challengers were doing was “very bad for our country,” and that the plaintiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation, had “a beautiful name, but even their name is FAKE.”

“This is a terrible, tremendously harmful case to the United States of America, and all it stands for!” Woodward also wrote to the court in the ballroom litigation.

More recently, Woodward has been especially critical of judges who have been making moves to rein in Trump administration priorities.

Woodward last weekend submitted a filing to Reyes asking for her recusal in the golf course case — a challenge to Trump’s plans to turn the course, which is accessible to the public at a modest price, to a more exclusive, championship-level venue. Woodward argued that the judge’s heated reaction to a sudden move by the administrations to cut down hundreds of trees showed a bias against the administration, and that her demeanor on the bench exhibited “histrionics.”

And on Tuesday, in unrelated cases in Minnesota, Woodward took aim at two different senior judges who are overseeing federal court cases for immigrants. The requests that senior judges Patrick Schlitz and John Tunheim recuse because of recent comments they made in the press that were critical of the administration’s immigration enforcement mirrored how Woodward approached Reyes by submitting the court filings separately from other Justice Department attorneys involved in the cases.

“The American people must be able to trust the impartiality of our Nation’s judges. Unfortunately, some judges have breached that trust … This [Justice Department] will not let that stand,” Woodward posted on the social media site X on Wednesday.

Chief legal punching bag

The prominent role Woodward has taken defending Trump’s wishes in court has, at times, made him the administration’s chief legal punching bag — including among critics of Justice Department leadership on the right.

Last week, the prominent far-right influencer and Trump ally Laura Loomer repeatedly attacked Woodward for his shepherding of cases over veterans’ claims and settlements following decades of water contamination in the 20th century at the US Marine Corps base Camp Lejeune.

Loomer has frequently pointed out that Woodward has past ties to Democrats as a lawyer in Washington.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has publicly defended him several times.

Blanche worked alongside Woodward on legal defenses around Trump in 2023 and 2024, where the now-attorney general represented Trump personally and Woodward represented a co-defendant —Trump’s aide Walt Nauta — in the classified documents case.

“You are dead wrong about Stanley,” Blanche wrote to Loomer Tuesday on his official X account. “He is a patriot who is fighting for POTUS and the American people every day … Find a different obsession other than going after one of DOJ’s best fighters.”

A Justice Department spokesperson said the department and Woodward’s work on Camp Lejeune settlements and efforts to protect veterans are “in lock step” with the Pentagon and the White House.

Woodward didn’t comment for this story

Amid the attorney general’s defending Woodward from attacks from the conservatives, Woodward has continued to attempt to maintain his place in the DC legal community, which largely leans liberal.

This spring, he attended the retreat for the lawyers and judges of the DC federal courts, called the Circuit Conference, in Williamsburg, Virginia. His attendance surprised many of the lawyers there.

People who attended social events with Woodward in the evenings told CNN they witnessed him trying to chat with former Biden administration Associate Attorney General Vanita Gupta. But he also took flack in person from Matt Olsen, a former top national security attorney in Democratic administrations, who indicated to Woodward he thought he was a disgrace to his job. Both Olsen and Gupta declined to comment.

A Justice Department spokesperson responded to questions about those interactions by saying “being called a disgrace by a top deep state lawyer,” meaning Olsen, “should be viewed as a badge of honor” and that Woodward “of course can have respectful conversation with the former associate attorney general,” meaning Gupta.

Redefining the role

The traditional role of the associate attorney general has been to oversee civil litigation handled by Justice Department headquarters in Washington, as well as cases related to the environment and natural resources, government approval of corporate mergers and tax-related matters.

“The associate position is one where the individual can have a pretty large say in how they execute the authority. There’s obviously a lot of civil litigation attorneys under the associate’s supervisory chain,” said Ed O’Callaghan, who served as a top Justice Department official during the first Trump administration.

“What I see him doing is saying, I am the top political appointee below the attorney general itself to argue the policies of the administration.”

O’Callaghan noted that some associate attorneys general in the past have argued in court at their choosing, as Woodward is doing now, including Kevin O’Connor in the George W. Bush administration, who regularly appeared in federal appellate court arguments.

“It’s not easy to do,” O’Callaghan added.

During Woodward’s daylong appearance in Reyes’ courtroom Monday, he was surrounded by no less than eight other Justice Department lawyers and officials in court.

He jumped in several times when Reyes was grilling a greener, career-level Justice Department attorney about the administration’s handling of the case.

“Someone is going to have to take responsibility for what is said in court,” Reyes said later in the all-day hearing on Monday after a Justice Department lawyer was unable or unwilling to answer Reyes’ questions.

Woodward jumped up and walked toward the front of the courtroom, ignoring the requirement to speak into a microphone.

“That’s why I’m here! He knows the law. Yell at me, not him,” he told Reyes.

The associate attorney general also took the lead objecting to questions posed to officials from the administration as they were asked to testify about conversations they may have had with government lawyers, or with the president himself.

At one point in the hearing, Woodward had objected so many times — citing executive privilege, confidentiality around government deliberations, or attorney-client communications — that he barely stood up from his chair to interject, staring at the counsel’s table in front of him as he listened.

“I’m sorry, your Honor,” Woodward said, apologizing for interrupting, hunched over and still looking down.

“Ok, you’re getting good at this,” Reyes said, referring to his success in shielding witnesses from answering, and without looking at him, she sustained his objection. The judge moved on to the next question.

At another point in the hearing, Woodward scrambled to object to questions lawyer Abbe Lowell was asking Department of Interior official Gregory Wischer, who visited the East Potomac golf course property with Trump and others in June.

Woodward noted he knew the case law around executive privilege because of his work on White House adviser Peter Navarro’s criminal contempt of Congress case in 2023, as he and Reyes discussed whether he would get a letter from the White House formally asserting privilege in the golf course litigation.

“I don’t speak to the president directly,” Woodward told the judge.

A Justice Department spokesperson later clarified that Woodward does meet and speak to Trump, just not regarding official executive privilege assertions.

CNN’s Evan Perez, Catherine Shoichet and Kit Maher contributed to this report.

text:
Walking into a green card interview in downtown Minneapolis, William Lizardo expected to take another step towards citizenship.

Instead, the Canadian-born dentist and father left in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

Lauren Lizardo, Will Lizardo's wife, said she learned what happened through their attorney, who was present at the interview and for the detainment.

"It was my worst fear that I never thought would happen and now it's happening," she said.

Lauren Lizardo said that she never thought it would happen because she believed she and her husband had done everything right. The pair met at the University of Minnesota School of Dentistry and got married shortly after graduation. They now have an 18-month-old baby girl.

Lauren Lizardo said she helped sponsor Will Lizardo as he applied for a green card. In January of this year, they learned that he had been denied. While he hasn't been allowed to work, Lauren Lizardo said that her husband has been volunteering at a low-cost dental clinic in Burnsville, Minnesota. At the time, Lizardo didn't think it would be an issue. They didn't have the money post-graduation to apply with an attorney, but they decided to take a second crack at it with legal representation.

"We thought we were doing everything right; the attorney said we were doing everything right. He said we would have no problem getting a green card," Lauren Lizardo said.

The attorney, David Whalen, told WCCO that when it came to achieving a green card, Will was "probably the best candidate I'd ever had."

Whalen said he was with Will Lizardo on Friday when the woman interviewing him stood up at the end of the conversation, left the room and returned with two ICE agents.

"It's very straightforward that they [the government] screwed up," Whalen said.

According to Lauren Lizardo, she and her husband learned for the first time on Friday that there was actually an order for deportation for Will Lizardo. It came after he didn't respond to a notice to appear before an immigration judge. Lauren Lizardo said that the federal government had sent the notice back in February to a Virginia address that they hadn't lived at for more than two years.

"We had no way of knowing there was this notice to appear, but they still detained him because he didn't appear to something we didn't know was happening," Lizardo said.

Lauren Lizardo explained that they have been meticulous with their record-keeping and check an online immigration portal related to Will Lizardo's case daily. She said that he has seen immigration officials in recent months for fingerprinting and that they receive official communications from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services at their current address in Victoria, Minnesota. But no one has brought up anything about a deportation order or appearance notice, according to her.

As of Friday night, ICE, which commands the largest law enforcement budget in the country, has not acknowledged WCCO's request for information about what happened.

Whalen said Friday that they would be filing an emergency motion for Will Lizardo's release. Lauren Lizardo is left to wonder what comes next and when she'll get to see her husband.

"I want a fair chance and I want to be treated with compassion and kindness. I feel like I haven't been given that opportunity, and Will hasn't either," Lauren Lizardo said.

title: Courts Reject Trump's Attempt at Deploying ICE to Intimidate Voters | Truthout
authors: Zack Kligler, Mike Ludwig, Sasha Abramsky, Tyler Walicek, Jessica Corbett, Bruno Malheiro, Simón Rodríguez, Shahad Ali, Chris Walker, Kenny Bruno
description:
Feds Investigate Voters, Non-Profit Groups Janovsky said sending agents door-to-door in states where Republicans face headwinds could suppress turnout.
With billions of dollars in funding from Congress, the Trump administration has transformed ICE into a powerful tool of intimidation.
ICE agents have injured and killed people in multiple high-profile cases since Donald Trump took office again.
Under Trump’s mass deportation campaign, ICE has detained at least 506 U.S. citizens as well as many legal permanent residents.
Activists are preparing for the potential deployment of ICE agents to the polls, which Trump officials have said is not a priority but also could not be ruled out.
text:
The Trump administration is attempting to intimidate Latino voters and naturalized citizens with the threat of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and arrests ahead of the midterm elections, democracy advocates are warning.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has deployed federal agents in multiple states to knock on doors and demand voters verify their identities and registration as part of an “Unlawful Voter Initiative” launched in August. In response to a lawsuit filed on October 19 by labor and voting rights groups, a federal judge in California ruled the DHS initiative violates the Voting Rights Act and ordered federal agents to halt “elections-related field operations and field interviews” in California, Wisconsin, New York, Missouri, Connecticut, Nevada, Georgia, Pennsylvania, and Washington.

“I look at this list of states, and I can think of some high-profile races that may be anticipated to be close in a lot of those jurisdictions,” said David Janovsky, senior policy analyst and acting director of the Constitution Project at the Project On Government Oversight, in an interview. “So, I think there is a reasonable question in all of this about how the federal government is choosing to focus these efforts, and the motivation that is behind that.”

Critical contests in these states include the tight race between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia, which could decide which party has a majority in the Senate. In California, New York, and beyond, multiple races could help to determine control of the House or pad a Democratic majority.

Feds Investigate Voters, Non-Profit Groups

Janovsky said sending agents door-to-door in states where Republicans face headwinds could suppress turnout. Indeed, since the 2024 election, polls suggest that Latinos and many other voters turned against the GOP as ICE invaded major cities such as Chicago and Minneapolis, causing chaos, fear, and death.

By deploying federal immigration agents to go door-to-door hunting for so-called “voter fraud” ahead of Election Day, the Trump administration may also be preparing the ground for meddling with election results and suppressing dissent if Republicans perform poorly and lose their congressional majority.

With billions of dollars in funding from Congress, the Trump administration has transformed ICE into a powerful tool of intimidation. ICE agents have injured and killed people in multiple high-profile cases since Donald Trump took office again. Under Trump’s mass deportation campaign, ICE has detained at least 506 U.S. citizens as well as many legal permanent residents. People arrested by ICE are often jailed in facilities where dozens have died amid complaints of medical neglect, including a lawful permanent resident who was found dead in a Texas ICE jail last week.

Trump’s Justice Department has been trying for over a year to get voter rolls from every state and hand them over to DHS investigators searching for evidence of widespread fraud that experts say does not exist. DHS uses voter data to create “target lists” of potentially fraudulent voter registrations, according to Wednesday’s court order.

“With Homeland Security agents knocking on people’s doors asking them if they are properly registered to vote, there is a very real concern, and it’s pretty well known, that the federal government doesn’t have accurate data,” Janovsky said. “It could freak people out, like, ‘maybe I don’t want to register to vote and put myself on this list.’”

Under an executive order issued in May 2025, the Department of Justice demanded voter rolls from states to share with DHS so agents could scour for non-citizens attempting to vote, which is exceedingly rare. States run elections, not the federal government, but many red states handed voter data over voluntarily. Another 26 states, including those named in Wednesday’s order, saw lawsuits filed by the Justice Department over voter rolls dismissed by federal courts.

“That effort has largely been rejected by the courts, because basically the federal government has no real business micromanaging every state’s voter rolls,” Janovsky said.

Unable to force states to hand over voter data, DHS gathered more than 48 million voter records through independent and commercial sources “of questionable provenance” in order to search for potential fraud, according to Wednesday’s ruling. DHS records obtained by Democracy Forward under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) link these efforts to Heather Honey, a prominent 2020 election denier who has supplied Trump with conspiracy theories and is currently serving as a senior advisor to DHS and ICE.

The FOIA records also reveal that the Trump administration considered sending undercover agents to investigate pro-democracy groups that register people to vote, particularly in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

Critically, the court order halting the DHS door-knocking initiative highlights the significant likelihood that such investigations would result in errors and the misidentification of citizens as non-citizens, potentially preventing them from voting, according to Elizabeth Laird, director of equity at the Center for Democracy & Technology.

“This decision continues to establish the legal basis that it is not only unethical but illegal to weaponize personal data in ways that lead to irreparable harm to individuals who are wrongly targeted,” Laird said in a statement on Thursday.

While Laird said the initial ruling is a promising step forward, the case underscores the “significant dangers” of the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to compile and weaponize personal information from across federal and state agencies.”

“That is the high-level problem,” Janovsky said of the administration’s exploitation of voter data. “Then you have these targeted enforcement operations happening in a handful of states, including California.”

ICE and DOJ Ramp Up Arrests

California may be a testing ground of sorts, Janovsky said. Immigrant advocates have confirmed a rapid increase of ICE arrests in the Central Valley and beyond, with more than 100 farmworkers arrested last week alone. As California’s KQED reports, fear and rumors spread whenever ICE conducts large enforcement operations. People stay home as a result, causing Latino businesses to suffer, schoolchildren to miss classes, and patients to forgo seeing the doctors.

Advocates warn the Trump administration is betting that ICE could keep Latino voters away from the polls as well, but Democratic California Rep. Lateefah Simon says the intimidation campaign will not work. Indeed, election officials are seeing a surge of interest in early voting, with 21 million people casting early ballots as of Friday morning, NPR reports.

“We know what Republicans are trying to do — intimidate Latino citizens so they stay at home and don’t exercise their right to vote,” said Simon in a statement to local media on October 16.

Activists are preparing for the potential deployment of ICE agents to the polls, which Trump officials have said is not a priority but also could not be ruled out. In Arizona, the grassroots LUCHA coalition has trained hundreds of volunteer “constitutional defenders” to respond to federal intimidation if it were to occur on Election Day, according to communications director César Fierros.

“Masked agents in tactical gear threatening people in line or attempting to raid polling locations would be an assault on democracy itself, and it’s the greatest threat facing our nation,” Fierros told Truthout in an email. “We are preparing, but hoping for the best.”

On Monday, the Justice Department announced it was charging 28 non-citizens in California with election crimes, a development Janovsky is watching closely. On October 15, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against California that asks a federal court to order California officials to stop processing ballots from thousands of people the Trump administration identifies as “likely non-citizens.”

Before filing the lawsuit, federal officials delivered a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them for fraudulent voter registrations. When local and state officials refused to do so, citing security concerns and potentially faulty data, Trump wrote online that, “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”

The administration’s data has already proven to be faulty in the neighboring state of Nevada, where DHS officials recently claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote on state rolls. However, that number fell to 185 after further inquiry, and then to zero after state officials confirmed that those individuals were all U.S. citizens.

While Janovsky said the circumstances surrounding the charges of election crimes against 28 individuals are unclear, the Trump administration has consistently claimed to be fighting widespread voter fraud that does not exist — but such enforcement backs up bogus claims about fraud that Trump has made since losing the 2020 election.

“It’s entirely possible that some of these folks are citizens who were properly registered to vote and the feds have bad data — and that is the basis for the court injunction issued on Wednesday,” Janovsky said.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court will hear several cases during its current nine-month term.

Here’s a look at some of them; rulings are expected by the end of June.

1. Climate suit

The justices heard arguments Oct. 5 in a bid by ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colo. The companies appealed after Colorado's top court allowed Boulder's lawsuit, which seeks monetary damages and accuses the companies of violating state law. The Trump administration backed the companies. The justices voiced concerns about unduly limiting states’ authority to pursue climate-related litigation, as well as the potential to unleash chaos if local governments across the country were permitted to sue these companies.

2. Immigration detention

The court will decide the legality of President Donald Trump's policy that subjects millions of immigrants in the U.S. illegally to mandatory detention during deportation proceedings. The justices took up the Trump administration's appeal of a lower court's ruling against the policy in a case involving a Brazilian national. The administration abandoned the longstanding interpretation of federal law that immigrants living in the U.S. could be released on bond while their cases play out in immigration court. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

3, Deportations

The justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own — so-called "third countries" — without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. On Sept. 29, the court paused a federal judge's ruling that deemed removing migrants to third countries unlawful. More than 25,000 migrants were deported to 29 countries under the policy, according to human rights groups.

4. Asylum and terrorism

The court will hear the Trump administration's bid to deny asylum to a ​man who was forced to prepare meals for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen, which U.S. officials considered to be a terrorist organization, in Nigeria — a case that could expand what officials ‌may deem terrorist activity under U.S. immigration law. The Justice Department appealed a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba that said cooking did ​not qualify as "material support" for terrorism. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

5. Firearms

The justices will hear arguments Dec. 2 in a challenge to the legality of state prohibitions on assault-style rifles, another chance to expand gun rights in a case that ​involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings. Lower courts upheld bans on powerful ‌semiautomatic rifles, such as AR-15s, in Cook County, Ill., and Connecticut. The lower courts rejected arguments that the measures violate the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and bear arms." Gun rights groups and other challengers said Supreme Court precedents concerning the ​Second Amendment protect these firearms, which they described as in "common use."

6. Voting rights

The justices will hear arguments Dec. 8 in a Republican-led bid to revive voter restrictions in Arizona that would stiffen proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registrants ‌and purge state voter rolls of alleged noncitizens. Republicans appealed after a lower court halted provisions of Arizona's law because they were found to violate a federal voting registration statute. Critics said the Arizona measure adds extra mandates for voting ​that unfairly target Latino, Native American and student voters. Those groups tend to favor Democratic candidates.

7. Race in admissions

The justices will consider whether to revive a lawsuit against a Maryland county's lottery admissions policy for four elite public middle ​schools that some parents claim unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants. The case has the court delving again into the contentious issue of race in student admissions. A coalition of parents appealed a lower court's decision rejecting their claim that Montgomery County's policy violates the U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment guarantee of equal protection under the law. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

8. LGBTQ+ rights

The justices will hear arguments Nov. 3 in a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver ​and other Catholic entities to be exempted from a Colorado preschool funding program's ‌nondiscrimination requirement. The Catholic plaintiffs objected to the state's requirement ⁠that schools receiving funding under the program give all children "equal opportunity" to enroll in preschool regardless ​of certain characteristics, including the sexual orientation or gender identity of students or their family members. A lower court found the program did not violate ​the religious rights of the plaintiffs under the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment.

9. DOGE

The justices will decide whether the Trump administration can avoid handing over records to a watchdog group about its Department of Government Efficiency, an initiative that slashing agency budgets and workers spearheaded last year by the president's former adviser Elon Musk. The administration appealed a judge's order for DOGE to respond to requests by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington for information about its operations. The judge found DOGE likely is a government agency covered by the federal Freedom of Information Act, or FOIA. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

10. Home distilling ban

The court will decide the legality of a federal ban on ​home distilling of alcoholic spirits enacted in 1868 to crack down on liquor tax evasion. The dispute pits the Trump administration, which defends the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds Congress’ authority under the U.S. Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states backed the legal challenge ​to the statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

11. Apple suit

Justices will hear Apple's bid to escape being found in contempt ​in its legal fight with "Fortnite" maker Epic Games after the iPhone maker was deemed in violation of a ‌judicial order mandating sweeping changes to its App Store in the antitrust litigation. Apple appealed a lower court's ruling upholding a decision by an Oakland, California-based federal judge finding Apple in contempt in Epic's 2020 lawsuit contesting App Store fees. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

12. PepsiCo trademark

The court will hear arguments in a bid by ​canned-coffee maker Rise Brewing to hold PepsiCo liable for alleged trademark infringement ‌concerning Pepsi's morning energy drink "Mtn Dew Rise." Rise appealed a lower court's ruling rejecting the company's claim that the product name "Mtn Dew Rise" infringes its trademarks and creates customer confusion with ​its coffee brand. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced.

title: Trump administration can hold immigrants in ICE custody without bond, court rules - San ...
authors: Uriel J. García, The Texas Tribune, Uriel J. García, The Texas Tribune
description:
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.
Friday’s ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.
A policy change by the Trump administration Under federal immigration laws, the government can quickly deport undocumented immigrants who recently crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without giving them a chance for a bond hearing.
Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.
The Trump administration appealed some of the cases to higher courts, leading to conflicting rulings.
text:
Immigrants who entered the country illegally don’t have a right to seek bond while they’re in custody and going through deportation proceedings, even if they’ve set roots in the U.S., a federal appeals court ruled Friday.

In a 10-7 ruling, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled that current immigration laws allow the federal government to hold detained immigrants until they’re deported — regardless of whether they have made a life in the U.S. and lack a criminal history.

Trump-appointed Judge Cory Wilson wrote in the court’s ruling that if undocumented immigrants have not been legally admitted to the U.S., they are only entitled to whatever rights Congress has spelled out in immigration laws. He added that if undocumented immigrants in custody want to be free from detention, “they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country.”

In a concurring opinion, Judge Andrew Oldham agreed.

“Because such aliens remain legally unadmitted, they receive exactly the same due process rights that they would have if they had come through a legal port of entry — which are whatever rights Congress chooses to give them,” Oldham wrote.

Judge Leslie Southwick, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote in his dissent that the ruling has created an “impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents.”

Rebecca Cassler, senior litigation attorney at the American Immigration Council, who argued the case before the 5th Circuit, said the court’s ruling is an attack on constitutional due process rights, which have been guaranteed to anyone living in the U.S., regardless of immigration status.

“The right to due process is a fundamental constitutional protection, and it is meant to protect every person in this country. Because of today’s decision, that right is hollow for immigrants in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi,” she said. “But the logic of the 5th Circuit’s decision threatens everyone in this country: When courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences.”

Mass deportation efforts

The case stems from the arrest of three men in Texas by state troopers between November 2025 and February 2026 during routine traffic stops. All three have lived in the country for at least 14 years, worked during that time and have children who are American citizens. The troopers turned the men over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who held them in detention without allowing them to see a judge.

Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, Miguel Angel Gomez Alvarado and Alejandro Villegas Angel were eventually released from ICE custody after federal judges found that holding them without a chance for a bond hearing violated the men’s due process rights. The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.

Friday’s ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.

“Big win in the Fifth Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens, a principle codified in 1996 legislation but ignored by the deep state for decades,” James Percival, a lawyer in the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said on social media, referring to Clinton administration immigration law that expanded the list of immigrants who can be more easily deported.

‘Rejecting due process’

Gracie Willis, an attorney with the National Immigration Project, which is representing the three Texas men, said the general public should be concerned that a federal court believes the government can hold people indefinitely without justification.

“We look at this case as an affront to due process, as the 5th Circuit rejecting due process,” Willis said. “It’s really a shocking extension of this attempt to criminalize immigrants and to hold immigrants in detention without any opportunity for them to be released, thereby creating an environment of fear.”

Willis said her organization is still assessing what legal action to take and has not decided if it plans to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

She said immigration lawyers are anticipating how district courts are going to react to this ruling. Many district judges have ruled that immigrants being held in detention centers have a right to bond as long as they are not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Even though Friday’s ruling is limited to the 5th Circuit, which includes Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the Trump administration has transferred many immigrants from other states to detention centers in Texas.

A policy change by the Trump administration

Under federal immigration laws, the government can quickly deport undocumented immigrants who recently crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without giving them a chance for a bond hearing. But for those who have lived in the U.S. for months or years before being detained, the law gave them the right to challenge their detention.

In July 2025, the Trump administration announced a policy change, saying that anyone who has been arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — regardless of how long they’ve been in the country — doesn’t have a right to bond.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear a separate but similar case that directly challenges the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy.

According to ProPublica, immigrants filed more habeas corpus petitions — a legal procedure that allows a person detained by the government to challenge their imprisonment — in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration than in the past three administrations combined.

Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.

Friday’s ruling doesn’t prohibit other detainees from filing habeas corpus petitions if they entered the country legally.

Politico found that more than 400 federal judges — appointed by presidents of both major political parties — have ruled in favor of immigrants’ right to due process in more than 5,000 cases since the Trump administration’s policy change last year.

In comparison, 41 judges have sided with the administration’s interpretation of the law in 250 cases, according to a Politico analysis of federal government data.

The Trump administration appealed some of the cases to higher courts, leading to conflicting rulings.

Immigration: Haynes Calls for Abolishing ICE Haynes delivered one of his strongest policy statements when asked about immigration enforcement, border security and the protection of immigrant families.
He questioned the consistency of American immigration policy, particularly the treatment of migrants from different racial and national backgrounds.
His campaign message combines traditional civil rights advocacy with a more expansive vision of federal economic intervention and institutional reform.
text:
By Patrick Washington | The Dallas Weekly

DALLAS — Rev. Dr. Frederick D. Haynes III has spent decades challenging political power from the pulpit. Now, as a candidate for Texas’ 30th Congressional District, the longtime Dallas pastor says he wants to take that fight directly to Congress, where he believes legislative action can address the economic and social inequalities affecting millions of Americans.

In an interview with The Dallas Weekly, Haynes outlined an ambitious congressional agenda centered on economic justice, immigration reform, government accountability and protecting civil rights. He also offered pointed criticism of the Trump administration and white Christian nationalism, arguing that the country faces a pivotal moment requiring more than political rhetoric.

For Haynes, the transition from ministry to electoral politics represents an extension of his life’s work rather than a departure from it.

“Public policy is so personal,” Haynes said, recalling the environmental crisis surrounding Shingle Mountain in southern Dallas, where a massive pile of discarded roofing shingles exposed nearby residents to environmental hazards.

Haynes described a member of his congregation who developed lung problems after living near the site. While his ministry offered prayer and advocacy, he said the experience demonstrated the limits of those efforts without legislative authority.

“We not only fought and prayed for her and fought to remove the shingles, but we also had to fight to change public policy,” he said.

He pointed to former U.S. Rep. Adam Clayton Powell Jr., who also served as pastor of Harlem’s Abyssinian Baptist Church, as an example of religious leadership translated into legislative influence.

For Haynes, Congress offers the opportunity to change the policies that determine whether communities can afford housing, access economic opportunity and protect themselves from discrimination.

Beyond the Minimum Wage: Addressing Dallas’ Affordability Crisis

One of Haynes’ central economic proposals is replacing the traditional minimum-wage debate with what he calls a “true cost-of-living wage,” a framework intended to account for differences in living expenses between communities.

He argues that proposals for a $20 hourly minimum wage, while an improvement over the federal minimum of $7.25, fail to reflect the financial realities facing Dallas residents.

“$20 an hour is no money in Dallas,” Haynes said.

He explained that a uniform national wage standard does not adequately recognize the differences in housing and living expenses between cities such as Dallas and Midland.

Haynes said he wants Congress to consider policies that tie wage standards more closely to the actual costs families face in their communities.

His economic agenda also includes protections for longtime residents of neighborhoods experiencing new investment and rising property values.

Asked how federal policies could encourage development without accelerating displacement, Haynes proposed property-tax protections for existing homeowners.

“As property values go up, that we see a freeze on property taxes for the traditional residents of the area,” he said, explaining that such protections could allow families to remain in neighborhoods undergoing economic transformation.

He referenced redevelopment discussions surrounding Redbird Mall as an example of the importance of ensuring that existing residents benefit from investment.

Haynes also emphasized that economic justice cannot be separated from racial justice.

“I have no problem with bringing racial justice as a component to economic justice,” he said.

He argued that historically discriminatory policies, including unequal access to New Deal-era programs and veterans’ benefits, demonstrate why broadly written economic legislation may still leave marginalized communities behind.

Without targeted protections, he warned, new investments and economic programs risk reproducing longstanding inequalities.

Immigration: Haynes Calls for Abolishing ICE

Haynes delivered one of his strongest policy statements when asked about immigration enforcement, border security and the protection of immigrant families.

“We need to abolish ICE. ICE has become the new KKK,” Haynes said, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

He argued that the agency’s enforcement practices have created fear in immigrant communities and that reforming its existing structure would be insufficient.

“You do not tweak a system. You do not tweak a pattern. You have to basically undo it and redo it,” he said.

Beyond abolishing ICE, Haynes called for comprehensive immigration reform that establishes a nondiscriminatory pathway to citizenship.

He also connected immigration to American foreign policy, arguing that U.S. intervention and economic exploitation have contributed to instability in countries whose residents subsequently seek refuge in the United States.

Haynes advocated what he described as a “moral foreign policy,” drawing on the teachings of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to argue that the United States should prioritize international goodwill, economic development and humanitarian investment.

He questioned the consistency of American immigration policy, particularly the treatment of migrants from different racial and national backgrounds.

Haynes said immigration reform must recognize the nation’s responsibility toward people displaced by persecution, instability and economic hardship.

Congressional Oversight and the Possibility of Impeachment

Haynes was equally forceful when discussing the role Congress should play in checking presidential authority.

Asked what measures he would support to address alleged corruption, conflicts of interest and executive overreach under President Donald Trump, Haynes argued that Congress has failed to exercise its constitutional responsibilities.

“The responsibility of Congress is to serve not as the doormat for the president, but instead to provide guardrails,” he said.

Haynes called for congressional investigations and hearings into potential wrongdoing by the administration if Democrats gain control of Congress.

He also expressed support for legislative action limiting executive overreach and restoring government functions he believes have been weakened.

While acknowledging that rebuilding federal institutions would require time, funding and strategic planning, Haynes suggested the country could be approaching an opportunity for what he described as a “third reconstruction.”

The candidate also made clear that he would not rule out impeachment proceedings.

“I am not taking impeachment off the table. If you break the law, you should have to face the consequences,” he said.

His comments reflected a broader argument that the nation’s system of checks and balances must be actively enforced rather than simply assumed to function.

Haynes accused the administration of undermining democratic institutions and using federal authority against political opponents. Those allegations were presented as his assessment of the administration, rather than findings established during the interview.

Confronting White Christian Nationalism

As a prominent religious leader seeking federal office, Haynes occupies an unusual position in the debate over the relationship between Christianity and American political power.

Asked how he would confront white Christian nationalism while protecting constitutional religious freedoms, Haynes distinguished between an individual’s right to hold extremist beliefs and the government’s responsibility to prevent those beliefs from infringing on the rights of others.

He said that, while he strongly opposes racist and discriminatory religious ideologies, he would defend the constitutional rights of those who espouse them.

However, he argued that religious freedom does not authorize discrimination or political domination.

“White Christian nationalism is so much more white than it ever will be Christian,” Haynes said.

He criticized what he described as the historical construction of a white image of Jesus used to justify slavery, colonialism and racial oppression.

Haynes argued that contemporary Christian nationalism represents a continuation of those traditions rather than an entirely new political movement.

He also invoked biblical teachings emphasizing justice, mercy and faith, arguing that religious institutions must be judged by how they treat vulnerable communities.

“If you ain’t about justice, you ain’t about Jesus,” he said.

Haynes said he intends to use the visibility of congressional office to challenge religious extremism while defending the First Amendment rights of all Americans.

From the Pulpit to Public Policy

Throughout the interview, Haynes returned to a central theme: the relationship between public policy and everyday life.

Whether discussing environmental injustice, housing affordability, immigration enforcement or federal accountability, he argued that political decisions have direct consequences for communities historically excluded from economic and political power.

His campaign message combines traditional civil rights advocacy with a more expansive vision of federal economic intervention and institutional reform.

But moving from advocacy to legislation would present significant challenges. Proposals such as restructuring federal immigration enforcement, establishing new wage standards and strengthening congressional oversight would require legislative support, political negotiation and, in some cases, cooperation across different levels of government.

Haynes acknowledged the difficulty of rebuilding institutions and policies he believes have been weakened.

“It doesn’t take a lot to demolish in terms of time, but to reconstruct, to rebuild, it takes what? An architect with drawings. You’ve got to finance it. You’ve got to have the material,” he said.

For Haynes, the opportunity to serve in Congress is ultimately about translating decades of ministry and activism into the authority to shape public policy.

His candidacy presents District 30 voters with a choice about the kind of representation they want in Washington: a continuation of outspoken civil rights advocacy, coupled with an agenda that seeks to turn those principles into federal legislation.

As the campaign progresses, the central question will be how Haynes intends to transform those ambitions into achievable legislative priorities.

This article is based on an October 23, 2026, interview conducted by Patrick Washington for The Dallas Weekly.

title: ICE detained me after speaking out on Gaza. I'm not alone | Opinion - USA Today
description:
I have lived in the United States for over 25 years as a contributing, law-abiding member of my community.
Now, the same government I showed up for is the one holding me in a cage in rural Georgia.
DHS later falsely claimed that my protected speech and social media posts indicated I endorsed terrorism.
Ultimately, this is about what happens when the government decides which speech it is willing to tolerate and which it won’t.
If they can lock me up and strip me of my protected status because they don’t like what I post, film or say in public, who’s to say who – or what – they’ll go after next?
text:
A little over a year ago, as I pulled out of my home in Arlington, Texas, on an otherwise ordinary October morning, I suddenly found myself surrounded by a dozen armed agents, one of them pointing a gun at my face, shouting obscenities.

I was shackled and, after a few weeks, transferred to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in Folkston, Georgia, far away from my family, my community and my home, in what I believe to be retaliation for my protected speech on Palestine, upholding due process rights and refusing to betray my community.

The government claimed that my advocacy, social media activity and commentary were an indication I "engaged in terrorist activity." In reality, I was simply protesting the mistreatment of political prisoners and speaking against the genocide in Gaza. More than 20 members of Congress have since called for my release, raising serious concerns about the government’s reliance on my political and religious expression.

I have lived in the United States for over 25 years as a contributing, law-abiding member of my community. As an airline safety specialist and first responder, I was part of the Cooperative for Assistance and Relief Everywhere (CARE) team that supported the grieving families of the 67 people who died in Washington, DC, when a regional jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided over the Potomac River in January 2025.

Now, the same government I showed up for is the one holding me in a cage in rural Georgia.

I want to make America better. ICE is tearing it apart

My connection to this country runs deep.

My great-grandfather and great-uncle were both posthumously awarded Congressional Gold Medals in 2020 to honor their U.S. military service during World War II.

In 2001, I immigrated here from the Philippines when I was 14 years old with my family. Shortly after our arrival, my father lost his sponsored job as an aircraft mechanic after the aviation industry suspended new hires in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks. In 2012, I applied to become a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient, a status I held until Citizenship and Immigration Services stripped me of it last year.

I have always aspired to help the most vulnerable, preserve life and stand up against injustice. These are values instilled in me early on by my mother, a highly respected district nurse who is now cancer–stricken and unable to speak – a calamity made all the more difficult to bear due to my prolonged confinement.

As a photojournalist, I've spent years documenting community events and rallies on Palestinian rights, the impact of the "War on Terror" on Muslim Americans, and other critical human rights issues pertaining to civil liberties.

Then came Gaza. Like most people of conscience, I felt compelled to use my voice and my platform to speak out against what was widely recognized as an unfolding genocide being committed by Israel, armed and funded by our taxpayer dollars, and to oppose ICE’s seemingly targeted campaign against anti-war organizers and student activists. I attended protests, interviewed organizers and posted on social media – only to find myself in the same position.

In November 2023, as my lawyers have detailed in federal court filings that have been widely reported, a joint terrorism task force identified me as a subject of interest and sought to recruit me as a confidential informant, invoking my immigration status and my connections within the Muslim community and the Palestine organizing space as leverage. One officer called me the perfect poster child for the way you're supposed to do it.

I declined. They then initiated an immigration-record review, and almost two years later, terminated my DACA and arrested me. DHS later falsely claimed that my protected speech and social media posts indicated I endorsed terrorism.

Speaking out against injustice is not terrorism

Since when has speaking up against genocide and the mistreatment of prisoners, irrespective of what they've been charged with, been a crime?

My detention is not only unlawful, but un-American. In August, a federal judge ruled that the government cannot use immigration law to punish or deport noncitizens for constitutionally protected First and Fifth Amendment speech. But the Trump administration continues to push the limits. For the sake of future generations – and for the sake of America herself – we have to push back.

The foundational values of this country – free speech, dissent and due process – are under attack by an administration that wants to rule with an iron fist and an unchecked arrogance of power. But as the late Sen. J. William Fulbright reminded us, true patriots are not only those who uphold this country’s values, but they're also those willing to be the first to hold power accountable when things go wrong.

Instead, we have seen the Constitution desecrated through the systematic silencing of dissent.

My confinement is part of a broader pattern targeting advocates of Palestinian rights, including Mahmoud Khalil, Leqaa Kordia and Salah Sarsour.

Each of us has a different story, but we're all test cases in this administration's attempt to see how far it can stretch immigration law – visa technicalities, foreign policy grounds and, in my case, the Immigration and Nationality Act’s terrorism provisions – to punish protected speech in defense of Palestinian life and critical of Israel.

A magistrate judge in southern Georgia ruled that my habeas petition can proceed, denying the administration's effort to dismiss my case – a small victory in a fight for my freedom from prolonged ICE detention, and for my status to remain in the country that I have called home for decades. Twenty-three members of Congress have also called for my release, demanding answers about my unconstitutional arrest.

I have spent much of my life believing in the promise of this country, serving its communities, comforting its grieving families, and speaking up when I believed injustice was being done. I never imagined that exercising those same values could cost me my freedom.

Ultimately, this is about what happens when the government decides which speech it is willing to tolerate and which it won’t. If they can lock me up and strip me of my protected status because they don’t like what I post, film or say in public, who’s to say who – or what – they’ll go after next?

description:

Friday’s ruling addressed a separate question: whether the Constitution requires bond hearings even when the law requires detention.
Some lower-court judges in the circuit nevertheless ordered bond hearings or released detainees after finding that prolonged detention violated due process.
HIGH COURT WILL REVIEW TRUMP’S MANDATORY DETENTION POLICY FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS A separate 5th Circuit panel later ruled that the Constitution required bond hearings in three cases.
text:
Judge Cory Wilson, an appointee from Trump’s first term, wrote the 159-page majority opinion in Sosnava Rodriguez v. Ortega. He was joined by eight other judges.

The men’s detention “presented no constitutional issues” that required their release, Wilson wrote. Judge Priscilla Richman, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, agreed with the result but not the majority’s legal reasoning. Seven judges dissented.

The men were protected by the Fifth Amendment, Wilson wrote. But because they had never been admitted to the United States, they were not entitled to extra hearings beyond those provided by Congress.

“Due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal,” Wilson wrote.

The 5th Circuit had already ruled that federal immigration law did not give people in these cases a statutory right to a bond hearing. Congress has broad authority over immigration and can set rules for noncitizens that would not be acceptable if applied to citizens, Wilson wrote.

The Trump administration adopted the detention policy last year. It began treating illegal immigrants who had lived in the U.S. for years as people “seeking admission,” the same legal category used for people who had just entered the country.

That interpretation placed them under a provision of immigration law that requires detention while removal cases proceed. It also prevented them from asking an immigration judge to decide whether they should be released on bond.

The policy led to a wave of lawsuits from illegal immigrants who said their detention was unlawful.

The decision added to a major split among federal appeals courts. At least nine other appeals courts, including the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 6th Circuits, have ruled against the administration’s interpretation. The 8th Circuit has upheld the policy.

The Supreme Court agreed Oct. 1 to review the broader legal dispute in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha. The justices are scheduled to hear arguments Nov. 4 and are expected to issue a ruling by June.

That case will address whether federal law requires the government to detain people who entered illegally and were never admitted. Friday’s ruling addressed a separate question: whether the Constitution requires bond hearings even when the law requires detention.

In February, a 5th Circuit panel upheld the Trump policy as a matter of statutory interpretation. Some lower-court judges in the circuit nevertheless ordered bond hearings or released detainees after finding that prolonged detention violated due process.

HIGH COURT WILL REVIEW TRUMP’S MANDATORY DETENTION POLICY FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

A separate 5th Circuit panel later ruled that the Constitution required bond hearings in three cases. The full court vacated that ruling in July and agreed to reconsider the constitutional question.

The petitioners are represented by the National Immigration Project, the American Immigration Council, and Garza & Narvaez PLLC.

text:
A two-part conversation on how to study U.S. immigration courts through data, ethnography, and advocacy. Bringing together academics, students, lawyers, community advocates, and data scientists, the panel explores what court records reveal, what they miss, and how collaborative research can illuminate asylum adjudication and access to justice.

Hosted by: UCLA Center for the Study of International Migration

Tuesday, November 10, 2026

This two-part panel examines how interdisciplinary, collaborative methods, including ethnography, legal advocacy, and data science, can deepen understanding of U.S. immigration courts. At a moment of intense political pressure on asylum adjudication and immigration enforcement, it asks how researchers and practitioners can make these courts more visible, legible, and accountable. Panelists will explore both the promise and the limits of large immigration court datasets, showing how quantitative analysis can reveal patterns in adjudication, representation, and inequality. They will also consider what such records miss: the lived experience of hearings, the daily work of advocates, the role of students in courtwatching and research, and the human consequences of legal procedure. Bringing academics, lawyers, impacted community members, and data practitioners into conversation, the panel highlights how collaborative research can deepen public understanding of immigration courts and support advocacy in the current climate.

This event is organized by Lauren Heidbrink and Amelia Frank-Vitale.

Lauren Heidbrink is an anthropologist, Professor of Human Development, and Director of Research for the College of Liberal Arts at California State University, Long Beach. She is the author of Migrant Youth, Transnational Families, and the State: Care and Contested Interests (U. of Pennsylvania Press, 2014), an ethnography of unaccompanied child migration and detention in the United States, and Migranthood: Youth in a New Era of Deportation (Stanford U. Press, 2020), which examines the deportation of Indigenous youth to Central America.

Amelia Frank-Vitale is Assistant Professor of Anthropology and International Affairs at Princeton University. An anthropologist of migration and violence in Central America and Mexico, Dr. Frank-Vitale has documented the dangers facing people migrating across Mexico and the strategies they develop – including coming together in caravans – to manage those risks and defy restrictions on movement. Her book, Leave If You Can: Migration and Violence in Bordered Worlds, examines how Honduran youth navigate life after deportation, illuminating the changing nature of deportation as a consequence of the externalization of borders and connecting regimes of mobility control - and the creative ways people challenge them - across scale and space.

Justino Mora is a full-stack software engineer, immigrant rights activist, and community organizer. Over the past 15 years, he has built technology that has reached hundreds of thousands of people in service of immigrant and other vulnerable communities, through work at organizations including Emerson Collective, RAICES, UndocuMedia, Dreamer Innovation Labs, and Mobile Pathways.

Laura Giselle Romero is a Justice in View courtwatcher and immigration advocate. Her work centers on documenting immigration court proceedings and supporting the rights and dignity of immigrant communities.

Paulina Mendez is a Justice in View courtwatcher and a graduate student in International Affairs at California State University, Long Beach. Her work focuses on observing and documenting how immigration law and policy shape the experiences of people navigating the court system.

Ingrid Eagly is a professor of law at UCLA School of Law and serves as Faculty Co-Director of the Criminal Law and Policy Consortium. Her research on U.S. immigration courts has explored the expansion of videoconferencing in immigration courts, the rise of courtrooms inside prisons and detention locations, and the challenges of access to counsel for immigrants facing removal proceedings.

Catherine L. Crooke is a lawyer and PhD candidate in the Department of Sociology at UCLA. She uses ethnography to study law, migration, work, and organizations. Her dissertation examines the experiences of social justice-oriented immigration attorneys to understand how professionals sustain moral commitments within institutional environments defined by constraint.

Erik Garcia is the Organizing and Program Director with ÓRALE (Organizing Rooted in Abolition, Liberation, and Empowerment), a Long Beach-based immigrant-led movement organization. Erik has organized for progressive movements for change over the past 12 years, primarily in California, with a few years in Colorado. Erik Garcia leads Orale's campaign and policy advocacy, community organizing, and the community defense network.

title: Detained migrants have no constitutional right to bond hearings, US court rules | WKZO
description:

The Supreme Court this month agreed to consider the issue, which has divided lower courts.
Numerous ​lawsuits by migrants arguing they were being unlawfully detained have flooded the courts as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, implemented Trump’s mass deportation agenda.
The Supreme Court is considering only ⁠whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the ⁠Constitution, the issue the 5th Circuit addressed with Friday’s decision.
