text:
A petition calling for the release of Dian Zhao Lin from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention is gaining support in Mount Morris, where community members say the longtime restaurant owner has been part of the community for more than two decades.

Supporters are urging ICE and the Department of Homeland Security to release Lin while his immigration case proceeds through the legal system, according to the petition.

"For more than 20 years, Mr. Lin has called Mount Morris home," the petition states. "He has raised his family here, operated a successful business, contributed to our local economy, and been part of the community we all share."

The Lin family has operated Mun Yuen Chinese Restaurant in Mount Morris since 2005. The family did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What does DHS say about Lin’s immigration case?

The Department of Homeland Security said Lin was apprehended Tuesday during an enforcement operation in Mount Morris, Livingston County. The agency described him as a Chinese national who entered the United States illegally in 1998.

DHS said Lin was also known as Sin Zhao Ling. According to the agency, Lin entered the country illegally in 1998 and was released into the United States by the Clinton administration. An immigration judge ordered him removed in 1999, DHS said.

In July 2023, the Board of Immigration Appeals denied a motion to reopen his case, according to the agency.

DHS said Lin would remain in ICE custody pending removal.

“To be clear: work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the United States,” the agency said.

Petition highlights Lin’s ties to Mount Morris

“Mr. Lin is not a stranger to Mount Morris. He is our neighbor,” the petition states.

Supporters say Lin’s family ties, history in the community and contributions as a local business owner should be considered as federal authorities review his case.

"After more than 20 years of calling Mount Morris home, Mr. Lin deserves the opportunity to be with his family and have his case heard fairly," the petition states.

Mount Morris mayor expresses support for Lin family

Mayor Kelly Bacon voiced support for the Lin family in a written statement and on her Facebook page.

“Mr. and Mrs. Lin operate a successful Chinese restaurant in our village that has been a cherished part of our local business community for many years,” Bacon said. She described the couple as hardworking, kind and generous neighbors who have raised their children in the community.

“As Mayor, I cannot overstate the positive impact they have had on the life and culture of our small village,” she said, adding that the village would offer support in helping reunite Lin with his family.

Hochul speaks with DHS secretary about detained New Yorkers

Gov. Kathy Hochul said Thursday evening that she had spoken with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin about Lin’s detention and the case of German Machado Guillen, a Venezuelan-born SUNY Brockport employee who was taken into ICE custody the previous week.

Hochul said Machado Guillen was accused of overstaying his authorized stay in the United States by nearly a decade.

“I want their families to know that I’m doing everything in my power to bring their loved ones home,” Hochul said in a social media post. “I’m encouraged by the Secretary’s willingness to engage, and I’ll continue pushing for their swift return.”

name: Human Rights
title: New York Banned ICE Contracts. Pro-ICE Sheriffs Could Stand in the Way. - Bolts Mag
authors: Daniel Nichanian, Felipe De La Hoz, Alex Burness
description:
Arteta says no longer renting space to ICE in the local jail will hurt the county budget.
Immigrants’ rights groups, meanwhile, say they’re focused on the health and safety of detainees in Orange County.
New York Lawyers for the Public Interest published a report late last year based on reviewing medical records of over a dozen of ICE detainees.
The office of Orange County Executive Steve Neuhaus also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
If and when the jail stops housing ICE detainees, that doesn’t end the conversation over immigration detention in the county.
text:
This story is part of Bolts’ series on sheriffs in the run-up to the midterms; read more on Maryland, North Carolina, Washington, and Wisconsin.

When New York legislators approved the state budget earlier this year, they folded in legislation to protect immigrant communities from President Donald Trump’s aggressive crackdown. The legislation, which bars localities from contracting with federal immigration agencies, was a victory for immigrants’ rights advocates but they knew it was only part of the battle; ensuring compliance would be crucial to actually reducing ICE’s presence in the state.

The most visible sort of cooperation that New York barred was participation in the 287(g) program, which effectively deputizes local law enforcement to carry out some of the functions of immigration agents. But lawmakers also restricted county detention contracts, which allow ICE to hold detainees in local jails in exchange for federal money—a practice that exploded last year as ICE arrests surged.

Orange County, a populous community some 30 miles northwest of New York City whose jail had become a sort of waystation in ICE’s national detention network, has quickly become a test of the law’s aftermath.

The jail is run by Sheriff Paul Arteta, a Republican who is holding ICE detainees there in accordance with a contract that the county first entered into in 2008, and that has long drawn scrutiny due to the dismal conditions immigrants have endured. The new state law is forcing Orange County to terminate this relationship, though so far the transfer of immigrant detainees out of the jail has been opaque.

Arteta has resisted the law, joining a group of law enforcement officials to sue over its implementation in late August. The lawsuit also includes sheriffs in counties like Broome that were in the 287(g) program. Now, Arteta and other Republicans are railing against the law as the midterm elections approach. Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, the GOP nominee for governor who had joined 287(g) last year, is attacking Governor Kathy Hochul for “making New York less safe.”

ICE cooperation is also an issue in the sheriff’s race between Arteta and Democratic challenger Bernie Rivers, who has criticized the county’s ties with the agency. Arteta says no longer renting space to ICE in the local jail will hurt the county budget.

Immigrants’ rights groups, meanwhile, say they’re focused on the health and safety of detainees in Orange County. This summer, Dignity Not Detention, a statewide coalition that has long advocated for the termination of ICE contracts, began preparing people held in Orange County for transfers and teaching them their rights, said Kate Johnson-Powers, post-release manager at Envision Freedom Fund, an organization that supports immigrants. “But of course, none of us knew what to expect, besides the legal definitions.”

An earlier generation of debates over county detention contracts with ICE—including in neighboring New Jersey during the first Trump administration—pitted advocates who wanted local jails to stop holding people for ICE against people who were typically their allies, immigration public defenders and families of those detained. The latter pointed out that cancelling the contracts would not necessarily mean anyone would be released from detention, but instead merely moved elsewhere, probably much further away in southern states like Louisiana.

But during the second Trump administration, constant transfers have been the norm for ICE.

Observers of the Orange County jail, or OCJ, told Bolts that, starting in early 2025, it became increasingly routine for federal authorities to bring people to Orange County after arresting them in New York City or upstate, but then quickly transfer them out of state while bringing in people from far away.

“We have seen our clients at OCJ get transferred sometimes in batches, sometimes just individually across the country multiple times,” said Rosa Cohen-Cruz, immigration policy director at the Bronx Defenders. “Often during those processes they lose medication, they’ll get to their new facility and won’t have commissary, so won’t be able to make a phone call, they lose property in the transfer.”

The agency is under no legal obligation to hold people near where they were detained or where their attorneys are.

Ben McCoubrey, data and advocacy manager at Envision, has tracked detainees at OCJ using data obtained by the Deportation Data Project as well as Envision’s own information on detainees it’s in touch with. He told Bolts that before the start of the second Trump administration, the jail consistently had 40 to 50 ICE detainees.

He, too, stressed that federal authorities have been cycling people in and out of OCJ quickly. “They started booking tons of people in, transferring a ton of people out to make space, and just continued,” he said. In recent months, the immigrant population has hit a high of around 120 at once, many either recent arrests, recently transferred in, or on their way out.

“I’ve seen guys come in one night, and the next day they’re shipped out,” said Samuel, a former ICE detainee who spent roughly seven months at OCJ, through the end of August (his name was changed to protect his identity, as he has an active immigration case).

While Samuel was able to win release through a habeas petition, most of his fellow detainees have not. “This guy I know got sent to Texas, he got sent with another guy then came back from Texas, then went to Louisiana, came back from Louisiana,” he said. “They don’t explain nothing to you. Besides what your lawyer explained to you and the [immigration judge] explained to you, whether you get denied or post bond, that’s the only information you get to know.”

From his time in the OCJ, he described how corrections personnel kept shortening the time that they would notify detainees that they would be transferred after some started refusing and trying to barricade themselves inside their cells.

Other detainees backed up this account of cyclical transfers. “They’ll take people over to go suffer over there and then bring them back to Orange County, from Pennsylvania and Louisiana,” said Mateo (also a pseudonym), a detainee who was picked up by ICE while going to work in November 2025 and held until this July.

New York City funds public defender organizations to provide legal defense to immigrants arrested in the city—a service that people ICE arrests elsewhere are not entitled to since immigration removal proceedings are civil procedures.

But on occasion, detainees arrested in NYC and brought to OCJ have been moved so quickly that public defense providers do not even become aware they were there until after they’re already out of state, according to local advocates, hampering their ability to actually provide representation.

Most advocates believe this bedlam to be strategic, helping the Trump administration to make what is supposed to be civil, non-punitive detention more punishing and exhausting in a bid to get people to just give up on their cases and accept removal.

Orange County’s jail has been hampered by allegations of poor conditions affecting detainees, particularly those arrested by ICE.

New York Lawyers for the Public Interest published a report late last year based on reviewing medical records of over a dozen of ICE detainees. They alleged a pattern of delayed, inconsistent, and ineffectual medical care at the facility by both corrections staff and outside medical contractors. The sheriff’s office denied the validity of the report without offering specifics, and stressed that many detainees had been accused of “severe crimes.”

Genesis Ramos, the Democratic leader of the county legislature, told Bolts that her office had followed up on these concerns but had not been able to specifically substantiate them. “What we’ve been assured over and over again is that the jail is subject to a lot of scrutiny and different audits, different levels of certification that the jail has to go through,” she said. “As a legislator, we only have but so much authority in terms of the data and operations in the jail.”

Ramos added that she had visited the jail twice during her time as a local legislator, and “never saw anything that was nefarious in nature or that was alarming or concerning per se.” According to Samuel, though, staff would repaint, clean, and provide better food whenever auditors or legislators would visit. Samuel also complains of medical deficiencies. After he was diagnosed with diabetes in jail, he said the food he was served remained the same and his medical appointments kept being delayed; he is now concerned he may have permanent vision problems.

The actual status of the ICE detainee population at the jail remains unclear. Since the law barring local collaboration with ICE went into effect, detainees were transferred out in large numbers, though some were only transferred after the Aug. 25 date at which the county was required to exercise the termination clause of its ICE contract.

A large group of detainees was transferred to the Brooklyn Metropolitan Detention Center, a federal prison, as part of the process to wind down the ICE contract. According to McCoubrey’s tracking, detainees were also sent to the GEO Group-run ICE facility in Jena, Louisiana, which is also where Mahmoud Khalil was held for months; to the deadly Delaney Hall in New Jersey; to the troubled Miami Correctional Facility in Indiana; and to other institutions in Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and Texas.

But advocates at Envision and some public defenders say they caught wind of additional book-ins after Aug. 25. Under state law, localities have until Nov. 25 to certify that they are in compliance, though receiving new detainees in that interim period could arguably run afoul of it.

Johnson-Powers, of Envision, said the fund had received a call to its hotline from an ICE detainee at OCJ as late as Sept. 15. The next day, James Potter, the captain of the corrections division at the sheriff’s office, told a meeting of the county legislature’s public safety committee that “the ICE detainee count was 171 for August and as of this morning it was zero,” per meeting minutes. Potter also noted year-to-date “boarder revenue,” i.e., income from renting jail beds to ICE, was $8.13 million.

In response to Bolts’ questions about the current ICE detainee population, transfers, conditions at the jail, and compliance with state law, the sheriff referred all questions to ICE, which did not respond.

The office of Orange County Executive Steve Neuhaus also did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A spokesperson for New York Attorney General Letitia James, who has the power to go after jurisdictions in noncompliance, did not address specific questions about Orange County, but clarified that the office views Nov. 25 as the compliance deadline.

If and when the jail stops housing ICE detainees, that doesn’t end the conversation over immigration detention in the county. In late June, Project Salt Box reported that the federal government leased a massive warehouse in Newburgh, a city in Orange County, with some indication that it could be used for ICE detention, including the requirement that it have a sally port large enough for detainee buses and vans.

The prospect has led to significant community pushback this fall.

ICE detention is also a point of contention in November’s sheriff race between Arteta and Rivers, a rematch of the 2022 election in which Arteta easily prevailed.

Rivers, the Democratic challenger, has criticized Arteta for signing on to the lawsuit against the immigration legislation, arguing that the sheriff should keep their focus local: “Orange County residents deserve a Sheriff who is focused on their needs, not one chasing national headlines at the expense of public trust,” he said in a Facebook post in August. He has also warned that the debates are set to continue given the Newburgh warehouse, telling Bolts that immigration detention was a “hot-topic button… with the federal government for the second time looking to purchase or lease facilities here in Orange County to house ICE detainees.”

“I’m not saying the federal government doesn’t have a right to enforce immigration law; they have every right to enforce immigration law, but the way they’re doing it is just wrong,” he added.

Still, he doesn’t see himself as a “standard-bearer” for the anti-ICE movement in the county. “It does come into the political conversation. People want to talk about ICE,” he told Bolts. “I really didn’t want and don’t want to focus the sheriff race totally on what’s going on in ICE.”

Rivers said he would still consider notifying ICE about detainees when appropriate. But he could not immediately say when it would be, telling Bolts he’d look into the laws and regulations when in office. If elected, Rivers also committed to looking into concerns over food and medical care at OCJ, including for people held there on criminal charges.

But Rivers also lamented that the main reaction he was getting from would-be voters was surprise that there was even an election for sheriff, a reality he partly chalked up to the collapse of local media.

Several of the community organizations that participated in the Dignity Not Detention coalition and pushed for the cancellation of the Orange County ICE contract told Bolts that they’re staying out of the race and had no comment on it. Attention now is focused on support for those who are being moved out, including the group sent to Brooklyn MDC, a federal facility housing roughly 1,400 people that was denounced by a judge in 2024 for its “dangerous, barbaric conditions.”

“The levels of security and just degradation and lack of humanity through this intense security, it’s just very different from being in a small county jail,” said Johnson-Powers.

Still, even if the closure of OCJ to ICE detainees won’t address the broader issues of an administration committed to mass deportation and armed with enormous funding, advocates say the law restricting local cooperation with ICE and the contract’s cancellation have value.

McCoubrey, the advocate at Envision, stresses “the multiplier effect that every ICE bed has,” telling Bolts, “70,000 [total detention] beds is already a scary number. But the fact that that facilitates hundreds and hundreds of thousands of deportations every year really brings home the value of any amount of any dent that you can make in local detention capacity.”

text:
A funeral will be held Monday for the Dallas man who died in an ICE processing center in Laredo last weekend.

As the family of Emilio Andrade Covarrubias prepares to lay him to rest, questions remain surrounding his death at the Rio Grande Processing Center.

The 56-year-old man originally from Hidalgo, Mexico, was a lawful permanent resident of the U.S. who had lived in Dallas’ Casa View neighborhood with his wife and four kids for decades.

Immigration officials had taken him into custody in June, alleging he had obtained his residency fraudulently for failing to disclose a 2004 arrest.

His family alleges he was denied his medication while in detention. ICE maintains he received proper medical care.

“We believe he did not receive the medical attention he desperately needed,” his daughter Stefani Andrade wrote on the GoFundMe page she had set up for her father. “His passing has left our family devastated, heartbroken, and struggling to come to terms with such an unexpected loss.”

In a statement earlier this week, Mexico’s Secretary of Foreign Affairs called on U.S. officials to conduct an “exhaustive and transparent investigation” into the circumstances surrounding Andrade Covarrubia’s death.

According to the statement, this is the 18th death of a Mexican citizen while in ICE custody in the U.S. since January 2025.

Mexican authorities also called on the Webb County district attorney to investigate Andrade Covarrubia’s death.

He is the seventh person to die in ICE custody in Texas this year and the second at this facility.

Andrade Covarrubias’ family was in Laredo earlier this week to pick up his belongings and meet with Mexican authorities.

A spokesperson from the Mexican Consulate in Laredo told KERA that Mexican officials were waiting for the autopsy certificate.

The spokesperson said the Consul of Protection and Legal Affairs, a Mexican diplomat who protects the rights of nationals, had been in contact with the family, but did not have further information to release.

Andrade Covarrubias will be laid to rest at Laurel Oaks Memorial Park in Balch Springs.

“My father was more than just a name,” Stefani Andrade wrote. “He was a father, a loved one, and someone whose life meant so much to our family. He deserved to be treated with dignity, compassion, and care.”

text:
Why It Matters

The Trump administration has terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 13 of the 17 countries that held designations when President Trump took office in January 2025, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. ​

The 13 terminated designations covered approximately 1,103,390 beneficiaries as of June 25, based on Department of Homeland Security figures provided to CRS. Four designations currently remain in effect: El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Lebanon.

The Big Picture

Congress created TPS in 1990 to provide safe haven to noncitizens from countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disaster or other extraordinary circumstances. The Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security may designate a country for six, 12 or 18 months and must terminate a designation upon determining that the country no longer meets the conditions.

The 13 terminated countries, with termination dates and beneficiary counts from the Federal Register, are:

Afghanistan: July 14, 2025 (11,740)

Burma: Jan. 26, 2026 (3,970)

Cameroon: Aug. 4, 2025 (5,460)

Ethiopia: Feb. 13, 2026 (5,010)

Haiti: Sept. 2, 2025 (353,160)

Honduras: Sept. 8, 2025 (70,070)

Nepal: Aug. 5, 2025 (12,160)

Nicaragua: Sept. 8, 2025 (3,850)

Somalia: March 17, 2026 (1,080)

South Sudan: Jan. 5, 2026 (230)

Syria: Nov. 21, 2025 (6,100)

Venezuela: April 7, 2025 and Nov. 7, 2025, covering two concurrent designations (627,750 combined beneficiaries)

Yemen: May 4, 2026 (2,810)

CRS notes that several terminations were subject to litigation that delayed their effective dates, but it does not identify which terminations or whether any cases remain pending.

The four remaining designations covered 343,800 beneficiaries as of June 25: El Salvador (224,070), Sudan (2,020), Ukraine (117,170) and Lebanon (540).

The Bottom Line

DHS stated on Sept. 9 that Salvadoran TPS holders "retain protection including work authorization" until an announcement is made, and provided matching statements for Sudan and Ukraine to CRS on Oct. 20. Lebanon's designation expires Nov. 27.

authors: Eleanor Fitzgerald | San Antonio Report, www.tpr.org, eleanor-fitzgerald

text:
San Antonio Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones wrote to federal agencies seeking protections for qualified military family members following another instance of immigration officials targeting a Texas family.

In an effort to protect military readiness and preserve interest in military service in San Antonio, Jones asked U.S. Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to allow military families lawfully seeking citizenship to move through that process undeterred, with the strongest preference for approval of that status.

Last month, South Texas Democratic Congressional candidate Bobby Pulido posted the video to social media highlighting a the story of a local military family.

“Giovanna was tricked. They called her to the base to pick up her military IDs. Instead, ICE was waiting. Now she faces deportation,” Pulido said in the video.

Giovanna Perez had applied for a program called military parole in place through her husband Pedro Gutierrez, who recently enlisted in the U.S. Army, she told The Atlantic last week.

The program is designed for qualifying non-citizen family members of service members and veterans to have access to a legal pathway to citizenship, in an effort to protect military readiness.

Perez, a mom of four kids who was brought to the U.S. from Mexico when she was 6-years-old, was confronted by U.S. Immigration and Customs agents in September while going to pick up her military IDs at the Naval Air Station in Corpus Christi.

Jones said in the letter that the recent report of a military spouse being apprehended and detained by federal immigration officials on base in Corpus Christi is “deeply troubling.”

“According to the report, the spouse was seeking to obtain an identification card needed to access healthcare and other family benefits while her soldier spouse was away,” she added.

The military has long advertised parole in place in recruitment efforts, but that appears to be changing. The U.S. Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard no longer tout the program as an enlistment benefit. The Army and National Guard still do.

For family members applying for parole in place, wait times have nearly tripled over the last year. According to USCIS data, the processing time for military parole went from 4.5 months in fiscal year 2025 to 12.5 months in fiscal year 2026.

Jones said she worries targeted immigration enforcement against military families is a recruitment deterrent, that harms San Antonio’s military reputation.

“We fear such actions may dampen interest in military service, while introducing unneeded stress during a time of heightened military operations,” she wrote.

“As Military City USA, we recognize and appreciate the service of everyone courageous enough to support and defend the Constitution, and the family members — irrespective of citizenship — who make that service possible.”

Perez’s case comes after a similar situation struck a San Antonio family in August.

U.S. Rep Joaquin Castro (D-San Antonio) said the mother of a U.S. Navy midshipman that he had nominated to the Naval Academy this year was detained by ICE at her green card appointment.

One week later, he said Maria Rocio Rocha was deported to Mexico, splitting up the San Antonio family as her son David Garcia continues his service.

The parole in place policy hasstretched back to the George W. Bush administration, when DHS attempted the deport a military spouse while her husband was missing in action in Iraq. Public outcry halted the deportation, and the policy was born from that instance.

By 2013, United States Citizenship and Immigration Services had officially issued a policy memorandum outlining parole for undocumented spouses, children and parents of armed forces personnel and veterans.

In 2016 the policy was expanded even further, with military branches actively advertising it in their recruiting efforts. The policy is not a guarantee of citizenship, but it provides a pathway by allowing qualifying family members to remain in the country legally as they move through the process with their service member sponsor.

Since President Donald Trump took office in 2025, the way the government has dealt with immigration cases involving service members or their families is changing.

In 2025, a new ICE policy was issued, “ICE values the contributions of all those who have served in the U.S. military; however, U.S. military service alone does not automatically exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws,” it stated.

An Associated Press investigation in August found that more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty service members have been detained during the second Trump administration.

Perez said in a video this month that she was able to call her husband, who is still in basic training at Fort Benning, in Georgia. She recounted what he told her.

“Don’t let them get you intimidated, or anything. We have four kids that we have to stand up for. I hope I see you soon, I’m willing to die for y’all, if I have to,” she retold.

Jones asked that Hegseth and Mullin reconsider the practice of detaining military families like theirs as they work to obtain lawful permanent status.

“These families are among the very best of our communities, and it is only to our benefit to embrace their commitment to our country,” Jones concluded.

text:
After Wrongly Flagging 185 American Citizens in Nevada, Trump Administration Sues California for Refusing to Disenfranchise Voters and Threatens Election Workers With Prosecution

Washington, D.C. (October 23, 2026)—Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, and Rep. Joe Morelle, Ranking Member of the Committee on House Administration, demanded answers from Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the Trump Administration’s use of baseless noncitizen voting claims to bully states into disenfranchising American citizens ahead of the midterm elections.

“The stakes for our democracy in this offensive could not be higher. Under the Constitution, the States are primarily responsible for election administration and Congress has the final say on the time, place, and manner of federal elections. To the extent DHS has a role in elections at all, it is only to fulfill Congress’s assigned statutory purposes. The Department should be focused on providing the states resources that Congress has appropriated to it to support State and local elections officials at their request. Instead, DHS and President Trump are engaging in increasingly brazen bully tactics to force states to illegally remove eligible voters hand-picked by the Administration from their voter rolls,” wrote the Ranking Members.

In July, Secretary Mullin and President Trump publicly claimed that DHS had identified more than 250,000 potential noncitizens illegally registered to vote in California, New Jersey, Nevada, and Pennsylvania. But the Administration’s allegations fell apart in Nevada. DHS initially claimed to have identified 15,903 potential noncitizens, then supplied just 185 names it said it had “confirmed” were not U.S. citizens. Nevada officials reviewed their records and determined that all 185 were American citizens eligible to vote(link is external). In essence, the Administration tried to deprive American citizens of their right to vote with false accusations.

Rather than admitting that failure and learning from it, the Trump Administration has escalated its intimidation campaign in California. In an October 13 letter(link is external), the Department of Justice (DOJ) imposed an arbitrary 48-hour deadline for California to review 20,000 names(link is external)supplied on a thumb drive, require Los Angeles County to set aside ballots already received from those individuals, and stop sending them mail-in ballots. The letter provided no explanation of how DHS determined that the individuals were noncitizens.

When California refused to submit to this lawless and unworkable ultimatum, DOJ sued. It then threatened to prosecute election officials who knowingly count ballots cast by people federal agencies identify as noncitizens(link is external), even as DHS conceded that the people it flagged were only “likely” noncitizens.

Noncitizen voting is vanishingly rare(link is external). Yet the Trump Administration continues to weaponize these claims to target voters and intimidate the local officials and citizen volunteers responsible for administering our elections.

Ranking Members Raskin and Morelle requested a briefing as soon as practicable on the evidence behind DHS’s allegations, the data and methods used in its supposedly “rigorous manual review process,” and whether DHS took steps to distinguish recently naturalized Americans from noncitizens before targeting their voter registrations.

text:
The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers during a violent anti-immigration, anti-protest crackdown in the state earlier this year, state officials said in recent court filings.

Minnesota officials sued the Trump administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings.

The family of Good, 37, earlier this month sued over her death when she was shot by a federal officer with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as she drove her car away during a protest in January.

Pretti, also 37, was shot dead in the street by a border patrol agent as he went to the assistance of a fellow protester on the icy city streets during fierce demonstrations against the crackdown. Both Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) and ICE are under the umbrella of the Department of Homeland Security.

The shootings of the two protesters, both US citizens, was a turning point in the government’s approach after weeks of violent action by ranks of militarized, masked federal immigration enforcement in Minneapolis, which local leaders called a siege, after months of similar mass operations in major cities.

There were immediate disputes over the investigations into Good’s and later Pretti’s killings between state and federal authorities.

The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.

The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.

State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Hennepin county attorney Mary Moriarty said at the time that the state expected to receive “all the evidence.”

But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the US attorney’s office for Minnesota, the state outpost of federal prosecutors, told her on 10 September that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely “in light of challenges with DC”, according to the documents, referring to Washington and the federal authorities.

State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they “have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations”.

In a reply filed on Tuesday, attorneys for the US justice department argued it is within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities.

Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota bureau of criminal apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good’s clothing, the cell phone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view. Bystanders captured footage of the shooting death of Good in her car and Pretti on the street, in each case contradicting key parts of what the administration said prompted the killings. No criminal charges have been filed.

Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Trump's DOJ Is On A Denaturalization Crusade. Ilhan Omar Is Just One Of Its Targets
description:
Back in 2019, the last time the Trump administration directed federal authorities to comb through Omar’s immigration records, they found no evidence of wrongdoing.
Between 1990 and 2017, the Justice Department filed an average of 11 denaturalization cases per year.
Additionally, researchers at the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse have identified more than 100 denaturalization complaints filed by the Trump administration so far this year.
Another database, maintained by Democracy Forward, shows nearly 200 civil denaturalization cases filed since January 2025.
And it is waging a denaturalization crusade that aims to make equal membership in society depend on race, ancestry, and Trump’s singular will.
text:
Around 6 AM on Monday, October 12, roughly two dozen federal agents raided the Washington, D.C., residence of Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat and the first Somali American member of Congress. The raid was part of the Trump administration’s sprawling investigation centered on Omar’s citizenship status. Over the past two weeks, federal officials have seized her phone, passport, notebooks, and computers. They’ve issued grand jury subpoenas to her family members. They’ve floated the possibility of criminal charges and prison time, and claimed that the probe may allow the Trump administration to strip Omar of her citizenship and facilitate her deportation.

Back in 2019, the last time the Trump administration directed federal authorities to comb through Omar’s immigration records, they found no evidence of wrongdoing. But actual legal wrongdoing is not the point. What’s “wrong” for Trump is the idea that a Black and Muslim woman he deems inferior could come to the United States and be granted rights as his equal.

Omar arrived in the United States in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee of the Somali Civil War, and was naturalized as an American citizen in 2000. For years, Trump has disparaged Omar and other Somali Americans as “garbage,” and claimed that people from “the worst countries” should not come to the United States and start “telling us about the Constitution.”

Under federal law, “having opinions about the Constitution” does not appear on the list of permissible reasons to revoke someone’s citizenship. Congress has authorized the Justice Department to pursue civil denaturalization proceedings only when the government alleges that someone should not have become a citizen in the first place—for example, by procuring that status “by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation.” Longstanding Supreme Court precedent requires the government to prove those allegations with “clear, unequivocal, and convincing evidence which does not leave the issue in doubt.”

The Supreme Court has also recognized that “citizenship obtained through naturalization is not a second-class citizenship,” and that a legal system in which “a group of citizens temporarily in office can deprive another group of citizens of their citizenship” is “completely incongruous” with “the very nature of our free government.” Accordingly, actual revocations of citizenship have been exceedingly rare in the modern era: Fewer than 150 Americans were denaturalized between 1968 and 2013, compared to more than 18 million Americans who were naturalized in that same period. And when the rare denaturalization does occur, the targets have tended to be people suspected of war crimes or terrorism.

The Trump administration is trying to change that. Between 1990 and 2017, the Justice Department filed an average of 11 denaturalization cases per year. During Trump’s first term, the average rose to 25 cases per year. Now, the Trump administration has directed the Department of Homeland Security to “supply” the Justice Department with “100-200 denaturalization cases per month,” and the DOJ has further instructed all employees in the Civil Division to “prioritize and maximally pursue denaturalization proceedings.”

Trump’s Justice Department is acting on these instructions. In April 2026, administration officials informed federal prosecutors that they had identified 384 Americans to target in a first wave of denaturalization cases. And earlier this month, the DOJ announced that it had filed 40 such denaturalization actions between August 21 and October 2. Additionally, researchers at the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse have identified more than 100 denaturalization complaints filed by the Trump administration so far this year. Another database, maintained by Democracy Forward, shows nearly 200 civil denaturalization cases filed since January 2025.

The federal government’s ongoing attacks on Ilhan Omar are part of the Trump administration’s attempt to act as sole arbiter of who gets to be an American. It issues orders purporting to rescind birthright citizenship. It deploys federal agents to surveil, detain, and deport people of color en masse. And it is waging a denaturalization crusade that aims to make equal membership in society depend on race, ancestry, and Trump’s singular will.

text:
NEW HAVEN — About 30 members of the New Haven Immigrants Coalition and representatives of the Yale Law School's Jerome N. Frank Legal Services Organization took their concerns about ICE to Tweed New Haven Airport this week, protesting outside the airport and in the board room.

About 18 protesters then took their concerns about ICE arresting or detaining Tweed travelers in recent months inside to the Tweed New Haven Airport Authority's monthly meeting, where several people addressed the authority board during the public comment session at the end.

ICE, which stands for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, was not visible either at the protest or in the Tweed Authority meeting. ICE spokespersons did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

Protesters made it clear that they don't think ICE should be at Tweed or the City of New Haven or Tweed Airport should be cooperating with the agency.

They offered a list of demands to the Tweed Authority, including that Tweed ensure that every ICE officer granted unrestricted access at Tweed has undergone a full background check; maintain a comprehensive identification system for ICE agents; administer training, including on Public Act 26-14 which prohibits civil arrests without a judicial warrant, before granting ICE access to secured areas, and maintain records of all ICE arrests at Tweed.

Their concerns echoed those of New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker, who sent a letter to Tweed New Haven Airport Authority Chairman Robert Reed last month in the wake of at least two recent ICE detentions at Tweed, asking that Tweed "not exceed any federal requirements by extending additional assistance to ICE" beyond what's required by law.

"No agency is above the law!" said the Rev. Scott Marks of New Haven Rising, a member of the coalition, speaking at a gathering at Burr Street and Fort Hale Road, just outside the airport entrance. "Our state and local governments do not do the bidding of Immigration ... I say today, enough is enough!" he said.

"Here in New Haven, we don't like that fear to be part of our community," said Kiana Cintron of the NHIC, a student at the University of Connecticut. "Nobody should be afraid that their loved ones are not going to" return home, she said.

Article continues below this ad

Coalition member Leslie Blatteau, president of the New Haven Federation of Teachers, said New Haven's schools "are open to everyone, regardless of their immigration status" and "the same should be true for Tweed."

She called what ICE does, including at Tweed, "immoral" and "unacceptable," and said, "it is why we are here, to say that we must abolish ICE!"

While there have been two high-profile detainments of students in recent months, protesters said there actually have been at least four, including two other community members. Coalition spokesperson Anne Watkins declined to identify them.

A spokesman for Avports, the private company that operates Tweed on a contract with the Tweed Authority, also said he was unable to identify any detainees.

Article continues below this ad

Representatives of the Jerome N. Frank Legal Services Organization's Worker & Immigrant Rights Advocacy Clinic said they submitted a request under the state Freedom of Information Act to the Tweed Authority Wednesday, seeking a number of documents related to ICE's presence at Tweed.

"The Tweed New Haven Airport Authority should not be granting access to unvetted ICE agencies, said Trinh Truong, a law school intern with the clinic who said the documents they seek are "to prove that all agents have been" subject to proper vetting procedure. Among the items they are seeking is a roster of all ICE employees with access to Tweed, she said.

Tweed Authority Chairman Reed welcomed the protesters to the meeting, telling them, "We recognize those that have come out today and respect the public's right to demonstrate, peacefully ... Our responsibility is to maintain a safe, secure and orderly environment" for both travelers and others, he said.

Reed said he understands the public's interest and "I can assure you that those steps are being actively pursued ... We ask everyone to help keep the airport safe and accessible for people to use it."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Among the speakers at the meeting was Rose Murphy, a teacher at Career High School who lives in Branford. She said she used to bring students to Tweed on field trips but doesn't feel comfortable doing that now with ICE at the airport. She urged Tweed officials to adhere to the Trust Act, which limits municipal cooperation with federal immigration enforcement efforts.

New Haven resident Jessica Light said she came "to ask Tweed Airport to uphold federal law and Connecticut law and make sure ICE agents have judicial warrants before they detain anyone."

Avports spokesperson Andrew King said Thursday that "we recognize the concerns these incidents have raised in the community. Our responsibility is to maintain a safe, secure airport for everyone who travels through or works here."

With regard to background checks, he said, "federal regulations specifically address government employees, including law enforcement officers, whose employment investigation included a criminal records check."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Under the law, "airport operators must authorize unescorted access for those qualifying individuals. That provision recognizes the government employment investigation rather than requiring a separate airport-administered fingerprint check in every case," King said in an email.

"Airports are not federally authorized to create their own credentialing standards or impose requirements that conflict with the federal regulatory framework," he said. Credentialing "is governed by TSA regulations, not ad hoc local rules. This is not a matter of airport discretion. All airport badges and access privileges remain subject to the airport’s TSA-approved security program."

Access to secured areas of the airport "is governed by federal credentialing requirements and the airport’s TSA-approved security program," King said. "Public Act 26-14 addresses the circumstances under which officers may make civil arrests. Those are separate legal questions. An airport credential authorizes access; it does not authorize an arrest or constitute airport approval of an enforcement action."

The airport "does not direct ICE operations," King said. "...Questions about the legality of a particular arrest belong with the appropriate law enforcement agencies and courts. Our focus remains the safety of passengers, employees, and everyone using the airport."

Regarding Elicker's request, "our focus remains on passenger safety and adherence to applicable laws and requirements," King said. "We continue to revisit our policies and procedures to confirm total compliance."

title: Cubans facing deportation are being sent to third countries despite legal challenges, uncertainty
description:
Third-country deportations allow for the removal of immigrants even when their home countries refuse to take them back.
More than 25,000 people have been sent to 29 countries, according to the Third Country Deportation Watch, a project of Refugees International and Human Rights First to monitor data on third‑country deportations.
In February, a federal judge in Massachusetts blocked third-country deportations, acknowledging deportees’ right to notice and to challenge their removal.
In such circumstances, migrants may agree to leave the country without understanding what they are signing, attorneys told The Trib.
Most Cubans in the United States live in Florida, with Miami-Dade County home to the largest concentration of Cubans outside the island.
text:
In the middle of the Arizona desert in June, at Eloy Detention Center, Dolores Freixa opened her eyes at 3 a.m. to the sound of an officer telling her to get up and collect her things. She was being transferred, but no one told her where.

Freixa described one other woman and about 40 men getting on the bus with her beneath the dark desert sky. She was the only Cuban. When she asked the men what was happening, they told her they had voluntarily signed up to return to their home country: Mexico.

Freixa had never agreed to be taken to another country.

Third-country deportations allow for the removal of immigrants even when their home countries refuse to take them back. More than 25,000 people have been sent to 29 countries, according to the Third Country Deportation Watch, a project of Refugees International and Human Rights First to monitor data on third‑country deportations.

In February, a federal judge in Massachusetts blocked third-country deportations, acknowledging deportees’ right to notice and to challenge their removal.

But The Trib found that the ruling did not stop ICE from attempting to take people to the border without notice while the judicial block was in effect, according to interviews with migrants and immigration attorneys. Transfers between detention centers and paperwork presented under stressful conditions, sometimes alongside warnings of worse consequences for refusing to sign, can leave detainees caught in bureaucratic confusion and turmoil. In such circumstances, migrants may agree to leave the country without understanding what they are signing, attorneys told The Trib.

Freixa refused to sign the paperwork and was taken back to Arizona, but she was an exception.

“We are seeing a pattern where they are put on a bus without being told anything, taken to the Mexican border, and forced to get off,” said immigration attorney Liudmila Marcelo. “It happened to a client of mine. In his case, he refused to get off. Others did get off, and once they did, they accepted their deportation. My client has also been asked several times to sign documents.”

A DHS spokesperson asked The Trib to identify the migrants by name and date of birth who relayed that they had been pressured to self-deport. When The Trib declined to disclose their identities, the spokesperson replied by email: “When the media refuses to give names, it makes it impossible to provide details on specific cases or even verify any of this even happened or that the people even exist. If you can’t do your job, we can’t do ours.”

The spokesperson also said, “It is categorically false we would pressure someone to self-deport.”

The U.S. Supreme Court has since allowed third-country deportations to resume.

As of May, Cubans were the largest group of deportees to third countries, most of whom had been taken to Mexico, according to a report by Human Rights Watch. Most Cubans in the United States live in Florida, with Miami-Dade County home to the largest concentration of Cubans outside the island.

Some Cubans who lost their permanent resident status after criminal convictions continued living in the country under orders of supervision, since the government could not carry out their deportations. They were required to report to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and, if they complied with their reporting requirements and had no new criminal offenses, could apply for work permits.

Under this arrangement, some spent decades rebuilding their lives in the United States – and most often in Florida.

Now, the government is seeking to deport them to third countries. That’s Freixa’s story.

She arrived at age 11 during the 1980 Mariel boatlift and was arrested in 2015 on charges including burglary, theft and fraud-related offenses. After serving her sentence, she was transferred directly to immigration detention earlier this year.

“The U.S. government wants to deport as many people as possible, and one way is creating contracts with countries around the world that will accept deportees for cash. Unfortunately, a lot of Cubans have removal orders, and they’re shooting fish in a barrel because these people have, for decades, been reporting to ICE offices, following the law and doing what they’re supposed to do,” said immigration attorney Andrea Jacoski.

The agreement with Mexico is not public, leaving questions about the Mexican government’s responsibilities when receiving these migrants.

In the same report, Human Rights Watch found that migrants dropped off in Mexico have no clear path forward. They are given 10 days of permission to stay in the country, after which they must begin their own asylum-seeking process. They are left with no clear path to shelter, food or health care. The organization also found that migrants are left in cities where they are vulnerable to smuggling networks, extortion rings and human traffickers.

In August, other Cuban residents of South Florida were deported as far as Africa, the Miami Herald reported. The deportations have prompted protests, particularly because some of the countries receiving migrants are under U.S. State Department travel advisories warning of widespread violence and insecurity.

“The law allows for third-country removal, but to a safe third country. And so that ‘safe’ is the operative and very important word, because so many of these countries where people are being deported to are not safe. They’re in the middle of civil war or there’s internal conflict, such that it’s not safe for people to go there,” said Jacoski.

A DHS spokesperson told The Trib that migrants who refuse to return to their home countries are sent to a safe third country, emphasizing that the decision to return home is theirs. “If an illegal alien chooses to file a claim in court refusing to go to their home country, we are required by law to find a safe and secure nation for them to go to. If an illegal alien chooses to go home, we will give them a free flight home and a $3,000 check. The choice is theirs,” the spokesperson said in an email.

When Freixa arrived at the border, she remembered a warning from her friend and fellow detainee back in Arizona and from her lawyer. She told the officer it was illegal to drop her off. She said the officer then showed her a self-deportation document and asked whether the signature was hers. It wasn’t.

She kept repeating that the removal was illegal and that they had to put her back on the bus.

Freixa was taken back to Eloy Detention Center, but the legal protections that allowed her to protest at the Mexican border have vanished after the Supreme Court allowed third-country deportations to resume.

“I think people have come to believe there’s a binary of deserving and non-deserving immigrants, and that people with criminal histories, regardless of their equities or their family ties or how long they’ve been here deserve to be deported,” said Jacoski, the immigration attorney. “When in reality, nobody deserves to have their human rights violated. Nobody deserves to suffer needlessly in a country that they don’t know. Nobody deserves to really be the poster child for human suffering.”

Zoe Millán is a journalist and graduate of the M.S. at Columbia School of Journalism and a summer 2026 fellow with The Florida Trib. You can reach Zoe at zoe.millan@floridatrib.org.

text:
HARRIS COUNTY, Texas – Two conflicting accounts emerge about an early morning crash between ICE agents and a truck driver in Northwest Harris County, one from a federal agency and one from the man’s family.

The Harris County Sheriff’s Office said the incident happened around 6:41 a.m. Tuesday in the 12400 block of Old Foltin Road in Northwest Harris County. Luis Eduardo Villanueva Loredo, 52, is currently being held at the Montgomery ICE Processing Center. His family tells KPRC 2 News they spoke with him by phone after the crash.

Through a translator, Villanueva Loredo’s sister-in-law Patricia Hernandez described what he told her happened.

“Earlier this morning, he left to go to work. He was getting out of the house. There were two or three cars following him with no lights, nothing at all,” the translator relayed.

The family says Villanueva Loredo became suspicious and believed he was about to be robbed.

According to the family, an ICE vehicle then struck him from behind.

“One of the ICE agents in the car hit him from behind in the corner of the truck. That’s when he lost the wheel. That’s when he came into that ditch right there,” the translator said.

DHS tells a different story.

According to an ICE spokesperson, agents activated their emergency lights and sirens before attempting to stop Villanueva Loredo. The agency says he drove into a ditch while trying to evade law enforcement. Federal officers stopped, believing the vehicle was stuck. Moments later, according to DHS, Villanueva Loredo’s truck pulled out of the ditch and struck the front driver’s side of the ICE vehicle. He then exited the truck and fled on foot before being taken into custody after a short foot chase.

The Harris County Sheriff’s Office confirmed the pickup went into a ditch during the pursuit. When the vehicle came back out, the two vehicles made contact, breaking a taillight on the truck.

While still at the scene, Villanueva Loredo complained of chest pains. EMS responded, found nothing immediately wrong and transported him to a local hospital as a precaution. He is expected to be okay.

DHS says Villanueva Loredo is a Mexican national who entered the United States illegally and was previously granted a voluntary return to Mexico on March 26, 2007. His family disputes DHS’s claim that he had prior deportation orders.

The Harris County Sheriff’s Office is investigating the crash in consultation with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.

text:
In a congressional race that has the chance to be competitive in the final weeks of the midterm election, Rep. Jeff Van Drew and Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock clashed for 60 minutes Thursday.

They sparred over President Donald Trump’s massive tax and spending law, over the release of government files involving convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and immigration.

The debate, sponsored by the William J. Hughes Center for Public Policy at Stockton University and The Press of Atlantic City, followed the House Democratic political arm’s announcement that it had added Van Drew (R-Dennis) to its target list, followed by a pro-Democratic super PAC announcing that it would spend $1.5 million against the incumbent.

The 2nd District is one of numerous districts across the country where Democrats see an opportunity to make inroads due to the unpopularity of President Donald Trump.

Van Drew was elected to the House as a Democrat in 2018, the last time Trump was in the White House. He was one of four Democrats to flip Republican-held seats in the Garden State. Van Drew switched parties after opposing Trump’s first impeachment.

In a state where 64% of voters in a recent Stockton University poll disapproved of Trump’s job performance with only 31% approving. Mullock wasted no time trying to tie Van Drew to the unpopular president.

“My opponent has sold out South Jersey, to data centers, to the war in Iran to doubling our health insurance prices, all for a pathetic undying support to Donald Trump,” Mullock said in his opening statement.

Van Drew talked about the money he brought back to the 2nd Congressional District, his successful effort to block plans to carve up the Federal Aviation Administration’s technical center in Egg Harbor Township, and the funds he got for beach replenishment.

Mullock repeatedly pressed Van Drew on his support for Trump’s massive tax and spending bill that gave 72% of the benefits to the richest 20% of Americans, and take away health care from 11.8 million Americans and nutrition assistance from two million, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The bill imposes new rules that wind up reducing overall spending spending for Medicare and Medicaid, according to the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Van Drew responded to Mullock’s charges by repeatedly accusing him of lying about his record. “He just never tells the truth,” he said.

And he pointed out that the Trump tax law Mullock opposes also cuts taxes on tips, on overtime pay, and for senior citizens.

Asked about energy prices, Van Drew blamed the Democrats.

“Energy companies have made record profits,” he said. “And they have been granted those increases by Democratic administrations.”

Mullock sought to blame high energy prices on the war with Iran, which has raised gasoline and diesel prices.

“The war in Iran has skyrocketed our energy prices,” Mullock said, blaming Van Drew for voting for the conflict.

“I never voted for that war,” Van Drew responded.

There technically was no vote to authorize the war; Van Drew and most of the House Republicans voted against a resolution requiring Trump to get congressional approval to continue the conflict.

“You had a chance to stop it and you didn’t,’ Mullock said, who later called the conflict “a war of stupidity.”

He interrupted Van Drew several times, accusing him of sending troops to Iran, which the lawmaker repeatedly said was untrue.

“I’ve never seen anything like it,” Van Drew responded. “You get the Pinocchio prize tonight.”

There was some agreement on the issue of Social Security, where reserve funds are scheduled to expire at the end of 2032, forcing Congress to either find more revenue or the federal government to cut benefits.

Both candidates said a solution to the problem could involve raising the income cap on Social Security taxes, now $184,500.

But there were many more disagreements. Van Drew said the state and localities should work with federal officials when they seek to take unauthorized immigrants into custody. He said New Jersey should not be a sanctuary state. He cited examples of people being killed by those in the U.S. illegally.

“You have angel moms come forward whose children were beaten, were raped, were murdered,” Van Drew said.

Mullock decried the Trump administration’s policies.

“What’s happening with masked agents in our streets with no accountability is insanity,” Mullock said. “Barack Obama deported more people than Donald Trump but we did it with decency and dignity. That is what we are as a country.”

title: Four in five immigrants deported under Trump 2.0 have no criminal record, study finds
description:
Majority of deportees had no criminal convictions According to the report, 80 percent of all deportations during the period involved people with no criminal record.
Among immigrants who had lived in the United States for two years or more, 71 percent of those deported had no criminal conviction.
Even among formal removals, where criminal offenders have traditionally represented a larger share of deportees, only 31 percent had criminal convictions.
The findings suggest that immigration enforcement has increasingly focused on migrants living inside the country rather than on recent border arrivals.
Expanded enforcement apparatus The findings come as the Trump administration has significantly expanded immigration enforcement resources.
text:
RIYADH: Of the 980,000 migrants deported during the first 18 months of US President Donald Trump’s second term, only 20 percent were individuals with a criminal conviction, according to a report published on Thursday by the Migration Policy Institute think tank.

The study, authored by Marc Rosenblum, a former head of the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Homeland Security Statistics, provides one of the most comprehensive assessments of immigration enforcement under Trump’s second administration.

The report found that the US Department of Homeland Security, through Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), carried out about 980,000 deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026.

Only around 190,000 of those deported had criminal convictions, despite Trump’s repeated pledges to target what he has described as “the worst of the worst” criminals living in the United States.

Majority of deportees had no criminal convictions

According to the report, 80 percent of all deportations during the period involved people with no criminal record.

Among immigrants who had lived in the United States for two years or more, 71 percent of those deported had no criminal conviction. The trend also extended to long-term residents, with 61 percent of deportees who had lived in the country for a decade or longer having no criminal record.

Even among formal removals, where criminal offenders have traditionally represented a larger share of deportees, only 31 percent had criminal convictions. The report said that was significantly lower than the 44 percent average recorded between fiscal years 2009 and 2021.

The findings suggest that immigration enforcement has increasingly focused on migrants living inside the country rather than on recent border arrivals.

Deportations rise but remain below early-2000s levels

The report said annual deportation levels under Trump’s second term have surpassed those recorded during former President Joe Biden’s administration and Trump’s first term.

However, deportations remain well below the levels routinely seen during the early 2000s.

Of the nearly 980,000 deportations recorded during the first 18 months of Trump’s second term, about 580,000 were classified as removals, 300,000 as enforcement returns and 110,000 as administrative returns.

The study also found a sharp increase in immigration arrests within the US interior. Deportations stemming from interior arrests rose from around 8,000 per month in early 2025 to about 19,000 per month by mid-2026, accounting for nearly 40 percent of all deportations nationwide.

Meanwhile, encounters along the US-Mexico border have fallen to historically low levels, shifting enforcement priorities deeper into the country, according to the report.

Expanded enforcement apparatus

The findings come as the Trump administration has significantly expanded immigration enforcement resources.

Congress approved $240 billion in immigration enforcement funding for DHS through fiscal year 2029, enabling ICE to hire an additional 12,000 officers, more than doubling the agency’s operational workforce.

The administration has also increasingly relied on voluntary departures and enforcement returns to speed up removals and avoid heavily backlogged immigration courts.

According to the report, about 170,000 deportations involved ICE grants of voluntary departure or return, a record level that allowed migrants to leave without going through formal deportation proceedings.

The study also questioned administration claims that more than three million immigrants have left the country through a combination of deportations and voluntary “self-deportations.” Researchers estimated total departures of immigrants who had lived in the US for at least one year at between 790,000 and 1.9 million.

Debate over crackdown continues

Trump has argued that his immigration crackdown and deportation campaign are necessary to improve public safety and enforce immigration laws.

The administration says expanded interior arrests help restore the rule of law and deter illegal immigration.

Civil rights groups and immigration advocates have sharply criticized the policies, arguing that they have eroded due process protections, fostered fear among immigrant communities and increased concerns about racial profiling.

The administration’s immigration measures have faced multiple legal challenges with mixed outcomes in US courts.

Separately, the State Department said this week that the Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 US visas during the president’s second term.

Among the revocations criticized by rights advocates were those involving pro-Palestinian demonstrators protesting Israel’s war in Gaza and foreigners whose social media posts referred to the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.

text:
A U.S. citizen says ICE agents pointed a gun at his face, broke his truck windows and detained him during an arrest in east Charlotte on Wednesday.

Atilio Portillo, who lives in east Charlotte, says he was on his way to work with his brother and nephew on Wednesday morning when ICE vehicles boxed in their pickup truck on Idlewild Road near W.T. Harris Boulevard.

Portillo says agents demanded identification and ordered him at gunpoint to open the driver’s door. He told them he was a U.S. citizen. Bystander video captures Portillo yelling, “I am a U.S. citizen.”

When he refused to open the door, Portillo says, agents broke the truck’s windows and pulled the three men out. He and his nephew, also a U.S. citizen, were handcuffed for nearly 30 minutes while agents checked their citizenship. Portillo says agents did not show him a warrant.

Portillo is from El Salvador. He says he came to the U.S. in 1988 and became a citizen in 2013.

“I feel frustrated and helpless because I couldn’t do anything,” Portillo told WFAE. “In fact, I couldn’t sleep last night. They didn’t just take me out of the truck; they pointed a gun at my face.”

ICE agents released Portillo and his nephew. His brother, whom Portillo says is undocumented, was taken to Stewart Detention Center in Georgia.

ICE has not responded to WFAE’s request for comment.

text:
The United States expelled 536 people between January 2025 and August 2026 to African countries that were not their own, denied them a meaningful chance to contest the transfers, and in several cases delivered them into prisons or onward deportations to the very countries US judges had barred them from being returned to, according to a recent report from Human Rights Watch (HRW).

The 125-page report, entitled “To Scare People: US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa,” draws on interviews with 24 deportees across Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, and South Sudan, along with court records and ICE data obtained through litigation. Human Rights Watch wrote to eight African governments and filed 26 FOIA requests with US agencies; none produced substantive answers.

“The point is to scare people,” an unnamed US official told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The official explained that the value of countries like Palau or Eswatini lies in the threat of dropping people somewhere remote, the official said.

The African transfers formed a small slice of a program that moved nearly 28,000 people to more than 50 third countries in the same period, under arrangements with at least 36 governments, 14 of them in Africa.

A March 2025 memo from then Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem allowed removal without further procedures wherever Washington held diplomatic assurances against persecution or torture, and a July memo from ICE set a 24-hour notice window that could shrink to six hours.

A federal district court vacated both memos in February 2026, an appeals court upheld that ruling in September, and the administration asked the Supreme Court for a stay. Meanwhile, immigration judges pretermitted 31,835 cases, closing asylum claims on the assumption they would be heard abroad.

Most of the people interviewed had already won withholding of removal, a finding by a US immigration judge that they would likely face persecution or torture at home, but were shut out of asylum on technical grounds such as crossing the border irregularly or missing a one-year filing deadline.

That status made them targets. ICE arrested them at routine check-ins, shuffled them between detention centers so lawyers could not locate them, and in several cases, put them on planes within days of a pending habeas petition. Officers told some they were headed to Chad when the destination was Cameroon, or to Ghana when it was the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Every interviewee described being shackled at the wrists, waist, and ankles for the entire flight, sometimes 18 hours or more, and one man was strapped into a full-body restraint after refusing to board. At least a dozen LGBT people, several of whom had been protected from returning home because of their sexual orientation, landed in countries that criminalize same-sex relations.

What awaited them varied by country but rarely included an asylum system. Eswatini locked 32 arrivals in the Matsapha maximum-security prison under a $5.1 million deal to take up to 160 people; a Senate minority report put the cost at $413,333 per deportee. Equatorial Guinea received $7.5 million, more than all US aid to the country over the previous eight years and confined roughly 65 people in a shuttered hotel ringed by armed police before returning about 30 to their home countries, among them a man who had escaped hereditary slavery in Mauritania.

Cameroon held 46 deportees in a Yaoundé facility where malaria spread and chronic conditions went untreated, after Washington withheld a $30 million UNHCR disbursement until the government signed. The Central African Republic accepted 92 people on three flights while the State Department still told Americans not to travel there, and police soon detained two of them in an extortion attempt. Of 15 South Americans flown to Kinshasa in April, none remained by late September; 11 went home despite US orders barring their return.

HRW has called on the United States to suspend all third-country removals and on African governments to refuse new agreements and terminate existing ones, in line with an African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights resolution adopted in October 2025 that warned states against migration partnerships carrying a real risk of serious abuses.

The watchdog contrasts the current arrangements with the 2002 US-Canada safe third country agreement, which was public, reciprocal, binding and enforceable in court, and concluded that none of the African deals plainly met the US legal standard requiring access to a full and fair asylum procedure. Washington, the report noted, paused visa services for countries that refused and withheld UN funding from one that hesitated.

text:
US Rep. Ilhan Omar said Wednesday that she plans to move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal agents searched the property last week, saying the raid had drawn unwanted attention and left her feeling unsafe, according to ABC News.

Federal agents searched the Minnesota Democratic representative's home last week as part of an ongoing criminal investigation into allegations of immigration fraud involving her family's immigration paperwork. Authorities have also issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives.

Omar was born in Somalia and is a naturalized US citizen, and denied the allegations in an interview with MS NOW on Wednesday, her first since the search.

She said she was “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong.”

The investigation comes amid longstanding allegations promoted by Trump supporters and conservative commentators that Omar entered into a fraudulent marriage with her brother and misrepresented details of her immigration history. Omar has repeatedly denied wrongdoing, and the allegations have not been substantiated.

Omar accuses Trump administration of political intimidation

Omar alleged that the raid was politically motivated and was intended to appease supporters of US President Donald Trump who have demanded action against her.

“They kept alluding to the fact that something was going to happen to me,” Omar told MS Now host Chris Hayes. “They had to do something, I believe, to say, ‘Hey, look, we raided her house.'”

In a social media post following the search, Omar accused the administration of weaponizing federal law enforcement against Trump's political opponents.

"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Trump denies involvement in raid, suggests she could go to jail

Trump denied any involvement in the investigation when questioned about the raid on Monday.

“I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he said, describing Omar as “totally crooked” and “a terrible person.”

“That’s really up to the DOJ; I have nothing to do with it,” he added.

Trump has repeatedly criticized Omar, including making personal attacks referencing her Somali heritage and questioning her loyalty to the United States.

During a recent exchange with reporters, he described her as a “sick, very dishonest person who hates our country.”

When asked whether or not Omar could face deportation, Trump suggested that she could also face criminal prosecution.

“Well, she could be. She could also go to jail," he said.

Trump claims Ilhan Omar using fake name, demands resignation from Congress

In a Truth Social post on Friday, Trump claimed that 'Ilhan Omar' is not Omar's real name, instead alleging that it is 'Ilhan Nur Said Elmi.'

"Therefore, because she used a fake name to be sworn in, I assume she must IMMEDIATELY resign from Congress," Trump wrote. "Please inform the Speaker of the House of Representatives, James Michael Johnson, that the Dumocrat Party has just conceded her seat."

Trump also accused Omar of having "openly admitted to FRAUD," and said that she would "not be legally allowed to be a Member of this August Body from this point forth."
