title: Immigrants seeking US citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown
authors: OLGA R. RODRIGUEZ, CLAUDIA LAUER, AMY TAXIN Associated Press, AMY TAXIN - Associated Press
description: Most of the immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud had applied for U.S. citizenship and now face charges related to lying on forms
text:
Homeland Security Investigations officers leave a home after arresting a suspect accused of illegally registering to vote during a federal operation in Commerce, Calif., Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

Homeland Security Investigations task force officers escort a suspect accused of illegally registering to vote during a federal operation in Commerce, Calif., Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

Acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter stands next to a display showing photos of people charged with illegally registering to vote during a news conference in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

A Homeland Security Investigations task force officer stands near police tape marking a perimeter during a federal operation targeting suspected illegal voter registration in Commerce, Calif., Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Most of the immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud had applied for U.S. citizenship and now face charges related to lying on forms or during interviews. Those charges could lead to years in prison and thwart their efforts to naturalize.

One of them is José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, who applied for citizenship in October 2025 after living in the country for 40 years and spending his entire adult life as a legal permanent resident. The federal government has alleged in charging documents that he improperly claimed to be a citizen in 2007 when registering to vote, then later lied about it on his immigration paperwork. The government hasn't accused him of casting a ballot.

Bañuelos-Díaz told The Associated Press he had no idea he had registered to vote until he was arrested Monday outside his Los Angeles home, though he recalls getting a driver's license around 2007. In California, people are prompted to register to vote when applying for a driver’s license.

“I have never voted because I know I can’t vote,” he said. “If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later.”

He was released from custody after his arrest but faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

Federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents in California in a crackdown on people accused of illegally voting or registering to do so. As of Thursday morning, the government had filed charging documents in 10 of the 28 cases, offering additional details about how authorities relied on voter registration data to pursue broader criminal charges around immigration status.

Most of the immigrants charged in California have lived in the country for at least five years, and some of them for decades. They could face deportation if they lied on their citizenship application.

Immigrants convicted of illegally voting in the United States face up to a year in prison. Those convicted of lying on applications to become American citizens face up to a decade.

The Justice Department said in a statement that six people would be charged with voting as a noncitizen, a misdemeanor. The 22 others were facing a combination of felony charges including lying on their naturalization application during interviews or on voter registration forms.

In one case, Homeland Security agents arrested Pamele Arbues Line immediately following her Oct. 15 naturalization interview in San Diego.

In charging documents, the federal government said Line had allegedly registered to vote five times and had submitted ballots in several elections but said in her paperwork and in the interview that she had never voted or claimed to be a U.S. citizen. She later admitted to registering to vote while getting her driver’s license renewed last year and said she voted once, according to the charging documents.

Line, who is from the Philippines, told authorities she thought she was a U.S. citizen because her mother had become naturalized after they moved to the United States more than four decades ago. But Line, now 56, was 19 at the time and not covered by her mother's citizenship, according to the government. She learned she was not a citizen in June when she went to get a renewed Social Security card, and she told agents she applied for naturalization the same day, according to the documents.

She faces at least 10 years in prison if convicted of two charges.

Thanks! You’re all set.

Watch your inbox for Daily Headlines.

The cases are part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare , difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

The Department of Justice has sued California for not complying with a request to verify the citizenship of roughly 20,000 registered voters it says may be noncitizens. California, which has more than 23 million registered voters, has argued the state complies with federal law and that the Trump administration's numbers are likely significantly inflated.

State election officials also noted once a ballot is mailed in, it is separated from any individual voter identification, making it impossible to separate based on the information provided by the federal government.

Beyond voting, the Trump administration has also ramped up immigration enforcement nationwide and slowed down the approval of naturalization applications. Government data shows officials approved 58,000 naturalization applications between April and June 2026, less than a quarter of the number approved in the same period in 2025, according to the data.

Immigrants can apply to become U.S. citizens after holding green cards for at least three years. They must answer extensive questions about activities related to voting, political activities and crime, pass background checks and a civics test and meet English language requirements.

The Department of Homeland Security did not say what initially drew attention to the immigrants charged but said in an email that the agency reviewed naturalization and other records in its investigation. Some of the court documents in the cases describe a benefits fraud audit performed by Homeland Security in August that started the process of identifying those charged this week.

“The voting rights of American citizens must be protected,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the charges this week.

Amandeep Kaur, who is among those charged, has lived in the country for eight years and is in the process of becoming a naturalized U.S. citizen, said her husband, Kulwinder Singh.

Singh said she got her driver's license in 2024 but took the written test at the DMV in Hindi because she struggles with English. He doesn’t know if she registered to vote then. He said she received and returned a ballot in 2024 but they both thought it was a registration form.

Now, he said his wife is distraught with the news that she may have done something illegal.

“All she does is cry. It’s heartbreaking,” said Singh, who is a U.S. citizen.

—

Lauer contributed from Philadelphia and Taxin from Santa Ana, Calif.

description:

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.
The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the "worst of the worst."

text:
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year, a new report released Thursday shows, as arrests ramp up across the country.

The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump's second administration. The numbers fall short of previous highs in the early 2000s and fail to meet the Trump administration's promise, made when it received the billions from Congress, that the money would allow for 1 million deportations annually.

The report, based on publicly available data obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, comes after the Trump administration in January 2025 stopped publicly releasing similar figures compiled by the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year -- when the Trump administration's immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear -- an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI's analysis, that's a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization were from Mexico and didn't often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the U.S. from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them.

And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

The report said voluntary departures -- when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country -- were at an "all-time high," with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025.

People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the U.S. But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country's interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28% of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by this July that had risen to 39%.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said -- 69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the "worst of the worst." Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: "President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history."

Trump administration no longer regularly releases immigration data

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent.

On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump's second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end Dec. 18, and the BBC's attorneys want to make sure they have Trump's deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defense said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also moved back.

Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, "Trump: A Second Chance."

The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump's claims that it defamed him.

READ MORE: Trump sues BBC for $10 billion, accusing it of defamation deceptive practices over editing of his Jan. 6 speech

Trump's lawyers say Jack Smith 'lacks personal knowledge' of issues in the case

To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump's lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.

The parties were expected to address the issue later in Thursday's hearing.

"Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter," they argued in the filing. "He was not present when President Trump's January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump's state of mind at the time the Speech was given."

Trump's side also argued that "Smith's testimony would be duplicative," because he published a lengthy report on the events of Jan. 6 and also testified for many hours. "The entirety of his testimony is publicly available," it argued.

The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of Jan. 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years.

"It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him," the BBC's lawyers argued.

"No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim."

“Today, the City Council approved my proposal to reestablish the Immigrant Legal Defense Fund, an important step toward protecting our residents, defending due process, and standing up against the Trump administration’s abusive immigration enforcement practices.

The City of Fresno has successfully challenged the Trump administration in federal court when it attempted to withhold critical federal funding from our city. We stood up to protect our city’s resources then, and we have a responsibility to stand up for our residents now.

If we can take the federal government to court to protect our city’s funding, we can and must provide our residents with the resources to defend themselves in court when their fundamental constitutional rights are at stake.

Our immigrant communities are an integral part of Fresno. They are our neighbors, coworkers, business owners, and taxpayers who contribute to our local economy, strengthen our neighborhoods, and play an essential role in our city’s continued growth and prosperity. They deserve dignity, fairness, and full Constitutional protection.

No president, federal agency, or immigration enforcement officer is above the law. Due process is not a privilege reserved for a select few; it is a fundamental constitutional protection afforded to every person in this country, regardless of immigration status.

Today’s action sends a clear message: Fresno will not turn its back on immigrant families facing fear, intimidation, or potential violations of their constitutional rights. We have fought to protect our city’s resources. Now, we are committing resources to protect our residents.”

During the meeting, Councilman Karbassi was putting forth a resolution about an old lawsuit when Councilman Arias interrupted and said he would like to say something, and said, "F-Trump and F-Pedophiles".

Can ICE agents legally operate at or near polling stations?

On Tuesday, Human Rights Watch called on the Trump administration to order ICE agents not to deploy near polling stations or other midterm election sites.
text:
Since returning to office for a second term, United States President Donald Trump has embarked on a campaign to root out and deport the country’s undocumented immigrants.

Spearheading that campaign is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal agency housed in the Department of Homeland Security.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls

list 2 of 3Key takeaways from Donald Trump’s controversial speech on election security

list 3 of 3Homeland Security Secretary Mullin reiterates Trump threats about elections

end of list

Under Trump, the agency has grown substantially, boasting 22,000 officers and agents as of January, a staffing increase of 120 percent.

Thanks to recent spending packages, ICE is also considered the best-funded federal law enforcement agency in the US.

But the agency, founded in 2003, has come under increased scrutiny for its aggressive tactics and expedited hiring techniques.

Immigration agents, under the authority of ICE and other agencies, have been responsible for at least 25 shootings since the start of Trump’s second term, six of which have been fatal. At least 60 people have also died in ICE custody since January 2025.

That track record has made democracy advocates and human rights groups worried about ICE’s activities in the lead-up to the November 3 midterm elections.

Organisations like Human Rights Watch and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) have voiced concern that the Trump administration could use ICE to intimidate voters.

The threat of encountering ICE agents could also keep some voters away from the ballot box, the groups say. One national poll, conducted in September by the University of California, San Diego, found that 40 percent of respondents expected ICE agents to be present near polling stations on election day.

Can ICE agents legally operate at or near polling stations?

Federal law prohibits the use of armed federal agents at polling stations. Some states have similar provisions.

The federal prohibition dates back to 1865. The law reads that it is illegal for anyone “engaged in the civil, military or naval service of the United States” to order or bring “any troops or armed men” to election sites.

There is, however, a loophole if such force is needed “to keep peace at the polls” or “to repel armed enemies of the United States”.

Another federal law prohibits members of the military from interfering with elections, and several other laws prohibit efforts to “intimidate” voters.

Those measures have been tested this year. During the primary elections for the midterms, there were at least two incidents – one in San Antonio, Texas, and another in Ventura County, California – where ICE agents reportedly conducted routine operations near polling stations.

In both cases, the ICE agents left after being asked to do so by local police.

How has the Trump administration used ICE agents before the election?

Though there are prohibitions against law enforcement near polling stations, advocacy groups say the Trump administration has nevertheless used ICE agents for election-related matters.

ICE has different offices under its control, one of which is Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).

In the months leading up to this year’s midterm elections, HSI has reportedly been ordered to prioritise its investigations of non-citizen voting, an illegal act. Only US citizens are allowed to vote in federal elections.

Starting in August, the Department of Homeland Security deployed HSI agents for “field investigations” in at least nine states to probe questions of voter eligibility.

Some have reportedly gone door to door, asking residents if they are citizens and if they plan to vote.

This week, a federal judge ordered the Department of Homeland Security to pause those investigations, citing the risk that a US citizen could be “wrongly swept up” and “subjected to intimidation”.

The judge also noted a “high likelihood of error” in how the federal agents were identifying alleged non-citizens.

Trump has pointed to non-citizen voting as support for his false claims of pervasive voter fraud.

Experts, though, say such fears are unfounded, with tiny numbers of non-citizens actually taking part in elections, despite Trump’s depictions of the issue as a widespread problem.

What has the Trump administration said about deploying ICE during the midterms?

Trump officials have refused to rule out using ICE agents to stop illegal voting, an effort that could extend to election day itself.

In May, Trump was asked by reporters: “For the midterm elections, would you send the National Guard or ICE to voting locations in November?”

Trump declined to answer directly. “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections,” he replied.

Other leaders in his administration have issued similar statements. In September, for instance, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin affirmed that ICE would not “patrol” polling stations, but he suggested its agents could be there for other reasons.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said.

Another member of Trump’s cabinet, Attorney General Todd Blanche, has questioned the uproar over the issue, framing it as misguided.

“Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations?” he asked in March at a conservative conference. “Illegals can’t vote. It doesn’t make any sense.”

What has been the response from advocacy groups?

The Trump administration’s rhetoric has raised alarm with a number of rights groups, who fear an ICE presence on election day could dampen voter turnout.

On Tuesday, Human Rights Watch called on the Trump administration to order ICE agents not to deploy near polling stations or other midterm election sites.

“ICE officers’ abuses have already seriously affected US citizens who have been stopped, beaten, detained, deported and even killed,” said Philippe Bolopion, the executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Voters should not have to fear being caught in an ICE dragnet when they head to the polls.”

On October 16, the rights group Amnesty International issued a similar appeal.

“Eligible voters must have the meaningful opportunity to participate in elections without discriminatory and arbitrary barriers, intimidation by armed forces, or fear of harm when seeking to exercise their rights,” the group said.

title: Trump's Justice Department Ditches Civil Rights and School Desegregation Cases
authors: Zack Kligler, Jessica Corbett, Josh Friedberg, Danny Katch, Shireen Akram-Boshar, Aallyah Wright, Johnnie Jae, Alecia Taylor, Petala Ironcloud, Adam Mahoney
description:
The new analyses of the cases — “Walking Away: DOJ’s Abandonment of Civil Rights Cases for People of Color” and “Filling in The Gaps: Tracking The 50+ School Desegregation Cases DOJ Says It Is Ending” — were developed by Democracy Forward’s oversight and accountability project Red Line for Civil Rights.
“People and communities rely on DOJ to pursue vital cases to address threats to civil rights under our nation’s laws.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 authorized DOJ to file its own school desegregation lawsuits against public schools or institutions of higher education and to join cases that families had already brought,” the paper explains.
“These school desegregation cases are how the promise of Brown reaches individual classrooms.
“Not only has the Civil Rights Division abandoned its work to protect the rights of our most marginalized students, but it is also weaponizing civil rights statutes against them.” Democratic leaders in the US House of Representatives also spoke out about the project’s findings.
text:
A pair of papers published Thursday by the legal group Democracy Forward detail how, under President Donald Trump, the Department of Justice has dumped dozens of cases focused on school desegregation and the civil rights of people of color, all while weaponizing the DOJ to serve “the most dangerous criminal in US history” and his allies.

The cases were previously taken up by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, currently led by Harmeet Dhillon, whose confirmation was controversial — like those of Trump’s first attorney general for this term, Pam Bondi, whom he fired in April and replaced with his former personal lawyer, Todd Blanche.

The new analyses of the cases — “Walking Away: DOJ’s Abandonment of Civil Rights Cases for People of Color” and “Filling in The Gaps: Tracking The 50+ School Desegregation Cases DOJ Says It Is Ending” — were developed by Democracy Forward’s oversight and accountability project Red Line for Civil Rights.

“People and communities rely on DOJ to pursue vital cases to address threats to civil rights under our nation’s laws. The Red Line for Civil Rights reports don’t just highlight the cases that have been abandoned, but also make clear the harm that DOJ’s abandonment of its mission retreat has caused,” said Democracy Forward president and CEO Skye Perryman.

The project found at least 36 abandoned cases and probes addressing discrimination against Black, Latino, and Native American people, from Voting Rights Act lawsuits and redlining settlements with banks to firefighter and police hiring issues.

There was United States v. Cobb County, Georgia, in which the DOJ alleged that credit checks and a written exam illegally screened out Black firefighter applicants, and United States v. Patriot Bank, a 2024 consent order over redlining of Black and Hispanic neighborhoods in Memphis, Tennessee.

In United States v. SouthEast Bank, the department argued that a student loan refinancing product discriminated against Alaska Native, American Indian, and Black applicants, and in United States v. City of Minneapolis, the DOJ concluded that police discriminated against Black and Native American in Minnesotans.

“The shameful withdrawal of DOJ resources from these cases and investigations highlights how this administration is abandoning communities across the country,” said Megan Marks, a former leader in the department who is now the project’s deputy director and managing editor. “Walking away from them doesn’t mean the discrimination has been addressed. It just means DOJ is no longer watching.”

In its second analysis, the project identified 56 school districts in 12 states where the department has moved to ditch or end a desegregation case, or did not oppose ending one — from Athens City, Alabama and Chesterfield County, South Carolina to South Bend, Indiana and Waterbury, Connecticut.

“The Supreme Court held in its landmark 1954 case, Brown v. Board of Education, that segregating public school students by race violates the 14th Amendment’s guarantee of equal protection,” the report notes. “Since Brown, DOJ has monitored and enforced desegregation orders, reviewing evidence and often working collaboratively with school districts and, in some cases, private plaintiffs to support progress.”

“This work was central to the Civil Rights Division’s history. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 authorized DOJ to file its own school desegregation lawsuits against public schools or institutions of higher education and to join cases that families had already brought,” the paper explains. “These school desegregation cases are how the promise of Brown reaches individual classrooms. Behind each of these cases are children, families, and a community that fought, sometimes at great personal risk, for the right to an equal education.”

Shaheena Simons previously oversaw the Justice Department’s desegregation docket but is now a senior adviser at the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. In response to the report, she said that the “DOJ’s haste to end these cases without deliberation or transparency is a betrayal of Black students who continue to face segregation and inequality in our schools.”

“This retreat is part of a much bigger picture,” Simons emphasized. “Not only has the Civil Rights Division abandoned its work to protect the rights of our most marginalized students, but it is also weaponizing civil rights statutes against them.”

Democratic leaders in the US House of Representatives also spoke out about the project’s findings. Education and Workforce Committee Ranking Member Bobby Scott (Va.) accused the “politicized” department of “turning its back on workers and students by abandoning entire categories of discrimination cases and ending the fight against school desegregation altogether.”

Democrats on his panel “are committed to the protection of civil rights and to guaranteeing that all Americans are protected from discrimination in accordance with the civil rights laws that so many Americans fought to secure,” pledged Scott, as his party prepares for next month’s midterm elections, in which Republicans could lose control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Fellow Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin (Md.), a constitutional scholar and ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, said that “Democracy Forward’s reports expose the Justice Department’s shocking betrayal of its central duty to protect Americans against race discrimination.”

“While DOJ devotes its resources to persecuting Trump’s political enemies, it has dropped protection of voting rights and is allowing discrimination to proliferate by abandoning school desegregation and job discrimination cases,” he said, as the Trump administration pursues everyone from former Federal Bureau of Investigation Director James Comey to New York Attorney General Letitia James and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).

text:
Hennepin County Sheriff Dawanna Witt is seeking re-election after taking fire from both sides in the aftermath of Operation Metro Surge, the ICE surge in Minnesota this year. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement threatened her with arrest for not helping the agency, while protesters accused her of being an ICE collaborator.

DFL delegates also denied her the party's endorsement in the nonpartisan race for sheriff.

Witt defended her record in an interview with WCCO's Esme Murphy, who asked how she answers the criticism that she was "too much in bed with ICE." Witt said her job is to protect everyone and that she can't discriminate based on whether someone is a Republican, a Democrat, the color of their skin or otherwise

"How am I not doing what I was elected to do?" Witt said. She added it "makes absolutely no sense" to say she is cooperating too much when she has "been served 18 subpoenas, threatening my arrest."

The New York Times reported that federal immigration officials began sending letters in July warning Witt she could face tampering charges. The dispute centers on when the Hennepin County jail turns people over to ICE. In February, Witt told WCCO the jail would cooperate with ICE if agents obtained a judicial warrant for an individual's arrest.

Sheriff's deputies were at the scene of protests, especially outside the Whipple Federal Building, an area that does not have its own police department.

Witt is also a key player in the coordinated law enforcement effort to target Somali gangs. At the podium in the fight against gang violence, she is often the only woman, and the only woman of color. Witt said it "doesn't feel so weird" now, but she said she initially worried about being judged for being a woman — and a Black woman — in the role.

Witt's opponent is Joseph Banks, who ran against her in 2022 and lost by about 30 points. Witt won that race as the first woman and first person of color to serve as Hennepin County sheriff. Asked by Murphy why he thinks he can win this time, Banks said he now has more name recognition.

Banks is a former police chief for the Lower Sioux Indian Community, home to Jackpot Junction Casino. He said that job meant dealing with thousands of people visiting the casinos every day.

Banks said he wants more cooperation with ICE.

"I think we have a responsibility to work with our federal partners to keep everybody safe," he said, adding he would "definitely make sure that we're in the room with Homeland Security."

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it resume building a border wall project through the Big Bend region of Texas.

The government filed an emergency appeal asking the justices to lift a lower court decision halting construction. That ruling marked a setback to one of President Donald Trump’s signature projects.

The administration has been racing forward with construction on a border wall and other infrastructure from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.

But in the Big Bend region, the administration has run into opposition from ranchers, residents, business owners and environmentalists who argue the projects are a waste of money in an area of historically low illegal immigration and that construction could harm the region’s scenic landscapes.

Opponents have filed numerous lawsuits seeking to stop the project, which in the Big Bend consists of a mixture of walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.

Ruling in one of those cases, Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 ordered the government to stop construction across the roughly 500-mile project area while the case plays out in the courts. It was a major victory for the bipartisan opposition.

The case hinges on sweeping waivers signed by the secretary of Homeland Security that allow U.S. Customs and Border Protection to bypass environmental and other regulations that would otherwise slow down construction of such a major project.

The government argued that the Big Bend sector is an area of high illegal entry, and said legislation dating back to 1996 explicitly gives the secretary these far-reaching powers as necessary to build physical barriers or roads near the border to stop people from crossing illegally.

Opponents disagreed, arguing that Congress gave that power to waive regulations specifically in areas of “high illegal entry.” They said Big Bend, a remote and rugged region, doesn’t fit that description.

Cardone sided with the opponents.

“The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their major questions doctrine claim that the Big Bend Waivers were issued in excess of the Secretary’s authority,” she wrote.

Trump has long vowed to build a border wall along the roughly 2,000-mile length of the southwest border. Last summer, Republicans in Congress allocated Homeland Security $46 billion to finish the project, which will be a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.

The opposition in Texas’s Big Bend region had been brewing for months, but it escalated in August when bulldozers were spotted clearing land in Big Bend National Park.

The preliminary injunction filed by Cardone stops construction there as well as land up and downriver from the park that is owned by private landowners or the state.

The government has argued that if this region is one of the only areas left without a wall or other border infrastructure, illegal immigration could end up funneling to the Big Bend. But opponents have argued that other forms of infrastructure such as drones or surveillance towers are just as effective and a lot less expensive than the wall plans.

text:
Congresswoman Pettersen at today’s immigration roundtable with representatives from Casa de Paz, Hispanic Contractors of Colorado, COLOR Latina, Mi Casa Resource Center, Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network, Mi Familia Vota, American Friends Service Committee, Adelante Community Development, Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition, CLLARO, and Lideres Latines

LAKEWOOD – Today, Congresswoman Pettersen (CO-07) convened local leaders to discuss the ongoing abuses by Trump’s rogue Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency and discuss with local leaders their shared priority to strengthen oversight and establish guardrails to protect immigrant communities in the next Congress. Pettersen also first announced to the group that she, alongside Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37) today introduced two bills to protect disaster survivors’ personal information from being used for the purposes of immigration enforcement. This comes after the devastating Aspen Acres and Willow Fires forced thousands of Coloradans to evacuate earlier this summer, raising concerns that data collected through the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and non-government entities to issue re-entry cards to affected areas in the wake of a natural disaster could be accessed by immigration enforcement.

“From the very beginning, Trump’s ICE agency has acted without regard for basic human rights and safety – killing innocent people, detaining people in inhumane conditions, ripping families apart, and spreading fear throughout our immigrant communities. We need to rein in this agency and look ahead to what the next Congress can do to put real guardrails in place, hold ICE accountable, and protect our communities,” saidCongresswoman Pettersen. “And no family fleeing a wildfire should have to wonder whether to ask for help or evacuate out of fear that their information will be used to target them. I’m so grateful for everyone who joined me today to have an honest discussion on how we can protect our neighbors and our community.”

“Every family deserves access to resources following a natural disaster without fear that their information will be used against them,” said Congresswoman Kamlager-Dove. “I am proud to join Rep. Pettersen on this package to prevent ICE from accessing data collected in response to a natural disaster. No one should be able to take advantage of our immigrant neighbors during a vulnerable time.”

“No family should have to fear deportation when seeking safety from a wildfire or asking for help after a disaster,” said Alex Sánchez, president and CEO of Voces Unidas. “These bills would help protect the personal information Latino and immigrant families share to get emergency assistance. We thank Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen for her leadership and urge Congress to pass these protections.”

The roundtable brought together leaders from Casa de Paz, Hispanic Contractors of Colorado, COLOR Latina, Mi Casa Resource Center, Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network, Mi Familia Vota, American Friends Service Committee, Adelante Community Development, Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition, CLLARO, and Lideres Latines to discuss how ICE’s enforcement practices are affecting immigrant communities across Colorado.

The group discussed the various abuses that ICE has carried out on communities, including the killings of multiple innocent people including American citizens, the long-term detention of individuals in temporary holding cells that lack basic access to sanitation, and repeated ICE operations in and around sensitive areas including schools and churches. Wait times for immigration cases, applications, and work authorization documents have also been affected, with certain applications now taking over 6 months to process – leaving families facing prolonged uncertainty about their immigration cases and ability to work. Pettersen focused the discussion on where gaps in services are leaving families without support as well as her priorities for the 120th Congress, including bipartisan opportunities to expand access to counsel, improve detention transparency, and strengthen protections for children and mothers.

During the discussion, Pettersen also announced the introduction of her two new bills, the Emergency Assistance Privacy Protection Act and the Disaster Data Protection Act. These bills prohibit FEMA from sharing disaster survivors’ personally identifiable information with ICE and prohibit ICE from obtaining disaster data collected by third parties without a judicial warrant, respectively. This followed the Congresswoman’s visits to areas affected by this year’s Willow and Aspen Acres Fires, which burned over 100,000 acres of land, including in Custer and Lake counties, and forced thousands to evacuate from their homes. Residents affected by the evacuations expressed concerns that the personal information collected by FEMA in the wake of a natural disaster to administer re-entry cards to evacuated areas could be accessed and used by ICE for non-targeted immigration enforcement. This raises larger concerns that members of the immigrant community would forgo evacuation orders or fail to properly identify themselves to first responders and other disaster response personnel out of fear that this information will be accessed by ICE.

Specifically, the Emergency Assistance Privacy Protection Act would:

Prohibit data sharing of any personally identifiable information collected by FEMA with ICE.

Full bill text can be found HERE.

Specifically, the Disaster Data Protection Act would:

Prohibit ICE from obtaining data collected by a third party during a disaster absent a criminal warrant.

Full bill text can be found HERE.

Under the Trump Administration, Congressional Republicans have repeatedly voted to send more money to ICE and immigration enforcement with no guardrails, including over $70 billion initially through H.R. 1 and an additional $70 billion this past summer for ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) over three years – even as the agency has come under fire for its conduct. Pettersen has consistently voted against allocating additional funds to ICE, calling for major regulatory oversight and guardrails to keep immigrant communities safe.

Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen has repeatedly pushed back against Trump’s harmful immigration policiesand efforts to pour billions more into ICE and CBP without meaningful accountability. She has voted against enforcement funding packages, backed legislation requiring agents to visibly identify themselves, and supported restoring protections for schools, hospitals, and places of worship. Alongside Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper, she demanded that the administration abandon plans for a new ICE detention facility in Hudson,Colorado. She has also pressed for answers about prolonged detention in field office holding cells and proposed safeguards to protect detained parents’ children and prevent immigration detainees from being held in federal prisons.

Isaac Apodaca and Kierra McCulley are set to be sentenced Th…

The complaint brings claims under the federal Trafficking Vi…



Capital High student J.J. Luévano, left, talks to a few dozen mostly south-side students gathered in the parking lot at the Santa Fe Place mall after a school walkout Wednesday to protest recent immigration raids on construction sites around town.

The students knew they would be marked with an unexcused absence for walking out.

Still, about 430 did.

“We don't care, because we’ve got to support our people,” said Milagro Middle School seventh grader Amaris Ortiz. “We've got to support our people who belong here.”

The hundreds of students, who left their campuses around lunchtime Wednesday, hailed from seven Santa Fe schools. Though only a few dozen — ranging from grades six through 12 — gathered at their planned endpoint in the parking lot of the Santa Fe Place mall, their message for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was unified.

“Today we walked out to show our support to the immigrants and to stop ICE and to try our best to abolish it,” said Giselle Garcia, a sixth grade student at Ortiz Middle School.

She clutched a sign reading “Ice should be in our drinks not in our cities.” Others pinned Mexican flags to their cars; some danced and chanted.

The anti-ICE walkout came amid a recent reported surge in arrests of immigrants nationwide — including in New Mexico. Last week, federal immigration agents raided a Santa Fe housing construction site and arrested several people; in August, ICE agents arrested others, including a man taking his daughter to a health clinic who was jailed for several weeks despite being a legal resident.

The headlines about the construction site arrests spurred Capital High School junior J.J. Luévano into action. “We need to do something; we need to solve this,” she said.

“We’re not aliens,” Luévano continued. “We’re Mexicans, we’re Latinos, we’re Hispanic. We are all people here.”

Leonardo Ramirez decorates his car with a hybrid Mexican and American flag as a few dozen mostly south-side students gather Wednesday in a parking lot at Santa Fe Place mall after a school walkout to protest recent immigration raids around town.

After talking with her mother, Earth Care community development coordinator Miriam Luévano, she created an Instagram account to spread the word about the walkout and coordinated with students at three other south-side schools.

Meanwhile, Santa Fe High School senior Genoveva Zuniga made a separate account to mobilize east-side students. When she heard about last week’s immigration arrests, Zuniga said she had to check on a close family friend who works in construction.

He did not have any encounters with federal immigration agents, Zuniga said, but she rejects the stereotypes she believes led those agents to construction sites in the first place.

“That’s their thing — that we’re stealing jobs, that immigrants are stealing jobs, that us teens, Hispanics, are stealing jobs,” Zuniga said.

Zuniga and Luévano — though they had never met before — messaged each other and started working together.

Santa Fe Public Schools sent out an email to students Tuesday as word of the walkout spread.

“Please be aware that students who leave campus during the school day without an excused absence or without following proper school procedures will be marked with an unexcused absence in accordance with district policy,” stated the email, which Zuniga posted to her Instagram page.

Some students — including 85 of the 105 who walked out of Milagro — returned to class later Wednesday, district spokesperson Joe Abeyta wrote in an email. Regardless, students’ parents or guardians would have had to call in to their school in order for their absence to be excused, he wrote.

“This protest was not initiated or promoted by Santa Fe Public Schools,” the district said in a statement. “Student safety remains our highest priority, and we believe schools are the safest place for students during the school day. We encourage families to speak with their children about the importance of remaining on campus and attending school as scheduled.”

The district also coordinated with police. Officers in the Santa Fe Police Department’s recently launched Real Time Operations Center monitored the walkouts with a drone, interim Chief Ben Valdez wrote in an email, “to ensure traffic was not being obstructed and no safety concern existed for participants and members of the community as they engaged in constitutionally protected activities.”

No criminal activity was observed or reported as a result of the walkout, Valdez wrote.

Some who gathered at the mall filmed the drone. Members of Santa Fe Rapid Response — a group of volunteers that fact-checks and responds to local reports of federal immigration agents — stood in the parking lot with whistles around their necks.

A few dozen mostly south-side students gather in a parking lot at the Santa Fe Place mall after a school walkout Wednesday to protest recent immigration raids on construction sites around town.

Though student protests aren’t the group’s typical scene, Rapid Response member Darby Begeman said they had received a request to keep an eye out for an ICE presence around the walkout.

“I’m heart-warmed to see that students are paying attention and are concerned about what’s going on,” she said. “I’m not surprised — a lot of these individuals have family members, loved ones, friends … who may not have papers. And so I imagine there are very, very many of them who are certainly concerned about what’s happening in our country right now.”

Mateo Garcia, a seventh grade student at Milagro, said his family is composed of immigrants but he was born in the United States. President Donald Trump, he said, “has no right” to remove innocent people “out of a land that promised them good stuff.”

“I feel like it’s bad for them to take my family, because I was born here,” Garcia said. “So I’d have nobody. And immigration has no right to take innocent people who did nothing.”

Lily Alexander is a state accountability reporter for The New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico, focusing on equity and transparency. Her position is part of the New Mexican Public Service Journalism Fund, and her stories are available to all readers without a paywall.

text:
10.22.2026

By Jennifer Andrus

Recent changes to federal immigration policy on visas, international travel and regulatory compliance are causing confusion and uncertainty for employees and their employers.

The New York State Bar Association’s Health Law Section focused on the implications for attorneys working in the healthcare industry in a recent continuing education course. The course was presented by Cianna Freeman-Tolbert, a health law expert from Whiteman Osterman and Hanna in Albany.

Freeman-Tolbert reported that more than 370,000 non-citizens work for a healthcare provider such as a hospital, home care provider or nursing home in New York State.

“Immigration impacts everyone from the technician to the occupational therapist to the surgeon,” she said. “Your organization may be impacted with a loss of staff or hefty fines if you are not prepared.”

Changes to Work Visas

Most international, college educated health care professionals obtain the H1B visa to work in the United States. This year, foreign workers applying to work in the U.S. will need to pay $100,000 for an H1B visa application.

Freeman-Tolbert says the fee applies to new applicants and not those who are traveling outside the U.S. who already have the visa and wish to reenter the country. She warns that health systems and research facilities may think twice about hiring a physician or researcher from abroad who needs a work visa.

Medical students who wish to work in America after graduation must pay $70,000 for a one-year work visa. Students must apply for the visa through the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services office and shoulder the cost. Previously, college staff were able to help students who were applying.

The rationale, Freeman-Tolbert explains, is to move the visa process directly to the federal government to track applicants better. Both visa fees are being challenged in the courts and remain under injunction.

Department of State Pauses Visa Processing

To add more barriers to the visa process, in August 2026, the U.S. Department of State paused all processing of immigrant visas in consulates and embassies, citing a need for additional staff training.

There is some processing happening, but Freeman-Tolbert said it has been a severe reduction in the workflow. She also reminded the attorneys that all visa applicants will undergo enhanced vetting of all social media accounts, which must be made accessible to the public. Failing to make an Instagram or Facebook account public will slow the approval process further.

Prepare Contingencies for International Travel and Work

Healthcare providers and other businesses that employ foreign nationals must prepare contingency plans for employees traveling abroad, Freeman-Tolbert warns. Customs and Border Patrol have more latitude when it comes to seizing and searching electronic devices and laptops at a point of entry to the United States. If an employee is detained for national security reasons, attorneys need to be ready to respond.

“When someone leaves the country, make sure you coordinate with your department head that you may be gone longer than you plan,” she advises. “You need to be proactive. If you are doing international travel, you need a policy.”

Plan for the ICE Visit Now

Freeman-Tolbert advises attorneys to prepare their clients now for a visit from Immigration and Customs Enforcement saying it’s not a matter of if they are coming but when.

“In a health care organization, when ICE comes, they are going to serve a notice of inspection and they will likely not have masks on,” she said. “You need to have a protocol in place for who gives consent for them to enter. You can’t have one front desk worker look at a warrant and let them in.”

ICE access is limited to designated public spaces in a healthcare setting such as a waiting room in the Emergency Department. Clear signage showing which areas are public and which are private or staff only will protect patients and employees.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- The Fresno City Council voted Thursday to re-establish the city's immigration legal defense fund amid what officials describe as increased Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in recent weeks.

Councilmember Miguel Arias said demand for legal assistance has increased significantly.

"We've seen in these recent ICE raids, citizens and legal immigrants have also been picked up and victimized, including those who are undocumented. They have a right to due process. The defense fund is designed to help residents' constitutional rights that have been violated by ICE," Arias said.

According to city officials, funding for the program would come from salary savings generated by keeping vacant city positions unfilled.

Opponents of the proposal argued that taxpayer dollars should not be used to benefit a single group of residents.

"If the real concern is due process when government acts badly, the answer is simple make the fund available to any Fresno resident harmed by government or political abuse," Fresno resident Niel O'Brien said.

Arias defended the proposal by comparing it to legal assistance provided in eviction cases.

"Eviction is a civil matter. Immigration is a civil matter. We have invested more than $6 million representing those who are legally evicted who are residents of Fresno. This is no different," Arias said.

The city has previously funded immigration legal defense efforts. In 2022, Fresno spent $200,000 on 18 immigration cases. Of those, eight remain open, and 10 were completed successfully.

In 2023, the city spent $100,000 on 17 cases. Sixteen remain open, while one was completed successfully.

In 2025, the city budgeted $100,000 for the program, but legal staff were instructed not to open any new cases.

The city attorney's office said there are several reasons many of the cases remain unresolved. In some instances, outside legal counsel is still awaiting documents. Other cases remain pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, while some hearings are scheduled years into the future.

As the council meeting continued inside City Hall, demonstrators gathered outside. State Assemblywoman Esmeralda Soria joined the protest following her announcement of $3 million for Central Valley community organizations that support immigrant families.

"We're saying ICE out. We want them to stop doing what they're doing. They are racially profiling people regardless of if they are citizens are not. And our families are scared," Soria said.

The vote could still face a challenge from Mayor Jerry Dyer, who has the authority to veto the measure. Dyer has previously described the proposal as premature.

"I try not to replicate or duplicate what other government entities are doing, like the county, the state or the feds, or nonprofits," Dyer said.

This fund will only apply to those with no criminal convictions, and they must be residents of Fresno.

text:
“Impartiality is imperative to ensuring public trust in our Nation’s judiciary,” the DOJ wrote Wednesday. “Judge Schiltz’s and Judge Tunheim’s on-the-record participation in a recent highly partisan New York Times Article, along with Judge Schiltz’s subsequent public comments, unquestionably calls into doubt whether they can be impartial in these cases.”

Schiltz, an appointee of former President George W. Bush and the chief judge of the U.S. District Court for Minnesota last winter, drew criticism from the administration after describing its actions as “a grave threat to the rule of law.” He previously clerked for the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia.

Tunheim, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, also drew criticism for comments about immigration arrests.

“They weren’t arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street,” Tunheim told the New York Times.

In his motion targeting Schiltz, Woodard argued that a judge who has taken a position on immigration enforcement should not preside over a case involving the administration’s effort to expand denaturalization proceedings.

“A judge who has publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement cannot then preside over a case concerning one of the Justice Department’s key immigration initiatives: pursuing the largest denaturalization effort in Department history to restore trust and integrity in U.S. citizenship,” Woodard wrote.

He argued that allowing Schiltz to remain on the case would undermine public confidence in the proceedings.

“Absent recusal, the American people will reasonably question whether Judge Schiltz can be impartial regarding this important matter defending the integrity of American citizenship,” Woodard wrote.

The Justice Department made a similar argument against Tunheim, claiming his comments to the news outlet suggested he viewed the charges against the South African defendant as unwarranted.

“To Judge Tunheim, the ‘rule of law’ apparently means ignoring the law when it comes to illegal aliens who have broken the law,” Woodward wrote. “In sum, Judge Tunheim’s statements and participation in the New York Times article, at a minimum, give rise to the appearance of bias in immigration-related cases.”

Schiltz has scheduled a hearing on the motion seeking his recusal for Nov. 23.

DOJ steps up fight with judges accused of bias and stalling Trump agenda

The filings follow another effort by Woodard to remove a federal judge from a case involving the Trump administration. Over the weekend, he sought to disqualify U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington, D.C., from overseeing litigation over the president’s efforts to overhaul a historic public golf course in the capital.

Reyes rejected the Justice Department’s request Sunday, accusing the department of using “selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion.”

text:
ELOY, AZ — Yesterday, Representatives Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07) and Maxine Dexter (OR-03), joined alongside Reproductive Freedom for All President Mini Timmaraju, for an oversight visit to the Eloy Detention Center to hear directly from women about their reproductive health experiences in immigration detention. Multiple pregnant women have previously been held at Eloy, including one who miscarried. This is a departure from the policies of previous administrations that typically did not hold pregnant people in detention.

“The inhumane conditions inside Eloy Detention Center are unconscionable. Maria, a high-risk pregnant woman, is being denied critical medical care and adequate food. My constituent, Lilianne, the wife of a U.S. citizen, was detained at her green card appointment and is now being denied basic feminine hygiene products. No one should be treated this way,” said Rep. Ansari. “All the while, the Trump Administration is pouring billions into ICE as private prison corporations like CoreCivic and GEO Group profit from detention. The level of cruelty and corruption is abundantly clear. This is a profound failure of human dignity, and we will hold this Administration accountable.”

This marked Ansari's fourteenth oversight visit to an ICE detnetion facility. This visit focused on the urgent need to protect reproductive health, ensure access to adequate medical care, and uphold the dignity of women in immigration detention. During the visit, the lawmakers heard from women about their experiences navigating pregnancy and accessing essential reproductive health supplies while detained. The lawmakers met with two women:

Maria Alejandra Valero Brinez, a 24-year-old Venezuelan woman and mother of a six-year-old son. She has valid employment authorization until 2029, a pending asylum petition, and no criminal convictions. She was living in Mesa, Arizona before she was detained in August. She is approximately five months pregnant, and described serious concerns about her pregnancy and access to adequate medical care while detained. She has experienced spotting and reported that she has to throw herself on the ground and plead for attention in order to receive medical care. When she was able to receive care, the doctors informed her she has a low-lying placenta — the same condition that led to a stillborn birth three years earlier. Despite having a high-risk pregnancy, she said she has not been able to receive images from ultrasounds or other information about her and her baby’s condition. Maria fears for their safety and well-being, especially given the lack of information about her pregnancy. She is also afraid to express any emotion about her current condition, as detainees are often placed into solitary confinement if they show any signs of emotional distress.

Maria also raised concerns about access to drinking water and food inside the facility. Despite clear doctor’s recommendations to receive double food portions, Maria reports that one guard routinely dismisses this and only gives her the standard single portion. Maria also reported that she was not given antibiotics following a dental abscess that led to a tooth extraction. Untreated bacterial infections have the potential to cause miscarriages. Earlier this year, Emmanuel Damas passed away due to complications from an untreated tooth infection after being held at the Florence Detention Center.

Lilianne (who only wishes to use her first name), a Cuban woman detained at Eloy, described difficulties obtaining sufficient menstrual hygiene products. She reported inconsistent access, with the number of products provided varying depending on the detention officer, raising concerns about the availability of basic necessities for women in custody.

“Maria and Lilianne’s stories show the deliberate cruelty at the heart of the Trump Administration’s immigration agenda. Their treatment is not just inhumane — it is a disgraceful failure of the government's legal duty to protect the people in its custody,” said Rep. Grijalva. “While private contractors rake in billions of taxpayer dollars, they are denying the most vulnerable individuals – including pregnant people – their most basic necessities, including medical care, clean drinking water, and adequate food. These corporations are profiting off human suffering, and the Trump Administration is footing the bill with our tax dollars. Maria, as well as all pregnant people in detention, deserve dignity, proper medical care, and immediate release.”

“Maria is desperate to protect the health and safety of her baby. The federal government, by blatantly ignoring medical guidelines and advice, is putting her and her baby’s life at risk,” said Representative Dexter, who is one of six Democratic doctors in Congress. “She must be released immediately. DHS is refusing basic human and civil rights to the people in these despicable facilities and shows zero concern for the lives of people in them. Pregnant women and children do not belong in ICE detention. I will continue to use my experience as a physician, a mother, and my power as a member of Congress to protect women and children in this country.”

“ICE is putting women’s health, pregnancies, and lives at risk—leaving them to plead for even the most basic care and access to menstrual products,” said Mini Timmaraju, President and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All. “I’m grateful to Reps. Grijalva, Ansari, and Dexter for shining light on this crisis, and Reproductive Freedom for All is with them every step of the way in demanding an end to this cruelty.”

text:
The Trump administration has halted its efforts to overhaul the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, ending a plan that could have blocked some U.S. workers from tapping the popular lending program.

In a filing on Wednesday, the Trump administration said it was dropping its appeal of a June 30 federal court ruling that found the overhaul unlawful, without providing an explanation for its decision. Advocates for student borrowers hailed the step. Dan Zibel, chief counsel of the advocacy group Student Borrowers, called it a "significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service."

The proposed rule changes to the federal Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PLSF) program, originally proposed in August 2025, would have prohibited people from participating if their employer engaged in certain illegal activities. The proposed revamp said that employees who work for organizations that support terrorism, violate immigration laws or are involved in what the rule described as the "chemical and surgical castration or mutilation of children" would be barred.

The Department of Education didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Here's what to know about the change.

What is the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program?

The PLSF is aimed at people who work for government agencies, public schools, fire and police departments, public hospitals, and nonprofits. The idea is to provide a pathway to student loan forgiveness for people who work in public service. The program cancels outstanding debt for eligible borrowers who make 120 monthly payments, or 10 years of participation.

Almost 720,000 federal student loans were discharged through the program between 2018 and mid-2025, according to the Education Data Initiative, which collects data about the U.S. education system.

What did the Trump administration want to change?

At the time the Trump administration announced the new rule, Department of Education Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent said the rationale for revamping the PLSF was "supporting public servants who strengthen their communities and serve the public good, not benefiting businesses engaged in illegal activity that harms Americans."

The rule sought to disqualify applicants from the program if their employer engaged in "a substantial illegal purpose." It included a list of activities such as violating immigration laws, terrorism, trafficking, violating state laws or "violence for the purpose of obstructing or influencing federal government policy."

The rule was finalized in October 2025.

Who challenged the overhaul?

The rule was challenged in the courts by multiple nonprofits and municipalities, including Public Citizen Litigation Group and Student Defense on behalf of the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, the American Immigration Council and cities including Albuquerque, New Mexico, Boston and Chicago.

The groups argued that the rule gave the Department of Education excessive latitude in deciding whether an organization was engaged in "a substantial illegal purpose."

Just before it was set to take effect in July, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun in Massachusetts vacated the rule, saying it overstepped the Education Department's authority and threatened to violate First Amendment protections for free speech. On the same day, District Judge Amir Ali in Washington issued a similar ruling in a case brought by nonprofit organizations.

Nonprofit leaders on Thursday said the administration's decision to drop the appeal will provide relief to many public servants.

"With the appeal dismissed, the court's order vacating the rule stands, and PLSF remains as Congress designed it," Diane Yentel, CEO of the National Council of Nonprofits, said in a statement.

She added, "This outcome gives nonprofit employees the certainty that the loan relief they've earned through years of public service will be there for them, so they can keep doing the work that strengthens the communities they serve."

The ICE Midwest Office told TV9 Carlos Tino Chic was arrested on Oct. 19.

They say Tino Chic had two prior removals and admitted to illegally reentering the United States near Laredo, Texas, at an unspecified date, saying “he does not have any legal status to remain in the country and has accepted a voluntary departure back to his home country.”

Dubuque Police Department Lt. Luke Bock wrote in an email that police had no confirmed details about any ICE activity.

“We weren’t notified by ICE that there was going to be activity in town. We weren’t asked for any assistance with any operations,” Bock wrote.

The plaintiffs argue the funding cut is particularly egregious given Congress appropriated more than $5 billion for fiscal year 2024 to deliver services to unaccompanied children, including funding for legal representation.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — The Department of Justice asked a Ninth Circuit panel Thursday to vacate a lower court’s order blocking the government from terminating legal funding for undocumented children who are in the United States without a legal guardian.

“The statute says nothing, and neither does the regulation, about whether to terminate funding or who to fund. That particular choice is particularly committed to our discretion,” Thomas Vaseliou, representing the government, said.

Vaseliou argued the lower court lacked jurisdiction because the plaintiffs’ claims arose from a breach-of-contract issue and belong in the Court of Federal Claims.

He objected to U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin’s description of a “complete abandonment” of the program.

“When we’re still providing pro bono services, which was true when we terminated direct legal representation, and we were still preventing manipulation, exploitation and trafficking of children, that’s enough to say it’s not a complete shutdown of the program,” he said.

Vaseliou told the panel Congress appropriated the money for legal services as a lump sum across multiple programs under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, and it was up to the government to decide how to use the funding.

“With a lump sum appropriation, however, we’re not required to because we can make a judgment call, a budget-making decision to allocate the funds in a different direction,” Vaseliou said.

U.S. Circuit Judge Lucy H. Koh, a Joe Biden appointee, questioned Vaseliou about the termination of funding without a backup plan to ensure the children had legal counsel, while U.S. Circuit Judge Consuelo M. Callahan, a George W. Bush appointee, focused on Martinez-Olguin’s orders regarding the government’s compliance with the preliminary injunction and the judge’s decision not to recuse herself from the case, despite previous employment at one of the plaintiff organizations.

However, Callahan and U.S. Circuit Judge Kenneth Kiyul Lee, a Donald Trump appointee, directed the majority of their questions to plaintiffs’ attorney Laura Sturges, focusing on jurisdiction and redressability.

“It does seem at its core a contract case. That contract was canceled; we don’t have the money that we would have received under the contract. So it seems like then it should go to the Court of Federal Claims,” Lee said.

Sturges told the panel the plaintiff organizations’ contract does not need to be reinstated for an adequate remedy; instead, the government only has to ensure it was providing the required legal services under the TVPRA — which mandates the government “shall ensure, to the greatest extent practicable,” that unaccompanied children receive legal counsel.

“If the government was able to provide services to the greatest extent practicable, as required by the TVPRA, that would redress our harms without money flowing to us,” she said.

She added the courts should have power to determine whether the government abused its discretion in terminating the funds.

“We think the government has an obligation to fund direct representation for unaccompanied minors to the greatest extent practicable, and the government thinks it does not. That is a question of interpretation, that that is a statutory question, that is a question for a court, and that is not a Court of Federal Claims issue or a breach of contract issue,” she said.

Representatives for the parties did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In March 2025, the plaintiffs — Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto, Immigrant Defenders Law Center and the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, among others — said the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Office of Refugee Resettlement and the Department of the Interior abruptly — and without explanation — terminated the contract that enabled the plaintiffs and their sister legal service organizations to provide critical services to thousands of unaccompanied children nationwide.

Last year, the groups say approximately 26,000 children were at risk of losing legal representation. Many children arrive in the United States without parents or legal guardians, often unable to speak English and lacking the resources to hire an attorney. The plaintiffs argue the funding cut is particularly egregious given Congress appropriated more than $5 billion for fiscal year 2024 to deliver services to unaccompanied children, including funding for legal representation.

Last April, Martinez-Olguin, a Joe Biden appointee, granted the plaintiffs a temporary restraining order, writing the Trump administration’s plan to terminate the funding raised serious concerns it would violate the TVPRA. Later that month, Martínez-Olguín issued a preliminary injunction to restore nationwide legal aid funding through the Office of Refugee Resettlement.
