text:
A man who was documenting federal immigration activity in Woodland says an ICE vehicle struck him Tuesday.

“I saw it just coming directly at me and before I knew it, it hit me in the chest rib area and I kind of went flying,” Woodland -resident Antonio Moreida told CapRadio.

Moreida said he had gone out after receiving an alert from NorCal Resist, an immigrant support organization based in Sacramento that tracks suspected immigration enforcement activity across 25 counties. He said he was trying to document the vehicles because they had no visible license plates or other clear markings identifying them as law enforcement.

Moreida was recording unmarked vehicles on a Woodland street on Tuesday when he said a Chevrolet Tahoe drove toward him and hit him in the chest. Moreida said he was taken to the hospital where he was checked for injuries.

The incident drew a crowd to a Woodland City Council meeting that evening where residents expressed concern about the federal operation.

Moreida said he was surprised by the support he received from community members and local officials.

“It’s not about me,” he said. “I’m only one of several of these occurrences that keeps happening with no accountability.

Woodland police review video as DHS disputes Moreida’s account

Woodland Police spokesperson Victoria Danzl told CapRadio the department is investigating the incident.

“We didn’t participate in the federal operation consistent with California law and our role is just to investigate the collision independently and establish any facts that exist with it,” Danzl said.

The Department of Homeland Security disputes Moreida’s account arguing in a statement that ICE did not hit a pedestrian.

“An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes,” the statement reads. “The agitator slid off the hood… Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation.”

However, the Woodland police said their review of video evidence from multiple angles contradicts key parts of DHS’s account. They argue that footage shows Moreida was struck by a vehicle driven by an ICE agent and that he did not jump onto the hood.

The police department also said the driver remained near the scene, contacted police and cooperated with officers during the initial investigation.

Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said the city plans to ask the Yolo County district attorney to get involved in the case.

NorCal Resist reports a sharp increase in enforcement

The Woodland incident is one of several reports of immigration enforcement across the region in recent weeks.

Giselle Garcia with NorCal Resist said her organization’s rapid-response hotline has been ringing more than usual since Oct. 8. Before the increase, she said a typical week brought about 10 to 20 reports.

“We’ve had about between 20 and 50 dispatches per day,” Garcia said. “And we are logging confirmed detainment intake almost every single day.”

The group’s records are not an official count of ICE arrests. Garcia said some reports cannot be fully documented because witnesses or family members lack information needed to identify a detained person or locate them in the immigration system.

The majority of the reports have come from Sutter, Yolo, Butte and Sacramento counties, according to Garcia.

The increase follows a September announcement by the Department of Homeland Security that ICE had begun what it called a “nationwide public safety surge in sanctuary cities.” The department said the effort would target immigrants it described as criminal offenders including murderers and gang members.

Garcia said NorCal Resist began tracking a surge in the Central Valley followed by increased activity in Northern California following the announcement.

“We are actually operating under the assumption that this is just the new normal,” Garcia said.

Families face obstacles finding detained relatives, legal help

UC Davis law professor Raquel Aldana said the legal community was already stretched before the latest increase in enforcement, as detainees continue having difficulty finding available attorneys to represent them.

“When I used to practice human rights law in Latin America, we used to call what is happening enforced disappearances and the only thing that would save people from being forcibly disappeared by the government was habeas corpus that lawyers would file on behalf of people,” she said.

Aldana said she sees some similarities in what the current administration is doing with detained immigrants, especially when it sends them to countries they’re not from — a tactic that the Supreme Court allowed to keep happening as it considers whether the policy is legal.

“And it’s just added a lot of new practices, including not [being] willing to disclose or confirm to family members once somebody has been picked up by ICE and where they’re being detained,” Aldana said. “And I think that is what’s scaring people.”

text:
PASADENA, Calif. (CN) — The Trump administration asked the Ninth Circuit on Thursday to end a 40-year-old injunction aimed at protecting unaccompanied minor migrants from agreeing to voluntarily leave the country without first being informed of their legal rights and allowed to speak with a relative or an attorney.

The administration is appealing an April decision by a federal judge in Los Angeles who denied the Justice Department’s request to terminate the injunction.

The government argues changes in immigration law since the injunction was issued in 1986 and, in particular, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 prohibit trial courts from issuing class-wide injunctions that pertain to enforcement of immigration law.

U.S. District Judge Michael Fitzgerald, however, agreed with attorneys representing the interests of migrant children that the subsequent Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 controls how federal immigration agents process so-called unaccompanied alien children in their custody, and the 1986 injunction pertains to this statute rather than the 1996 law.

“The responsibilities of immigration officers when they encounter children are dictated by the TVPRA, not by the covered provisions of the IIRIRA,” the Barack Obama appointee said in his April 6 ruling. “In light of Congress’ codification of the TVPRA, the court is hesitant to […] prohibit courts from imposing class-wide injunctive relief when it comes to the treatment of children under this statute.”

The argument before the Ninth Circuit panel in Pasadena, California, revolved largely around the issue of whether the 1986 injunction has a direct effect on provisions of the 1996 immigration law, which presumably would mean it can’t be enforced, or whether its effect is only “collateral.”

While the panel didn’t say how they might rule, they revealed their colors in their questions to the parties, with the two Donald Trump appointees, U.S. Circuit Judges Patrick Bumatay and Lawrence VanDyke, taking turns skewering the attorney for the immigrant children, and U.S. Circuit Judge Salvador Mendoza Jr., a Joe Biden appointee, taking aim at the government lawyer.

“It’s a blatant logical fallacy,” VanDyke told Public Counsel attorney Mark Rosenbaum, to assume the injunction couldn’t have a direct, non-collateral implication on both the 1996 law and the TVPRA.

“You can have an injunction that says don’t do A or B,” VanDyke said. “That directly affects two things, and you can’t say A is what it directly affects and therefore everything else is just collateral. That’s just wrong.”

Bumatay, in turn, challenged the attorney to define what it means to have a collateral impact.

Rosenbaum, however, pointed to a recent Ninth Circuit decision involving asylum-seekers in which a split panel upheld a class-wide injunction despite its impact on some provisions of the 1996 immigration law.

“It had a dramatic effect on removal,” the lawyer said. “Once the individual was free to perfect his asylum claim, then, Boom!, he’s not going to be removed. Whether you want to call that a direct effect, with a small ’d,’ this court called it a collateral effect.”

The 1986 injunction resulted from a class action brought by children who were detained by immigration agents and claimed they were coerced with threats and intimidation into agreeing to voluntary removal and, as such, into waiving their right to a deportation hearing.

The judge at the time agreed the children found themselves in an “inherently coercive” situation and ordered immigration agents to advise them of their legal rights and allow them to call a parent, relative, friend or attorney.

According to Public Counsel, legal services providers in the Rio Grande Valley area of Texas have reported children are already being pressured to sign expedited return forms under coercive circumstances during the 72-hour window between when they are apprehended and when they are to be transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement.

text:
What This Story Is About

Tennessee’s top four gubernatorial candidates are divided over whether the state should continue or end its partnership with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including the Memphis Safe Task Force and 287(g) agreements.

Why It Matters

The outcome of the race will determine the future of Tennessee’s cooperation with ICE, affecting enforcement practices, local workforce availability and the relationship between state and federal immigration authority.

What Happens Next

Whoever wins the governor’s race will set the direction of the state’s immigration enforcement policy, including whether to maintain, expand or end agreements such as the MOUs with ICE and the 287(g) program.

For Context

State leaders estimate nearly 19,000 immigrants in the country illegally have been removed from Tennessee since January of last year, and the state has operated as a testing ground for federal immigration policies, including the Memphis Safe Task Force.

Catch Up

Democratic nominee Jerri Green has pledged to end ICE agreements on day one if elected, independents Lauren Pinkston and David Hatley hold opposing views on enforcement spending and strategy, and Republican U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn supports expanding the state’s cooperation with ICE.

Election 2026: Early voting for Tennessee’s November 3 general election is underway

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - State leaders estimate nearly 19,000 immigrants in the country illegally have been removed from Tennessee since January of last year.

The state’s top four polling candidates for governor are divided on immigration enforcement, an issue that could determine the future of the state’s partnership with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

State’s relationship with ICE

Tennessee has had a close relationship with Immigration and Customs Enforcement for years, with most sheriffs’ offices partnering with federal leaders through the 287(g) program. The state became a testing ground for President Trump’s immigration policies, including the Memphis Safe Task Force.

Democratic nominee Jerri Green said she has seen the impact of that task force firsthand.

“What we are seeing is people being rounded up into private prisons run by CoreCivic, a large donor of my opponent,” Green said.

Green: End agreements with ICE

Green said if she is elected governor, addressing immigration enforcement would be one of the first issues she tackles.

“I will, on day one, end the MOUs with ICE, ask them to get out of our cities,” Green said.

Green said she has spoken with Memphis’ police chief and the head of the city’s crime commission, who she said does not believe ICE should be in Tennessee cities.

“I believe they are terrorizing our neighborhoods and making the job of enforcing crime harder for our police force,” Green said.

Green said the Republican supermajority in the legislature passed a law last year requiring sheriff’s departments to cooperate with ICE or risk losing funding.

“I’m going to tell you right now, this Democrat is not going to defund the police. That’s going to be on them if they want to do that,” Green said.

Green described an incident in which she said people were “rounded up indiscriminately at a bar in Memphis at 1 o’clock in the morning, zip-tied, put on buses and shipped off in the middle of the night.” She said one person lost their mother in the operation and still does not know her whereabouts, and that the next day was the child’s sixth birthday.

Green said people in her community are now walking around with their papers to be ready to show them, and are afraid to wait in food bank lines, go to the doctor or go to church.

Green also said fewer than 10% of the people ICE arrests have a felony, and that most do not have a misdemeanor.

“They have a paperwork mess up. And they’re being put in prison,” Green said. “Mothers, children, babies that are sick are being put in prison. A prison that is for profit, so they’re cutting the margins on humans.”

Green said, of the federal arrests made in Memphis that were prosecuted, most were dismissed or resulted in plea deals, and she said she believes about three resulted in convictions.

“So they’re not getting the worst of the worst. Why are we doing this to our neighbors? These are people who have come to America. They work. They pay taxes,” Green said.

When asked whether she would end the state’s centralized immigration office, created under legislation passed by the Republican supermajority during a special session, and whether she would oppose ICE presence at courthouses, such as in Robertson County, Green said she does not want anyone “terrorized anywhere in our communities.”

“We already have federal immigration. We already have the DOJ, the Department of Justice,” Green said. “I don’t want gangbangers. I don’t want drug dealers. I don’t want rapists on our streets. But we have ways to do that through our criminal justice system, through our federal justice system. It was working. ICE is a new creation. People act like it’s been around for forever. It is not. We have homeland security.”

Green said she stands with the community members she said have been harmed by enforcement actions, including the child whose mother, a waitress on a work permit, has not been located since being taken into custody.

“That’s the kind of people that we need to be protecting, not hurting,” Green said.

Pinkston: Tennessee being used as a ‘playground’

Independent candidate Lauren Pinkston said Tennessee has always been a state that believes in state sovereignty.

“What we’re looking at right now is a Washington D.C. that wants to use Tennessee as a playground. And I’m not okay with that,” Pinkston said.

Pinkston said Tennessee law enforcement officers have always coordinated with federal agencies when needed, but said that over the last year, the state has been used to carry out a desire of Washington, D.C., rather than the desire of the majority of Tennesseans.

“I say all the time, it is economically irresponsible to hunt and peck people off of the streets to address an immigration issue,” Pinkston said.

Pinkston, who said she has worked in counter-human trafficking for 15 years, said the state should instead pursue businesses that are exploiting the labor of migrant workers.

“If we want to address the issue of immigration, we start with where the push and pull factors are, and that’s with the hope of a job in Tennessee,” Pinkston said.

Pinkston said the hospitality, agriculture and construction industries have all reported losses of legal workers due to fear of being arrested by ICE.

“Immigration and the economy cannot be separated in this conversation. And so the workforce gap is a real one,” Pinkston said.

Pinkston also said children in Tennessee are not being given their constitutional rights because their parents are afraid to send them to school, citing a U.S. Supreme Court decision from 1986.

Pinkston said an enforcement strategy built around fear does not necessarily make communities safer.

“When people are afraid to walk out of their home, and they’re afraid to call law enforcement because even though their daughter may be being abused or their son has fallen into a swimming pool, that’s a problem,” Pinkston said. “That doesn’t make our streets safer.”

Pinkston said the state spent $221 million to outfit Hotel Indigo in Memphis, and said that money should have instead gone toward expanding the Memphis police force, which she said was down 50% after George Floyd’s death.

“That’s a good way to use your tax dollars, not chasing a headline,” Pinkston said.

Hatley: Double down on ICE partnership

Independent candidate David Hatley said the state should instead strengthen its partnership with ICE.

“Every single local department in this state needs to work with ICE. We need to get violent, illegal criminals out of this state. They have no place in this state. That’s what ICE is doing. And their job is to take violent, illegal criminals off the streets,” Hatley said.

Hatley said immigration is ultimately a federal issue over which he would have no control as governor, but said he believes in cooperating with the federal government and would like to see local counties do the same.

“We’re never going to have a sanctuary city in Tennessee when I’m governor. I can promise you that,” Hatley said.

Blackburn: Bolster ICE partnership

Republican U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn agreed with Hatley’s position and said Tennessee should continue working with ICE.

“If you look at Memphis and what we’ve done there with the Memphis Safe Task Force, there have been 900 arrests by ICE in that. And I think it’s 546 of those that ended in deportations,” Blackburn said. “We also have the 287 agreements, and we have 120 of those in the state. And those allow our local law enforcement to work with federal law enforcement on these immigration and deportation issues. And those are things that we need to bolster. We need to continue that.”

Blackburn said that, in talking with Tennesseans across the state, she hears about the cost of living, public safety, education, infrastructure and health care.

“But public safety is so vitally important,” Blackburn said. “We’ve got a lot of families who have lost loved ones because of accidents and adverse occurrences that have happened with individuals that are illegally in our country and in our state and in our communities. And they will tell you, these angel families will tell you that they want to see safety and security.”

Workforce gaps

With reports of workforce gaps tied to immigration enforcement, Hatley and Blackburn were each asked how they would fill those jobs.

Hatley, who said he works in manufacturing, said the state’s education system needs improvement, pointing to Tennessee College of Applied Technology schools.

“I think we have to make sure that we’re training and educating our people. It goes back to our education system. For one, our education system is failing us right now. We’re dead last,” Hatley said. “So that’s why I’m so passionate on improving that, our TCAT schools. I mean, let’s look at expanding these TCAT schools.”

Hatley said that as a manufacturer, he has had difficulty finding skilled workers, including welders, even at a starting wage of $25 an hour.

“There just isn’t enough people out there. There’s two retiring for every one coming into the workforce,” Hatley said. “So as someone from manufacturing, this is going to be a crisis at some point. We’re going to wake up and manufacturing drives this state.”

Hatley said some students do not want four-year degrees and would prefer trade school.

“So I think we have to focus on a better education system, and we have to focus on our TCAT schools. Give these kids options,” Hatley said. “I think we have to make sure that we’re training our kids and getting them in the workforce to make sure that our manufacturers have the talent that they need.”

Blackburn was asked specifically about hospitality and construction industries, which she said have taken “a bit of a hit” because legal workers are afraid to go to work out of concern they could be picked up by ICE.

“People that are legally here in the country ought not to fear going to work,” Blackburn said. “And if they are legal, they’ve got their papers, there is no reason that they should fear that they were going to be picked up.”

These are the three important things that we look at,” said Talavera when asked about what matters most to Latino voters.
text:
President Donald Trump’s immigration policies are troubling some of Maryland’s Latino Republican voters, who think he is taking things too far.

With midterm elections near, the concerns are not unique to Maryland.

In 2024, Latino voters helped Trump return to the White House: He gained 48% of the Hispanic vote, according to the Pew Research Center. That support appears to be slipping.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Oct. 5 found that just 26% of Hispanic registered voters plan to vote Republican in November, while 52% plan to back Democrats.

In Maryland, some local Latino leaders say even Hispanic conservatives may stray from the president’s fold or simply stay home.

“It’s sad, but a lot of Latinos are going the other way,” said Juan Leo Salazar, president of the Latin Republican Organization of Maryland.

Since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents nationwide have increased arrests, often carried out by masked agents, and some captured on video showing agents forcibly detaining people.

In Maryland, ICE arrests more than doubled between Jan. 20 and March 10, 2026, compared with the same period a year earlier, according to a CNS analysis of data from the Deportation Data Project.

“This administration, Mr. Trump, is overdoing it a little bit,” Salazar added.

Gabriela Lemus, executive director of the nonpartisan Maryland Latinos Unidos, said some Latinos who voted for Trump because they wanted a better economy have seen what she called “punitive actions” against the Latino community and now regret their vote. Those voters, she said, may simply stay home.

“The more conservative Latino is not necessarily comfortable with the Democrat, but they’re not going to vote for Trump, so they may not turn out,” Lemus said.

To be sure, other Latino Republicans say many are still solidly in support of Trump. They blame other forces for economic troubles and want to keep the Congress in Republican hands to help Trump implement his vision for the country. Alfonso Talavera, chair of the Maryland GOP Hispanic & Latino Outreach Committee, said Trump is simply enforcing immigration law.

“A law is a law,” Talavera said. “If I am drunk and I am driving drunk, and a police officer stops me, I’m going to have a DUI.”

The Hispanic-Latino community is a sizable voting group in Maryland, with a population exceeding 830,000, based on U.S. Census data. Roughly 39% are eligible to vote, according to a Pew Research Center analysis.

Some Latino Republican candidates have distanced themselves from the immigration enforcement actions of the federal administration. Josephine Salazar, a Republican running for the Montgomery County Council in District 5, said she left immigration out of her platform. (Josephine and Juan Leo Salazar are not related.)

“I didn’t touch immigration because it’s a hot issue,” she said. “It’s a hot, hot, hot issue.”

Although the issue is not included in her platform, Josephine Salazar told CNS that U.S. lawmakers have to find a legal path for immigrants who came illegally but pay their taxes, work hard and stay out of trouble.

Latino Republicans in Maryland say their community moved toward the GOP in the first place because they see it as the party of family values and stronger security.

“Many Hispanics told me that they had voted for President Trump because they were concerned about security,” Josephine Salazar said.

“They were telling me they were worried that a lot of people were coming in who were selling drugs from Mexico, Central America and South America,” she added.

The local leaders also cited President Ronald Reagan, who signed the 1986 law that gave legal status to nearly 3 million immigrants, as one reason some Latinos vote Republican.

Beyond immigration, Maryland Latino leaders agreed that the economy is the other issue weighing most heavily on Hispanic voters, as it is for Americans overall.

“Family, church and food. These are the three important things that we look at,” said Talavera when asked about what matters most to Latino voters.

Local leaders described families stretched to the limit by rising prices at the grocery store and the gas pump. Lemus said a Maryland Latinos Unidos survey last fall found families choosing between paying for food and paying utility bills.

“We have big families. We tend to need larger cars,” she said. “That continues to really weigh on people’s minds.”

Republican leaders blamed Democrats such as Gov. Wes Moore for the economic strain on Maryland’s Latino community. But across party lines, all agreed that families are feeling it.

“The economy is not doing very well,” Juan Leo Salazar said. “Whatever I say, it’s not going to be good news.”

title: Trump administration and Texas urge court to leave their agreement on deportation ...
description:
The Trump administration and Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday afternoon to leave in place their consent agreement abolishing a Biden-era regulation that had allowed immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings.
Texas went to federal court in Wichita Falls, Texas, in June, arguing that the EOIR does not have the power to adopt the administrative-closure rule.
The case was assigned to the only federal judge there, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor.
O’Connor denied that request, holding that the challengers lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing.
Moreover, Texas added, “[i]f any local government could establish standing whenever federal immigration policy might eventually change the number of resident taxpayers, nearly every immigration measure would be judicially challengeable by municipalities on both sides.”
text:
The Trump administration and Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday afternoon to leave in place their consent agreement abolishing a Biden-era regulation that had allowed immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the request from the challengers in the case – three cities, led by Baltimore, and a group that provides legal services to immigrants – to pause a federal district court’s ruling “attempts to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over” the challengers’ efforts to join the case “into a far-reaching attack on the merits of” the court’s approval of the agreement. For its part, Texas argued that granting the challengers’ request “would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties.”

The Executive Office for Immigration Review, which is part of the Department of Justice, adopted the regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” in 2024. The rule gives immigration judges the authority to suspend deportation proceedings in some scenarios – when, for example, a crime victim or witness is seeking immigration relief, such as asylum – while the immigrant’s appeal in the lower federal courts is ongoing.

Texas went to federal court in Wichita Falls, Texas, in June, arguing that the EOIR does not have the power to adopt the administrative-closure rule. The case was assigned to the only federal judge there, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor.

On the same day that the case was filed, the U.S. Department of Justice and Texas filed a motion to have O’Connor enter a final judgment for the state. The DOJ also asked O’Connor both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests.

Three cities with substantial immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – sought to join the case to defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, along with Centro Legal de la Raza, a group that provides legal services to immigrants. O’Connor denied that request, holding that the challengers lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit declined to pause O’Connor’s decision while the challengers appealed, prompting them to come to the Supreme Court on Oct. 9.

In their application to pause O’Connor’s decision, the challengers told the justices that the consent judgment was “indefensible.” “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” they argued, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”

In their briefs opposing the challengers’ request, both the Trump administration and Texas emphasized that the challengers do not have standing to intervene on appeal and therefore cannot challenge the consent judgment. Sauer noted that although the consent agreement throws out the administrative-closure rule, it does not require cases that have already been administratively closed to be returned to an immigration judge’s calendar. As a result, Texas said, any injury to cities would hinge on “a cascade of discretionary and unidentified events”: “an administratively closed case must be re-calendared; the alien must lose on the merits; a final removal order must issue; the Department of Homeland Security must execute it; and the person otherwise must have remained employed and paying a municipal income tax. No declaration identifies even one taxpayer for whom that chain is likely.” Any such effects on the cities “are too ‘indirect’ and ‘attenuated’ to” give them a right to sue, Sauer similarly contended.

Moreover, Texas added, “[i]f any local government could establish standing whenever federal immigration policy might eventually change the number of resident taxpayers, nearly every immigration measure would be judicially challengeable by municipalities on both sides.”

text:
A federal judge limited aggressive U.S. Department of Homeland Security field operations targeting alleged noncitizen voting in nine states in a Wednesday ruling.

The operation ordered a series of field interviews and stops that targeted alleged noncitizens accused of registering to vote. Pro-voting groups said the harassment campaign threatened legal voters. President Donald Trump has baselessly claimed for years that noncitizens voting is widespread. In reality, it’s something that rarely happens and never in enough numbers to affect the outcome of an election.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin in California agreed that DHS’s efforts amount to “ongoing intimidation” that would cause “irreparable harm” to legal voters.

Martínez-Olguin blocked any DHS agents from conducting operations against people they suspect are likely U.S. citizens in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. However, DHS can continue investigation of suspected noncitizens.

Despite that, Martínez-Olguin found that agents’ “target lists” were likely rife with errors, similar to other Trump administration attempts to use federal immigration data to assess voter rolls.

The plaintiffs include a California nurse’s association, two local governments and the nonprofit Voto Latino Foundation.

Their interests and “the public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens,” Martínez-Olguin wrote.

The ruling will not go into effect until Friday evening to give the government time to appeal, and it will automatically expire after Election Day.

DHS’ campaign, known as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” came under fire in September after a whistleblower alleged federal agents were ordered to illegally misrepresent themselves as voters on state websites to obtain voter information. Officials reportedly directed agents to complete at least 40 subject reviews per day — which meant officers could take no more than 12 minutes on each suspected voter.

In response, Sens. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin calling the department’s actions “alarming.”

Federal authorities have sought to repurpose immigration databases to target noncitizen voting, but they have produced significant errors.

DHS claimed nearly 16,000 potential noncitizens were on Nevada’s roll, but after state officials questioned that figure, the department’s claim fizzled from 15,903 possible noncitizens to 185 and eventually to zero.

The Trump administration has particularly targeted California and other Democratic states. In early October, the U.S. Department of Justice sued California and Los Angeles for refusing to set aside 20,000 ballots it claimed without evidence were illegally submitted by noncitizens.

At the time, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said the DOJ lawsuit was part of the Trump administration’s “authoritarian attempt to undermine our democracy.”

text:
Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year, when the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear, an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI’s analysis, that’s a 26 percent increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, another Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the United States without authorization were from Mexico and didn’t often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the United States from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them. And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

The report said voluntary departures — when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country — were at an “all-time high,” with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025. People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the United States.

But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country’s interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28 percent of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by July of this year that had risen to 39 percent.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said — 69 percent of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the “worst of the worst.” Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.”

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent. On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump’s second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

text:
Follow WTOP’s team coverage of Election 2026 online, on air at 103.5 FM or on the WTOP News app.

With the midterm elections less than two weeks away, Arlington County, Virginia, is taking the Trump administration to court over concerns that armed federal agents could be sent to polling places, potentially intimidating voters and disrupting the election.

The Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, seeking to block federal policies that county officials say would allow armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers and FBI agents to conduct enforcement operations at voting locations.

The lawsuit comes as early voting is already underway in Virginia ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

In an interview with WTOP, Arlington County Board Vice-Chair Member Maureen Coffey said statements from senior federal officials have raised concerns about the possibility of armed agents appearing at the polls.

Related stories

Immigration remains a key issue, but voters’ views are shifting ahead of the midterms

Why data centers are becoming a top economic issue ahead of this fall’s midterms

What’s motivating voters to cast midterm ballots in DC region

“When voters are seeing senior U.S. government officials saying that they can’t rule out or that they believe it would be lawful for federal agents to enter polling places, we’re hearing a lot of fear and concern about the disruption of our elections,” Coffey said.

The lawsuit challenges policies that Arlington officials argue violate a federal law dating back to 1865, which prohibits federal officials from ordering armed personnel to election sites, except under narrowly defined circumstances.

The county points to statements made by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in September suggesting ICE agents could conduct enforcement operations at polling locations, including serving warrants. FBI Director Kash Patel has also said armed FBI agents could be sent to polling places for election-related enforcement activities.

Arlington officials argue those statements have forced the county to divert resources toward preparing for possible encounters with federal agents, including developing new guidance and conducting emergency preparedness exercises involving election officials, police and prosecutors.

Coffey told WTOP that although no specific complaints have been received, officials believe the potential consequences are too serious to ignore.

“What ICE is doing has really created, I think, a culture of fear, and we can’t wait until voters are intimidated to protect everyone’s right to cast their vote freely and fairly,” Coffey said.

DHS pushes back

In a statement to WTOP, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations.

“ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action,” the spokesperson said.

The department also said DHS and the Justice Department are focused on prosecuting and removing noncitizens who vote illegally.

“DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson said.

DHS also pointed to comments Mullin made during his confirmation hearing, when he said federal immigration officers would only be at polling locations in response to a specific threat.

“The only reason why my officers would be there is if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation,” Mullin said.

But Coffey said the administration’s assurance that no operations are currently planned does not go far enough.

“I think that if the administration would like to say clearly and directly that they will not be sending federal agents to any polling places this Election Day or any Election Day, that would do a lot to ensure that voters do not have anything to worry about,” Coffey said.

She argued that waiting until after an incident occurs could leave voters without a remedy.

“We may be able to get a determination that their action is illegal, but we can’t rerun the election, and so that’s why it has to come before anything has happened,” Coffey said.

County seeks court intervention before Election Day

The lawsuit, brought with assistance from Democracy Forward and Public Rights Project, argues that the administration’s policies exceed federal authority, violate the Administrative Procedure Act and interfere with state and local governments’ authority to administer elections.

Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said the county is determined to protect voters.

“Threatening to send armed agents to polling stations is unlawful and contravenes the bedrock values of free and fair elections we hold dear in this country,” de Ferranti said in a statement. “These statements are a clear attempt to stoke fear and undermine confidence in our elections.”

The lawsuit asks the court to block the challenged policies and prohibit armed federal agents from operating at or near polling places, including early voting sites and ballot drop-off locations, except under circumstances permitted by federal law.

With Election Day approaching, Coffey said officials are hoping for a quick decision.

“We’re hopeful that we will get a pretty speedy response from the courts,” Coffey said.

WTOP’s Nick Iannelli contributed to this report.

text:
Paris, France – As France reels from violent clashes during protests, riots and looting, the blame game is on.

One argument making waves across the political spectrum – and across the Atlantic – is that migrants and open-border policies are responsible.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

list 1 of 4‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors

list 2 of 4‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence

list 3 of 4Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?

list 4 of 4France’s Macron says protesters won’t be allowed to ‘cause chaos’

end of list

“If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished,” United States President Donald Trump said at the White House on Monday. “When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred – that’s not about school. That’s about people coming into the countries that hate the country.”

French President Emmanuel Macron later slammed “stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders” about the unrest.

Speaking during a visit in Qatar, he said there was no evidence of foreign interference behind the riots.

Young student protesters in France were unimpressed by Trump’s intervention.

Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old student at the Paul Eluard high school near Paris, one of the first to witness protests, called it “stupid talk”.

“They can think whatever they like. We’re focusing on the main subject, which is the students’ demands,” Narjissi said. “The far right has to say these kinds of things because they base their politics and political programmes on instilling fear.”

Emmanuel Dupuy, president of the Institute for European Perspective and Security Studies, a think tank on diplomacy and political analysis, said Trump’s argument was aimed at American voters.

“It’s an artificial argument used as a political tool in the context of midterm elections,” he said. “They are trying to argue that what is happening in France would happen in the US if Democrats get elected.”

Trump’s comments came after largely peaceful high school student demonstrations in France descended into chaos over the weekend when rioters attacked city halls and looted stores, marking the most violent unrest in France in years.

More than 2,000 people were placed in police custody – the vast majority of them minors – and thousands of businesses were ransacked. Accused of letting the situation spiral, French authorities imposed partial and temporary curfews in certain cities across the country, including in areas of Paris.

While concerns over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes and teacher shortages were at the fore, the protest movement quickly catalysed wider discontent over the cost of living and social unease.

Italy, Albania and Spain have seen similar demonstrations.

French authorities have not linked crime with migration. The state does not share the identities of people arrested and sent to trial.

Under constitutional laws aimed at equality, it is illegal to collect data on ethnicity and race.

Both far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen and politicians from the centrist bloc, including Macron and Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, have accused hard-left groups of fomenting disorder.

The wave of protests seems to have struck a nerve across the European bloc, too.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was now “clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on immigration”, posting on X a video showing buildings burning in France.

Without explicitly referring to events in France, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk also weighed in. “Poland will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, nor will it pay for them,” he asserted on X a day after the mass demonstrations and looting in France. “We will be uncompromising on security.”

Dupuy said the origin of those who joined the violence was beside the point.

“These protesters were high school students; then professional black bloc and looters joined, too – whether they came from a third or fourth generation of former migrants is irrelevant,” he said. “Eventually, this is a problem of integration, not immigration.”

Vance attacks ‘Western liberals’ in Europe

The US is in campaigning mode as it gears up for key elections in early November that will determine who dominates Congress.

With all eyes on midterms, Republicans seem eager to capitalise on unrest in Europe to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement and its tough policies on immigration and border measures.

“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” US Vice President JD Vance said on X. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”

Some critics have argued that Trump is trying to divert attention from the US’s cost-of-living crisis. Costs are rising in the US amid the Iran war he launched and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has sent energy prices to new heights.

What is happening in France, Trump said, should be a cautionary tale for American voters.

“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said, doubling down at a rally in the US state of Kansas.

description:
Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful, warrantless civil immigration arrests.
However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk.
The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Michigan.
“When immigration agents make unlawful arrests, the damage reaches far beyond the person taken into custody,” said Attorney General Nessel.
The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful, warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia.
text:
LANSING – Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, as part of a coalition of 22 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief (PDF) in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful, warrantless civil immigration arrests. Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Michigan.

“When immigration agents make unlawful arrests, the damage reaches far beyond the person taken into custody,” said Attorney General Nessel. “Children miss school, workers stay home, and families become afraid to seek medical care or call the police when they need help, putting public safety at risk. The federal government has a duty to enforce immigration law, but it must do so legally. My colleagues and I will continue to hold this agency and administration accountable whenever they fail to follow the law.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. Michigan has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plain clothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusal to identify themselves while carrying out operations, has further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful, warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted, in part, a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Nessel joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

Tajik authorities have not published information on the case.
Boboev, who was deported from Germany on June 20, previously told media that Tajik authorities had opened a criminal extremism case against him because of social media posts criticizing the Tajik authorities.
Boboev is not the first Tajikistani whom Germany has deported, despite human rights groups’ concerns.

text:
A court in Tajikistan has sentenced Asadullo Boboev, an opposition activist deported from Germany in June, to 17 years in jail. Human Rights Watch and other groups previously warned the German authorities that activists like Boboev could face mistreatment and criminal prosecution on politically motivated charges if returned to Tajikistan.

Boboev, 54, had lived in Germany with his family since 2017. He was involved in the Reforms and Development of Tajikistan movement, an opposition group critical of President Emomali Rahmon’s government. After Boboev was convicted under three articles of the criminal code, including “extremism through the internet,” a court sentenced Boboev on September 21, according to a media report. Tajik authorities have not published information on the case.

Boboev, who was deported from Germany on June 20, previously told media that Tajik authorities had opened a criminal extremism case against him because of social media posts criticizing the Tajik authorities. He said that the German court gave him until July 1 to prove that such a case exists, but he was deported before this deadline.

Boboev was deported to Dushanbe with his adult son, Muhammad. Boboev was detained on arrival.

Boboev is not the first Tajikistani whom Germany has deported, despite human rights groups’ concerns. Three other opposition activists deported from Germany since 2023 were also imprisoned after being returned to Tajikistan. Abdullohi Shamsiddin, Bilol Qurbonaliev, and Dilmurod Ergashev were sentenced to 7, 10, and 8 years in prison, respectively, on charges that appear to be fabricated.

International law prohibits refoulement—returning anyone to a country where they face a real risk of irreparable harm on account of serious human rights violations. While the German government has committed itself to countering governmental transnational repression, important gaps remain.

Germany has continued to return Tajik nationals even as evidence mounts that doing so delivers critics directly to the hands of the repressive security services they had, in many cases, fled.

German courts and immigration authorities should not readily deport dissidents to Tajikistan. German authorities should explain why Boboev was deported despite the concrete warnings of serious human rights risks and should press Tajikistan to disclose information about his conviction, his treatment, and ensure that he has access to independent legal counsel.

text:
A newly-launched nonprofit group is calling on state and federal leaders to create a $2 billion border security fund for the Big Bend region as an alternative to the Trump administration’s border wall plans.

“The premise is that all of us have been against something — i.e. the barriers — now we need to be for something,” said Jerry Patterson, a former Texas Land Commissioner and board member of the new organization, dubbed Let Texans Do Texas.

The group shared with Marfa Public Radio a letter that it plans to send to elected officials on Friday, including Gov. Greg Abbott and members of the U.S. House from Texas. In the letter, the group writes that the Big Bend region — famous for its iconic parks and rugged terrain — needs a different, more collaborative border security solution. The group says a number of county judges and sheriffs from the area are backing the proposal.

“Instead of imposing a one-size-fits-all federal construction program, LTDT would bring Texas, affected counties, landowners, local law enforcement, and the federal government together to design a security system suited to the Big Bend,” the letter states.

The group notes that the federal government is looking to spend over $7 billion on border barriers in the region, which accounted for just 1.3% of apprehensions along the entire southwest border last year.

“The least-trafficked sector should not receive one of the most destructive security responses,” the letter states.

Specifically, the advocacy group is asking that funding for the Trump administration’s border wall plans — approved by Congress in 2025 — be reallocated to other border security solutions, like road improvements, equipment, communications, emergency medical services, vehicles, drones, aircrafts and more.

“ Walls and soldiers are not a 21st century solution,” said Susan Hays, Democratic candidate for Presidio County Commissioner and LTDT board member. “ Instead, we need a solution that has input from local communities and supports local communities economically. Not to mention preserving the nature of the Big Bend, our land and our water.”

The participating counties include Hudspeth, Culberson, Jeff Davis, Presidio, Brewster, Terrell and Val Verde.

The group’s letter, which includes draft federal legislation, calls for the creation of the “Permanent Trust for Big Bend Region Border Security.” It asks that Congress halt construction of the Big Bend border wall, cancel the awarded contracts and allocate $2 billion to endow the new trust.

It also calls for bipartisanship and the creation of a board to oversee the fund “designed to minimize political whims,” headed up by the Secretary of State and including former politicians, landowners and county officials. The Gov, Lt. Gov and Speaker will have the power to appoint board members, Patterson said.

“ We wanna give the Governor and the Legislature confidence that this is not gonna be a renegade outfit, that folks in Austin will also be apprised of what’s going on,” he said.

Under the group’s proposed legislation, the trust cannot fund any initiatives that involve the seizure of private property.

Patterson estimates that around 200,000 to 700,000 acres of Texas land could be effectively ceded to Mexico if the Big Bend border wall were to be built along the Rio Grande. But, he argued, private property rights and state sovereignty don’t need to be sacrificed to obtain a secure border.

“ Republicans always talk about local control. Republicans always talk about property rights and state sovereignty,” Patterson said. “We’re trying to broaden our support by focusing on those things as well as just stopping illegal immigration.”

Hays said other border security initiatives like Gov. Abbott’s controversial Operation Lone Star program — which offers grants to local law enforcement along the border — have been “performative” and ineffective.

“We have these political whims that whiplash the border. It’s like clockwork every 10 years or so and nothing ever changes,” she said. “It disrupts our lives and we wanna break that cycle.”

LTDT’s proposal also requests additional Congressional protections for Big Bend National Park, following bulldozing by border wall contractors that took place near Santa Elena Canyon and Mariscal Mountain earlier this year which “demonstrated the vulnerability of one of America’s most treasured national parks to large-scale federal construction projects,” the letter said.

text:
For audio listeners, you can listen to our audio version of the News Digest here. You can also join our Immigration News Digest Newsletter here.

Sudan and Ukraine TPS Protections Continue as DHS Guidance Remains Pending

Federal Court Orders State Department to Reopen FY 2027 Diversity Visa Lottery

Canada Introduces New Express Entry Priorities for High-Wage Occupations

India Raises Minimum Salary Requirement for Employment Visas

Sudan and Ukraine TPS Protections Continue as DHS Guidance Remains Pending

Temporary Protected Status (TPS) beneficiaries from Sudan and Ukraine continue to retain TPS protections and employment authorization despite the October 19, 2026, expiration of their previously designated TPS periods. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published an announcement on their website but has not yet published a formal extension term or termination notice in the Federal Register, creating uncertainty for employers regarding employment eligibility verification. For now, beneficiaries from both countries remain protected and authorized to work while DHS determines the future of their TPS designations. However, the agency has not provided updated Employment Authorization Document expiration dates or specific Form I-9 instructions for this interim period.

Under federal immigration law, TPS designations may automatically continue for at least six months when DHS does not determine that the conditions supporting a designation have ended. However, the absence of formal guidance leaves employers uncertain about how to document continued employment authorization.

For employers, the distinction between continued work authorization and acceptable Form I-9 documentation is particularly important. Although USCIS has indicated that affected individuals remain authorized to work, employers should not independently assign new EAD expiration dates or assume that a six-month extension applies to Form I-9 records without supporting government instructions. DHS is expected to provide additional guidance clarifying the future of both designations and the documentation requirements for affected workers.

Impact: Employers with Sudanese and Ukrainian TPS beneficiaries should continue monitoring USCIS and DHS announcements while carefully reviewing employment authorization records. Organizations should preserve relevant government guidance and coordinate Form I-9 decisions with immigration counsel to avoid unnecessary employment disruptions or compliance issues.

Federal Court Orders State Department to Reopen FY 2027 Diversity Visa Lottery

A federal district court in California has ordered the Department of State to open registration for the Fiscal Year 2027 Diversity Visa (DV) lottery following delays to the program. Under the preliminary injunction, the agency must begin accepting entries by November 1, 2026, and keep registration open for at least 30 days.

The court also established several deadlines for the State Department:

October 29, 2026: Publish official registration instructions, including eligibility requirements, application procedures, and opening and closing dates.

November 1, 2026: Open the FY 2027 Diversity Visa registration period.

December 3, 2026: Notify selected applicants of their lottery selection.

The order also requires the State Department to process eligible DV immigrant visa applications under its usual procedures, subject to applicable visa limits and deadlines.

The ruling follows litigation challenging the Administration’s suspension of Diversity Visa processing and delays to the FY 2027 registration period. The court previously established earlier compliance deadlines but subsequently extended them to provide the agency additional time.

Prospective applicants should also prepare for recently introduced registration requirements, including a $1 entry fee and valid passport information.

Importantly, the ruling is a preliminary injunction rather than a final decision on the underlying lawsuit. The government may appeal, and further court action could affect the registration schedule.

Impact: The decision provides a potential opportunity for eligible foreign nationals to participate in the delayed FY 2027 Diversity Visa lottery. Applicants should monitor State Department announcements closely, prepare required documentation, and remain alert for possible changes to registration deadlines as litigation continues.

Canada Introduces New Express Entry Priorities for High-Wage Occupations

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is introducing significant changes to its Express Entry permanent residence system beginning November 3, 2026. The reforms will prioritize candidates with Canadian work experience or qualifying job offers in designated high-wage occupations while simplifying certain employer sponsorship requirements.

Under the new Labour Market Integration factor, Express Entry candidates may receive additional Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points based on eligible Canadian work experience or a qualifying job offer. Candidates working in designated high-wage occupations may receive additional points, improving their competitiveness for invitations to apply for permanent residence.

Importantly, eligibility for high-wage occupation points will depend on IRCC’s published occupation list rather than an individual’s actual salary. Candidates who qualify through both work experience and a job offer will receive the higher applicable score, rather than combining the two.

The reforms also eliminate the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) requirement for qualifying job offers under the Federal Skilled Worker and Federal Skilled Trades programs. Employers must still demonstrate that job offers are genuine and meet applicable program requirements.

IRCC will automatically recalculate scores for candidates already in the Express Entry pool and temporarily pause invitation rounds beginning November 3. The recalculation process may take up to two weeks. Candidates relying on qualifying job offers should update their Express Entry profiles before implementation.

Impact: The changes could improve permanent residence opportunities for skilled foreign workers in designated high-wage occupations while reducing administrative requirements for employers. Organizations should review employee occupation classifications, work experience, and job offer documentation ahead of November 3 to prepare for the new scoring framework.

India Raises Minimum Salary Requirement for Employment Visas

India has reportedly increased the minimum annual salary requirement for foreign nationals applying for Employment Visas, introducing a significant change that could affect employers sponsoring international talent. The new threshold has increased from INR 1,625,000 to INR 2,400,000 annually, representing an approximately 47.7% increase.

The revised salary requirement is reportedly effective immediately and applies to both new Employment Visa applications and renewal applications submitted within India.

Although the Ministry of Home Affairs has not yet published a formal notification confirming the change, the higher threshold has appeared in endorsements on recently issued residence permits from local Foreigners Regional Registration Offices (FRROs). Immigration authorities have also reportedly confirmed the revised requirement verbally.

This marks the first reported adjustment to India’s minimum Employment Visa salary threshold since 2018. The increase could have a particularly significant impact on employers hiring foreign professionals whose compensation falls between the previous and revised minimums. Additional guidance from the Ministry of Home Affairs is expected to clarify implementation procedures and any potential exceptions to the revised salary requirement.

According to the hotline’s social media, there was another confirmed targeted arrest in Redwood City around 9:20 a.m. near the intersection of Ebener Street and Poplar Avenue, in the Palm Park neighborhood.

The last verified ICE arrests in East Palo Alto were on Aug. 25, 2025, according to Faith In Action Bay Area’s Instagram account. One woman who was arrested that day suffered a medical emergency and was transferred to Stanford Hospital. She was later released from custody.

title: Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of target - NBC10 Philadelphia
authors: Rebecca Santana | The Associated Press, Rebecca Santana, The Associated Press
description:
The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump's second administration.
Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration.
More people being deported, but not at all-time highs The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.
Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.
Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.
text:
President Donald Trump's administration is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year, a new report released Thursday shows, as arrests ramp up across the country fueled by billions of dollars meant to supercharge his immigration agenda.

The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump's second administration. The numbers fall short of previous highs in the early 2000s and fail to meet the Trump administration's promise, made when it received the billions from Congress, that the money would allow for 1 million deportations annually.

The report, based on publicly available data obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, comes after the Trump administration in January 2025 stopped publicly releasing similar figures compiled by the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

More people being deported, but not at all-time highs

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year — when the Trump administration's immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear — an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI's analysis, that's a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, another Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization were from Mexico and didn't often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the U.S. from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them. And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

Voluntary departures are increasing as are interior arrests

The report said voluntary departures — when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country — were at an “all-time high,” with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025. People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the U.S. But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country's interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28% of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by July of this year that had risen to 39%.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said — 69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the “worst of the worst.” Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.”

Trump administration no longer regularly releases immigration data

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent. On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump’s second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

text:
A federal judge in California is putting limits on pre-election field operations conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that the agency says is aimed at trying to find noncitizens who have illegally voted in nine states.

In recent weeks, armed Homeland Security Investigations officers have carried out field operations and visited homes to interview people suspected of illegally voting as noncitizens. The targets can include people who became citizens but voted before they naturalized.

In a 19-page order late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden, wrote that the federal government was using "flawed" data in the initiative and that its efforts likely violated the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.

Martínez-Olguín referenced a disclosure last month from a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower that alleged rushed efforts to match data to create a target list of potential noncitizens on voter rolls, and that the list includes U.S. citizens. She also pointed to HSI's social media posts, including one that showed agents handcuffing a California man accused of unlawfully registering to vote.

The judge wrote that the government's use of unreliable and incomplete data along with highly publicized arrests "lead to an objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote."

HSI field operations were planned in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, according to documents produced in the case and CNN reporting.

Martínez-Olguín barred DHS officers in those states from conducting field operations targeting people they "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens," or that are based "wholly" on USCIS matching data without further investigation.

In a declaration, USCIS official Nicolas Bartell had told the judge his team manually reviews records before referring them to HSI, but acknowledged the "low possibility" citizens could be "erroneously identified as potential aliens" in federal records. He wrote the risks were mitigated by safeguards his office takes "and any remaining risks were outweighed by the need to support the agency's law-enforcement and election-integrity mission."

It's unclear how much of an effect the judge's order will have on the federal government's highly publicized campaign to find noncitizen voters.

States reviews and audits have consistently found voting by noncitizens to be extremely rare.

"DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders," the agency wrote in a statement. "We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."

The order is set to take effect on Friday and would be in effect through election night, though the federal government could appeal.

The judge's ruling came in a lawsuit filed last month by a coalition that includes San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, the city of San Francisco, nursing unions and Voto Latino Foundation. Protect Democracy and the National Immigration Law Center are litigating the case against the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice.

"Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens – whether born here or naturalized – should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them," Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer with Protect Democracy, said in a statement.

"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," he added.

A court filing by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United described naturalized citizen members who no longer wanted to attend political rallies, sign up to be election poll workers, or vote in person because of the federal operations.

The order comes as the Department of Justice is suing California and demanding the state segregate 20,000 ballots from people federal officials say they believe are "likely" noncitizens.

A preliminary review of a sample of that list by Los Angeles County election officials found many of the registrations were canceled, inactive or had no voting history, and some pertained to people who indicated they were born in the U.S.

The DOJ announced charges against 28 green card holders across the state on Monday who are accused of illegally voting or registering to vote.
